- Malignant tumors invade and metastasize; benign tumors do not.
- Stem cells self-renew and differentiate: totipotent, pluripotent, multipotent; iPSCs are reprogrammed body cells.

lessons.title: Meiosis and sexual reproduction
lessons.body:
## A division that halves

Mitosis, from lesson 14, copies a cell exactly: same chromosome number, same genes. That is perfect for growth and repair, but it creates a puzzle for sexual reproduction. A human egg and a human sperm combine to make a new person. If each carried 46 chromosomes, the child would have 92, the grandchild 184, and so on. That does not happen, so something must halve the chromosome number before fertilization.

Biologists in the 1870s and 1880s saw this directly. In 1876 Oscar Hertwig, watching transparent sea urchin eggs, saw a sperm nucleus enter the egg and fuse with the egg's nucleus: fertilization is the joining of two nuclei. In 1883 Edouard van Beneden counted chromosomes in a roundworm (Ascaris) whose cells have very few: the egg nucleus and the sperm nucleus each brought 2 chromosomes, and the fertilized egg had 4. August Weismann then argued that a special "reduction division" must halve the number when sex cells form. That division is **[[meiosis]]**. This lesson explains how it works and why it makes every offspring genetically unique.

## Pairs of chromosomes

Look at the 46 chromosomes of a human body cell arranged by size and you will see they come in 23 pairs. One chromosome of each pair came from the mother's egg and one from the father's sperm. The two members of a pair are **[[homologous chromosomes]]** (homologs): they are the same size and shape, have their centromeres in the same place, and carry the same genes in the same order. They are not identical, though, because they can carry different versions of those genes; your mother's copy of a gene for a blood protein might differ slightly from your father's.

Of the 23 pairs, 22 pairs are autosomes, matched in everyone. The 23rd pair is the sex chromosomes: two X chromosomes in most females, an X and a Y in most males. The X and Y differ in size but pair up during meiosis through a small shared region. (Module 5 covers how sex chromosomes affect inheritance.)

A cell with two complete sets of chromosomes, one from each parent, is **[[diploid]]**, written 2n. A cell with one set is **[[haploid]]**, written n. In humans 2n = 46 and n = 23. Body cells are diploid. Sex cells, or **[[gametes]]** (eggs and sperm), are haploid. Fertilization joins two haploid gametes into a diploid zygote, the first cell of a new organism: n + n = 2n. Every species has its own number: fruit flies 2n = 8, dogs 2n = 78, garden peas 2n = 14.

## Meiosis step by step

Meiosis starts after a normal interphase, so the cell enters it with every chromosome duplicated into two sister chromatids. Then it divides twice: meiosis I and meiosis II.

*Meiosis I separates the homologous pairs.*

1. Prophase I. Chromosomes condense, and each pairs up with its homolog along their whole length. The paired homologs (four chromatids in all) form a tetrad. While paired, chromatids from the two homologs exchange matching segments, a process called **[[crossing over]]**. The X-shaped places where they cross can be seen under a microscope.
2. Metaphase I. The homologous pairs line up at the middle of the cell as pairs, side by side. Which homolog faces which pole is random for each pair.
3. Anaphase I. The homologs of each pair are pulled to opposite poles. Sister chromatids stay joined. This is the key difference from mitosis.
4. Telophase I and cytokinesis. Two cells form, each with one chromosome from every pair: they are haploid, although each chromosome still has two chromatids.

*Meiosis II separates the sister chromatids.* No DNA replication happens between the two divisions. Each haploid cell goes through prophase II, metaphase II (chromosomes line up singly), anaphase II (sister chromatids separate), and telophase II. Meiosis II works just like mitosis, but in a haploid cell.

The result: four haploid cells, each genetically different from the parent cell and from each other.

### Example 1

A fruit fly cell has 2n = 8. Track the number of chromosomes and chromatids from the start of meiosis I to the end of meiosis II.

Step 1: Before meiosis (after S phase): 8 chromosomes, each with 2 chromatids, so 16 chromatids.

Step 2: Metaphase I: still 8 chromosomes (4 homologous pairs), 16 chromatids.

Step 3: After meiosis I: each of the 2 cells has 4 chromosomes (one from each pair), each still with 2 chromatids: 8 chromatids per cell. The cells are now haploid (n = 4).

Step 4: Anaphase II: in each cell the sister chromatids separate, so each pole receives 4 chromosomes of one chromatid each.

Step 5: After meiosis II: 4 cells, each with 4 single-chromatid chromosomes. Halved from 8, ready to combine with another gamete (4 + 4 = 8).

## Mitosis and meiosis compared

| | Mitosis | Meiosis |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | Growth, repair, asexual reproduction | Making gametes for sexual reproduction |
| Divisions | One | Two |
| Homologs pair up? | No | Yes, in prophase I |
| Crossing over? | No | Yes |
| Daughter cells | 2, diploid (2n → 2n) | 4, haploid (2n → n) |
| Genetically | Identical to parent | Different from parent and each other |

## Three sources of variation

Siblings with the same parents (other than identical twins) are never genetically identical. Meiosis and fertilization shuffle genes in three ways.

1. **[[Independent assortment]]**. At metaphase I, each homologous pair lines up independently of the others. For each pair there are 2 ways it can face the poles, so with n pairs the number of different chromosome combinations in a gamete is $2^n$. For humans, $2^{23} = 8{,}388{,}608$. This chromosome-level shuffle is the physical basis of Mendel's law of independent assortment (lesson 18): genes on different chromosomes end up in gametes independently of one another. Genes close together on the same chromosome travel together unless crossing over separates them.
2. Crossing over. Exchanging segments between homologs makes recombinant chromosomes, mixing the mother's and father's versions of genes on the same chromosome. Every pair normally has at least one crossover, and longer chromosomes often have two or three, multiplying the possibilities far beyond $2^{23}$.
3. Random fertilization. Any one of the millions of possible sperm can fertilize any one of the millions of possible eggs. Ignoring crossing over, one couple could produce $2^{23} \times 2^{23} \approx 7 \times 10^{13}$ (about 70 trillion) different chromosome combinations.

Why does variation matter? A population whose members differ is more likely to include some individuals who survive a new disease or a change in climate. This variation is the raw material for natural selection (module 7).

### Example 2

A plant species has 2n = 6. How many genetically different gametes can independent assortment alone produce? How many different chromosome combinations could a zygote have from two parents of this species (ignoring crossing over)?

Step 1: n = 3 pairs, so gamete combinations $= 2^3 = 8$.

Step 2: Each parent can make 8 kinds of gametes, so the zygote combinations number $8 \times 8 = 64$.

Step 3: Check by thinking about one pair: each pair lines up 2 ways, so 2 × 2 × 2 = 8. Doubling the number of chromosome pairs to 6 would square the gamete count, giving 64, not double it.

## When meiosis goes wrong: nondisjunction

Sometimes a homologous pair (in meiosis I) or a pair of sister chromatids (in meiosis II) fails to separate. This is **[[nondisjunction]]**. The result is gametes with an extra chromosome (n + 1) or a missing one (n − 1). If such a gamete is fertilized, the zygote has 47 or 45 chromosomes instead of 46.

- Nondisjunction in meiosis I: both homologs go to one cell, so all four gametes are abnormal: two n + 1 and two n − 1.
- Nondisjunction in meiosis II: only one of the two cells is affected, so two gametes are normal, one is n + 1, and one is n − 1.

Most embryos with a missing or extra chromosome do not survive. A well-known exception is trisomy 21 (three copies of chromosome 21), which causes Down syndrome; people with Down syndrome share some physical traits and some degree of intellectual disability, and many live full lives into their 60s. The chance of nondisjunction rises with the age of the egg, which is why trisomy 21 is more common in children of older mothers. Module 5 returns to chromosome disorders and how karyotypes reveal them.

## Making eggs and sperm

In males, each cell that completes meiosis produces four sperm, and sperm are made continuously from puberty on. In females, meiosis divides the cytoplasm unequally: one large egg cell keeps nearly all the cytoplasm (stored nutrients for the early embryo), and the other products are tiny polar bodies that break down. So one meiosis yields one egg. Human egg cells begin meiosis before birth and pause in prophase I for years or decades, finishing only around ovulation and fertilization; that long pause is thought to be part of why nondisjunction rises with maternal age.

## Common mistakes

- Thinking meiosis II halves the chromosome number. The halving happens in meiosis I, when homologs separate.
- Calling homologous chromosomes identical. They carry the same genes but can carry different versions. Sister chromatids are the identical ones.
- Saying the DNA is copied again before meiosis II. It is copied only once, before meiosis I.
- Treating independent assortment as $2 \times n$. The count is $2^n$, because each pair's choice multiplies the possibilities.
- Thinking nondisjunction in meiosis I and II give the same results. Meiosis I nondisjunction makes all four gametes abnormal; meiosis II, only two.

## Key points

- Meiosis turns one diploid cell (2n) into four haploid gametes (n); fertilization restores 2n.
- Homologous chromosomes carry the same genes, one from each parent; they pair and cross over in prophase I.
- Meiosis I separates homologs (the reduction step); meiosis II separates sister chromatids.
- Variation comes from crossing over, independent assortment ($2^n$ combinations), and random fertilization.
- Nondisjunction gives gametes with n + 1 or n − 1 chromosomes; trisomy 21 is one result.
- Sperm: four per meiosis. Egg: one per meiosis plus polar bodies.

lessons.title: Mendel's laws and Punnett squares
lessons.body:
The last lesson followed chromosomes through meiosis: homologous chromosomes pair up, then separate, so each gamete gets one chromosome from every pair. This module asks what that means for the offspring. Why do two brown-eyed parents sometimes have a blue-eyed child? Why does a trait vanish in one generation and come back in the next? The rules were worked out by Gregor Mendel in the 1860s, decades before anyone had seen a chromosome. His results line up exactly with meiosis, and that match is one of the great "aha" moments in biology.

## Before Mendel: the blending idea

In the 1800s most naturalists believed in *blending inheritance*: offspring are a mix of their parents, like paint. A tall and a short parent should give medium children, and those should give medium grandchildren forever. Blending has a fatal problem: it predicts that variation should steadily disappear, and that a trait, once blended away, can never return. Farmers and breeders knew that traits do skip generations and reappear unchanged.

## Mendel's experiments with peas

Mendel, a monk and trained scientist in Brno (now in the Czech Republic), bred garden peas from about 1856 to 1863 and published in 1866. Peas were a smart choice:

- They have clear either/or traits: round or wrinkled seeds, yellow or green seeds, purple or white flowers, tall or dwarf stems. Mendel studied seven such traits.
- They normally self-pollinate, so he could start with lines that bred true (purple plants whose offspring were always purple), yet he could also cross-pollinate by hand, moving pollen with a brush after removing a flower's own pollen-making parts.
- They are cheap and produce many offspring, so he could count thousands of seeds and plants. Counting, and treating the counts as ratios, was Mendel's real innovation.

His basic experiment had three generations. The parental generation (P) was two true-breeding plants that differed in one trait, for example purple × white flowers. Their offspring are the first filial generation, F1. He then let the F1 plants self-pollinate to get the F2 generation.

The results were the same for all seven traits:

1. Every F1 plant looked like one parent. Purple × white gave all purple; the white trait seemed to vanish.
2. In the F2, the hidden trait came back in about one quarter of the offspring.

| Trait | F2 dominant form | F2 recessive form | Ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| Seed shape | 5474 round | 1850 wrinkled | 2.96 : 1 |
| Seed color | 6022 yellow | 2001 green | 3.01 : 1 |
| Flower color | 705 purple | 224 white | 3.15 : 1 |
| Stem length | 787 tall | 277 dwarf | 2.84 : 1 |

The white trait could not have been destroyed in the F1, since it reappeared unchanged. So the F1 plants must have carried something for white that did not show.

## Genes, alleles, and the vocabulary of crosses

Mendel called his units "factors." Today we call a unit of inheritance a **[[gene]]**: a stretch of DNA that affects a trait (module 6 shows how). A gene can come in different versions, called **[[alleles]]**. The flower-color gene in peas has a purple allele and a white allele.

Each pea plant, like you, carries two copies of each gene, one inherited from each parent (they sit on the two members of a homologous chromosome pair). We write alleles with letters: a capital letter for the **[[dominant]]** allele, which shows its effect even when only one copy is present, and the same letter in lower case for the **[[recessive]]** allele, which shows its effect only when no dominant allele is present. For flower color, P = purple and p = white.

- A plant's **[[genotype]]** is its pair of alleles: PP, Pp or pp.
- Its **[[phenotype]]** is the trait you can observe: purple or white.
- A genotype with two identical alleles (PP or pp) is **[[homozygous]]**; one with two different alleles (Pp) is **[[heterozygous]]**.

Since P is dominant, PP and Pp plants are both purple. Only pp plants are white. Two genotypes can give the same phenotype, which is why you cannot read a genotype just by looking.

## The law of segregation

Mendel explained his data with what we now call the **[[law of segregation]]**: the two alleles of a gene separate (segregate) when gametes form, so each gamete carries just one allele, and the two are equally likely. At fertilization, an egg and a sperm each contribute one allele, restoring the pair.

Meiosis is the physical reason. The two alleles sit on the two homologous chromosomes, and homologs go to opposite poles in anaphase I. A Pp plant therefore makes gametes that are half P and half p.

Run the experiment with this model. The P generation is PP × pp, so every F1 plant gets P from one parent and p from the other: all Pp, all purple. Each F1 plant makes P and p gametes in equal numbers. A cross of Pp × Pp gives the F2.

## Punnett squares

A **[[Punnett square]]** is a grid that lists one parent's possible gametes across the top, the other parent's down the side, and fills each box with the genotype that union produces. Because each gamete type is equally likely, each box is equally likely.

### Example 1

Cross two heterozygous purple plants, Pp × Pp. What fraction of offspring are white, and how many white plants would you expect among 400 offspring?

Each parent makes gametes P and p, each with probability $\tfrac12$.

| | P | p |
|---|---|---|
| P | PP | Pp |
| p | Pp | pp |

Count the four equally likely boxes:

- Genotypes: 1 PP : 2 Pp : 1 pp (a 1 : 2 : 1 genotype ratio).
- Phenotypes: PP and Pp are purple, so 3 purple : 1 white (a 3 : 1 phenotype ratio).

The fraction white is $\tfrac14$, and among 400 offspring we expect $\tfrac14 \times 400 = 100$ white plants. That is Mendel's 3 : 1, explained.

Notice two other facts hiding in the square. Of the purple offspring, $\tfrac23$ are heterozygous (2 of the 3 purple boxes). And any one offspring is heterozygous with probability $\tfrac24 = \tfrac12$.

## Ratios are probabilities

A Punnett square does not say that a family of four children will contain exactly one recessive child. It gives the probability for each child, and each child is an independent event, like each toss of a coin. With 7324 seeds, Mendel got very close to 3 : 1 (2.96 : 1). With 8 offspring, getting 4 white or none at all is not surprising. Large samples match the predicted ratios closely; small samples can stray far from them. Lesson 21 shows how to decide when a deviation is too big to be chance.

## The test cross

A purple plant could be PP or Pp. How can you tell? Mendel's answer was the **[[test cross]]**: cross the unknown individual with a homozygous recessive one (pp). The pp parent can only give p, so each offspring's phenotype shows directly which allele came from the unknown parent.

- If the unknown is PP, all its gametes are P: every offspring is Pp, purple.
- If the unknown is Pp, half its gametes are p: offspring are about 1 purple : 1 white.

### Example 2

A black guinea pig (black, B, is dominant to white, b) is crossed with a white guinea pig. Their litters over a year total 12 offspring: 7 black and 5 white. What is the black parent's genotype?

The white parent is bb and contributes only b. Every white offspring (bb) must have received b from the black parent too. So the black parent carries b: it is Bb. A single white offspring is enough to prove this. The expected result for Bb × bb is 1 : 1, so 6 black : 6 white out of 12; 7 : 5 is a normal chance deviation.

If instead all 12 offspring had been black, the parent is probably BB. "Probably," not "certainly": a Bb parent would give 12 black offspring in a row with probability $\left(\tfrac12\right)^{12} = \tfrac{1}{4096}$, which is very unlikely but not impossible.

### Example 3

A tall pea plant of unknown genotype (T = tall, t = dwarf) is crossed with a heterozygous tall plant, Tt. Of the offspring, 3/4 are tall and 1/4 are dwarf. Which genotype fits?

Try each possibility.

- TT × Tt: every offspring gets T from the TT parent, so all are tall. Doesn't fit.
- Tt × Tt: the Punnett square of Example 1 gives 3 tall : 1 dwarf. Fits.

So the unknown plant is Tt. Working backward like this, from offspring ratios to parent genotypes, is a common exam task: 3 : 1 points to two heterozygotes, 1 : 1 to a heterozygote crossed with a homozygous recessive, and all one phenotype to at least one homozygous dominant parent (or two homozygous parents).

## Common mistakes

- Writing a gamete as "Pp." A gamete carries one allele of each gene, never two.
- Mixing up genotype and phenotype ratios. Pp × Pp gives 1 : 2 : 1 genotypes but 3 : 1 phenotypes.
- Thinking "dominant" means "more common" or "better." A dominant allele can be rare (the allele for Huntington's disease is dominant and rare); a recessive one can be very common (the allele for blood type O).
- Expecting a family to follow the ratio exactly. Each child is a separate chance event; the ratio describes probabilities, not guarantees.
- Concluding that a dominant-phenotype parent is homozygous from a few dominant offspring. Only a recessive offspring settles the question for sure.

## Key points

- Mendel crossed true-breeding peas and counted offspring: the F1 all showed one form, and the F2 showed 3 : 1.
- Genes come in alleles; each individual has two alleles per gene. Genotype is the allele pair, phenotype is the observable trait.
- Law of segregation: the two alleles separate into different gametes, each with probability $\tfrac12$, because homologous chromosomes separate in meiosis.
- Aa × Aa gives 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa and 3 dominant : 1 recessive.
- A test cross with aa reveals an unknown genotype: all dominant suggests AA; any recessive offspring proves Aa.

lessons.title: Dihybrid crosses and probability
lessons.body:
Lesson 17 followed one gene at a time. Real organisms inherit thousands of genes at once, so the next question Mendel asked was: when two traits are inherited together, do they travel as a package, or does each gene go its own way? His answer leads to the second law of inheritance, and it also gives us a fast method for any cross: treat each gene as a separate probability problem and multiply.

## Mendel's two-trait experiment

Mendel crossed a true-breeding plant with round, yellow seeds (RRYY) with one that had wrinkled, green seeds (rryy). Round (R) is dominant to wrinkled (r), and yellow (Y) is dominant to green (y).

Every F1 plant was RrYy, with round, yellow seeds, as expected from two dominant traits. A cross that follows two genes in parents heterozygous for both, such as RrYy × RrYy, is a **[[dihybrid cross]]**. When Mendel let the F1 self-pollinate, there were two possible outcomes:

- If the parental combinations were locked together (R always with Y, r always with y), the F2 would show only the two parental types, round-yellow and wrinkled-green, in a 3 : 1 ratio.
- If the genes sorted independently, new combinations (round-green, wrinkled-yellow) would also appear.

His F2 counts:

| Phenotype | Count | Fraction of 556 |
|---|---|---|
| Round, yellow | 315 | 0.567 |
| Round, green | 108 | 0.194 |
| Wrinkled, yellow | 101 | 0.182 |
| Wrinkled, green | 32 | 0.058 |

All four combinations appeared, close to $\tfrac{9}{16} = 0.5625$, $\tfrac{3}{16} = 0.1875$, $\tfrac{3}{16}$ and $\tfrac{1}{16} = 0.0625$: a 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio.

## The law of independent assortment

The **[[law of independent assortment]]** says that the alleles of different genes separate into gametes independently of one another. Whether a gamete gets R or r tells you nothing about whether it gets Y or y.

For genes on different chromosomes, the cellular reason is the way homologous pairs line up in metaphase I of meiosis. Each pair orients at random, independently of the other pairs, so the chromosome carrying R is as likely to end up with the Y chromosome as with the y chromosome. An RrYy plant therefore makes four kinds of gametes in equal numbers: RY, Ry, rY and ry, each $\tfrac14$.

An important exception: genes that sit close together on the *same* chromosome tend to be inherited together because they ride on one piece of DNA. Such linked genes do not assort independently, although crossing over in meiosis sometimes separates them. Genes very far apart on one chromosome are separated by crossing over so often that they behave as if unlinked, but the reason is crossing over, not the random orientation of homologous pairs. Thomas Hunt Morgan's fruit-fly work around 1910 first showed linkage. Mendel's seven traits happen to behave independently, and in this module we assume genes are unlinked unless told otherwise.

## The 16-box Punnett square

With four gamete types from each parent, the Punnett square has $4 \times 4 = 16$ equally likely boxes.

| | RY | Ry | rY | ry |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| RY | RRYY | RRYy | RrYY | RrYy |
| Ry | RRYy | RRyy | RrYy | Rryy |
| rY | RrYY | RrYy | rrYY | rrYy |
| ry | RrYy | Rryy | rrYy | rryy |

Counting phenotypes: 9 boxes have at least one R and one Y (round, yellow), 3 have R but yy (round, green), 3 have rr but Y (wrinkled, yellow), and 1 is rryy (wrinkled, green). That is 9 : 3 : 3 : 1.

The square works, but it is slow and error-prone, and for three genes it would need 64 boxes. Probability rules do the same job much faster.

## The product rule and the sum rule

Two rules of probability cover nearly every genetics problem.

The **[[product rule]]**: the probability that two (or more) *independent* events both happen is the product of their separate probabilities.

$$P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A) \times P(B)$$

The **[[sum rule]]**: the probability that one *or* another of two mutually exclusive events happens (they cannot both happen) is the sum of their probabilities.

$$P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B)$$

Because genes assort independently, a multi-gene cross splits into one-gene crosses. Solve each gene with a tiny 2 × 2 square (or from memory), then multiply. For RrYy × RrYy:

- Seed shape, Rr × Rr: round $\tfrac34$, wrinkled $\tfrac14$.
- Seed color, Yy × Yy: yellow $\tfrac34$, green $\tfrac14$.
- Round and green: $\tfrac34 \times \tfrac14 = \tfrac{3}{16}$. The 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 is just $(3 : 1) \times (3 : 1)$.

The sum rule handles "either way" outcomes. Within one gene, Aa × Aa gives a heterozygote two ways (A from the mother and a from the father, or the reverse), each $\tfrac12 \times \tfrac12 = \tfrac14$, so $P(\text{Aa}) = \tfrac14 + \tfrac14 = \tfrac12$.

### Example 1

In the cross AaBbCc × AaBbCc (three unlinked genes, each with complete dominance), find (a) the probability of an aabbcc offspring and (b) the probability of an offspring with the dominant phenotype for A and B but the recessive phenotype for C.

(a) For each gene, Xx × Xx gives xx with probability $\tfrac14$. By the product rule:

$$P(\text{aabbcc}) = \tfrac14 \times \tfrac14 \times \tfrac14 = \tfrac{1}{64}$$

(b) Dominant phenotype for a gene: $\tfrac34$. Recessive: $\tfrac14$.

$$P = \tfrac34 \times \tfrac34 \times \tfrac14 = \tfrac{9}{64}$$

A 64-box Punnett square would give the same answers after a lot more work.

### Example 2

Parents AaBb × aaBb. What fraction of offspring will be heterozygous for both genes (AaBb)?

Gene by gene:

- Aa × aa: offspring are Aa or aa, each $\tfrac12$ (a test cross). $P(\text{Aa}) = \tfrac12$.
- Bb × Bb: $P(\text{Bb}) = \tfrac12$.

Product rule: $P(\text{AaBb}) = \tfrac12 \times \tfrac12 = \tfrac14$.

The parents don't have to have the same genotype, and the genes don't have to be in the same state; just handle each gene with its own parental pair.

## Dihybrid test cross

A test cross works for two genes too. Cross a round, yellow plant of unknown genotype with rryy. If the unknown is RrYy, it makes RY, Ry, rY and ry gametes equally, and the rryy parent adds only ry, so the offspring show all four phenotypes in a 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 ratio. If it were RRYy, every offspring would be round, and color would split 1 yellow : 1 green.

## Families: combining the two rules

Probability rules also answer questions about several children. Each child is an independent event, so the product rule applies across children too.

### Example 3

Two parents are both carriers (Aa) of a recessive condition. They plan two children. What is the probability that (a) both children have the condition, and (b) exactly one of the two has it?

For each child, $P(\text{aa}) = \tfrac14$ and $P(\text{not aa}) = \tfrac34$.

(a) Both: $\tfrac14 \times \tfrac14 = \tfrac{1}{16}$.

(b) "Exactly one" can happen in two mutually exclusive orders:

- first child affected, second not: $\tfrac14 \times \tfrac34 = \tfrac{3}{16}$
- first not, second affected: $\tfrac34 \times \tfrac14 = \tfrac{3}{16}$

Sum rule: $\tfrac{3}{16} + \tfrac{3}{16} = \tfrac{6}{16} = \tfrac38$.

With more children, count the orders. For exactly $k$ affected among $n$ children, the number of orders is $\binom{n}{k}$, so

$$P = \binom{n}{k}\left(\tfrac14\right)^k\left(\tfrac34\right)^{n-k}.$$

For example, exactly 1 affected among 3 children: $3 \times \tfrac14 \times \tfrac34 \times \tfrac34 = \tfrac{27}{64}$.

Also remember that the past doesn't change the odds: if the couple's first child is affected, the chance that the next one is affected is still $\tfrac14$.

## Counting gamete types

An individual heterozygous for $n$ unlinked genes can make $2^n$ different gametes (each heterozygous gene doubles the options; homozygous genes add nothing). AaBb makes $2^2 = 4$ kinds, AaBbCc makes 8, and AaBBCc makes 4 (A/a × B × C/c).

## Common mistakes

- Listing gametes with two alleles of the same gene (Rr) or none of one gene. Each gamete gets exactly one allele of every gene.
- Adding when you should multiply. "And" for independent events multiplies; "or" for mutually exclusive outcomes adds.
- Forgetting the orders in "exactly one" problems. One affected child of two can be first or second, so multiply by 2.
- Assuming 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 for every two-gene cross. It holds only for two double heterozygotes with complete dominance and unlinked genes. Work out other crosses gene by gene.
- Thinking a previous child changes the next child's probability. Each fertilization is independent.

## Key points

- Law of independent assortment: alleles of different (unlinked) genes go into gametes independently. For genes on different chromosomes, the cause is the random orientation of each homologous pair at metaphase I.
- AaBb makes four gamete types equally; AaBb × AaBb gives 9 : 3 : 3 : 1.
- Product rule for "and" (independent events), sum rule for "or" (mutually exclusive events).
- Solve multi-gene crosses gene by gene, then multiply.
- Exactly $k$ of $n$ children: $\binom{n}{k}p^k(1-p)^{n-k}$.
- A heterozygote for $n$ unlinked genes makes $2^n$ gamete types.

lessons.title: Beyond simple dominance
lessons.body:
Mendel's pea traits were tidy: one gene, two alleles, one allele fully dominant, and two clear phenotypes. Lessons 17 and 18 used that model. Many traits are messier. A heterozygote can look intermediate, or show both parents' traits at once; a gene can have more than two alleles; a trait like height can depend on many genes plus the environment. None of this overturns Mendel. Alleles still segregate and assort exactly as before. What changes is the link between genotype and phenotype, so the Punnett squares stay the same and only the way you read the boxes changes.

## Incomplete dominance

In snapdragons and four o'clock flowers, a cross between a true-breeding red plant and a true-breeding white plant gives F1 plants that are all pink. This is **[[incomplete dominance]]**: neither allele is fully dominant, and the heterozygote has an intermediate phenotype.

Is this blending after all? No, and the F2 proves it. Let the pink F1 self-pollinate. Using $C^R$ for the red allele and $C^W$ for the white allele:

| | $C^R$ | $C^W$ |
|---|---|---|
| $C^R$ | $C^RC^R$ red | $C^RC^W$ pink |
| $C^W$ | $C^RC^W$ pink | $C^WC^W$ white |

The F2 is 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white. Pure red and pure white come back unchanged, exactly as particulate inheritance predicts. Blending would give only pink forever.

A molecular reason is often dosage. If the red allele makes a pigment-producing enzyme and the white allele makes a nonworking version, one red allele makes about half as much pigment as two. Half the pigment looks pink.

With incomplete dominance, every genotype has its own phenotype, so the phenotype ratio equals the genotype ratio. That makes these crosses easy to check: you can count genotypes directly.

### Example 1

In four o'clock plants, a pink plant is crossed with a white plant. What fraction of the offspring are pink, and how many red plants would you expect among 80 offspring?

The cross is $C^RC^W \times C^WC^W$. The white parent gives only $C^W$. The pink parent gives $C^R$ or $C^W$, each $\tfrac12$. So offspring are $\tfrac12$ $C^RC^W$ (pink) and $\tfrac12$ $C^WC^W$ (white). The fraction pink is $\tfrac12$; red needs a $C^R$ from both parents, which is impossible here, so the expected number of red plants is 0.

## Codominance

In **[[codominance]]**, a heterozygote shows the full phenotypes of both alleles at once, side by side, rather than a blend. Two classic examples:

- Roan cattle: a cross between red and white cattle gives roan calves whose coats are a mix of individual red hairs and individual white hairs. Each hair is fully one color.
- The human AB blood type: a person with one $I^A$ and one $I^B$ allele makes both the A and B sugar markers on their red blood cells.

The difference from incomplete dominance is what you see in the heterozygote. Pink petals are an in-between color everywhere; a roan coat has both pure colors present. Both cases still give a 1 : 2 : 1 phenotype ratio when two heterozygotes are crossed.

## Multiple alleles: the ABO blood groups

A single person has only two alleles of a gene, but a population can carry many. A gene with three or more alleles in the population has **[[multiple alleles]]**. The ABO blood-group gene has three common alleles:

- $I^A$ puts the A antigen (a sugar marker) on red blood cells;
- $I^B$ puts the B antigen on them;
- $i$ puts neither.

$I^A$ and $I^B$ are codominant with each other, and both are dominant to $i$. That gives six genotypes and four blood types:

| Blood type (phenotype) | Genotypes | Antigens on red cells | Antibodies in plasma |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | $I^AI^A$, $I^Ai$ | A | anti-B |
| B | $I^BI^B$, $I^Bi$ | B | anti-A |
| AB | $I^AI^B$ | A and B | neither |
| O | $ii$ | neither | anti-A and anti-B |

The antibodies matter for transfusions: a person's plasma attacks red cells carrying an antigen they lack. Type O red cells carry no A or B antigen, so they can be given to people of any ABO type, while a person with type AB has no anti-A or anti-B antibodies and can receive red cells of any ABO type. (Real transfusions also match the separate Rh factor, controlled by a different gene, and other markers.)

### Example 2

A woman with type A blood and a man with type B blood have a child with type O blood. What are the parents' genotypes, and what is the probability that their next child has type AB?

A type O child is $ii$ and received $i$ from each parent. So the mother must be $I^Ai$ (not $I^AI^A$) and the father must be $I^Bi$.

Each parent gives either allele with probability $\tfrac12$:

| | $I^B$ | $i$ |
|---|---|---|
| $I^A$ | $I^AI^B$ (AB) | $I^Ai$ (A) |
| $i$ | $I^Bi$ (B) | $ii$ (O) |

All four blood types are possible, each with probability $\tfrac14$. So $P(\text{AB}) = \tfrac14$, the same as for each earlier child.

Blood types were once used to rule out a man as a child's biological father. In Example 2, a man with type AB ($I^AI^B$) could not be the father of the type O child, because he has no $i$ allele to pass on. Blood type can exclude but never prove parentage; DNA testing replaced it.

## Polygenic traits

Many traits don't fall into a few clear classes. Human height, skin color and many crop yields vary continuously. These are **[[polygenic traits]]**, controlled by the combined effects of many genes, each adding a small amount.

A simple model shows why polygenic traits form a bell-shaped curve. Suppose three unlinked genes each have an "adding" allele (A, B, C) and a "non-adding" allele (a, b, c), and each adding allele makes a plant 2 cm taller. Cross two AaBbCc plants. Each of the six allele positions in an offspring gets an adding allele with probability $\tfrac12$, so the number of adding alleles is like the number of heads in six coin tosses.

```plot
{"x": [-0.5, 6.5], "y": [0, 22], "xLabel": "number of adding alleles", "yLabel": "offspring out of 64", "bars": [{"x": 0, "height": 1, "width": 0.8, "label": "1"}, {"x": 1, "height": 6, "width": 0.8, "label": "6"}, {"x": 2, "height": 15, "width": 0.8, "label": "15"}, {"x": 3, "height": 20, "width": 0.8, "label": "20"}, {"x": 4, "height": 15, "width": 0.8, "label": "15"}, {"x": 5, "height": 6, "width": 0.8, "label": "6"}, {"x": 6, "height": 1, "width": 0.8, "label": "1"}], "caption": "AaBbCc × AaBbCc with additive alleles: 7 height classes in a 1:6:15:20:15:6:1 pattern"}
```

### Example 3

In the model above, what fraction of offspring have the maximum height (all six adding alleles, AABBCC)?

By the product rule, each gene must be homozygous for the adding allele: $\tfrac14 \times \tfrac14 \times \tfrac14 = \tfrac{1}{64}$. The middle class (3 adding alleles) is the most common, $\tfrac{20}{64}$. With more genes, the classes get closer together and the histogram becomes a smooth bell curve. Environmental effects (nutrition, sunlight) blur the classes further.

## Genes and environment

The environment can change how a genotype is expressed:

- Hydrangea flowers with the same genotype are blue in acidic soil and pink in more alkaline soil.
- Himalayan rabbits have a temperature-sensitive pigment enzyme: their ears, nose and paws, the coolest parts of the body, are dark, while the warmer body is white.
- Phenylketonuria (PKU) is a recessive condition in which a person can't break down the amino acid phenylalanine. Without treatment it causes intellectual disability; with a low-phenylalanine diet from birth, people with PKU develop typically. The genotype is the same; the outcome depends on the environment.

Phenotype is the product of genotype and environment acting together.

## One gene, many effects; genes that affect other genes

**[[Pleiotropy]]** is when one gene affects several traits. The sickle-cell allele changes one amino acid in hemoglobin, and that one change leads to sickle-shaped red cells, anemia, pain, organ damage and, in carriers, some protection against malaria.

**[[Epistasis]]** is when one gene changes or masks the effect of another gene. In Labrador retrievers, gene B controls pigment color (B black, b brown/chocolate), but a second gene E controls whether pigment is deposited in the fur at all. A dog that is ee is yellow whatever its B genotype. A cross of two BbEe dogs gives 9 black : 3 chocolate : 4 yellow, a modified 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 in which the two classes with ee are merged.

## Common mistakes

- Confusing incomplete dominance with codominance. Intermediate blend in the heterozygote (pink) is incomplete dominance; both traits fully present (red and white hairs, A and B antigens) is codominance.
- Calling incomplete dominance "blending inheritance." The alleles stay separate and pure, as the 1 : 2 : 1 F2 shows.
- Thinking a person can have three ABO alleles. Multiple alleles exist in the population; each person has two.
- Forgetting that type A or B parents may carry a hidden $i$ allele.
- Using a 3 : 1 phenotype ratio for a heterozygote cross with incomplete dominance or codominance; it is 1 : 2 : 1.

## Key points

- Incomplete dominance: the heterozygote is intermediate; phenotype ratio = genotype ratio (1 : 2 : 1 from two heterozygotes).
- Codominance: the heterozygote shows both alleles' traits (AB blood, roan cattle).
- ABO blood groups: three alleles; $I^A$ and $I^B$ codominant, both dominant to $i$; four blood types from six genotypes.
- Polygenic traits come from many genes with additive effects and give continuous, bell-shaped variation.
- Pleiotropy: one gene, many traits. Epistasis: one gene masks or modifies another (9 : 3 : 4 in Labradors).
- The environment affects how genes are expressed.

lessons.title: Sex-linked traits and pedigrees
lessons.body:
In every cross so far, it made no difference which parent carried which allele: Aa mother × aa father gave the same results as aa mother × Aa father. That's true for most genes, but not all. Some traits, such as red-green color blindness and hemophilia, show up far more often in males than in females. This lesson explains why, using the chromosomes that differ between the sexes, and then shows how geneticists study human inheritance when they can't run experimental crosses: by reading family trees.

## Sex chromosomes and autosomes

Human body cells have 23 pairs of chromosomes. In 22 of the pairs, the two members match in size and carry the same genes; these are **[[autosomes]]**. The 23rd pair are the **[[sex chromosomes]]**, X and Y. Most females have two X chromosomes (XX) and most males have one X and one Y (XY). (Some people have other combinations, such as XXY; lesson 21 covers how these arise.)

The X is a large chromosome carrying roughly 800 to 900 genes, most of which have nothing to do with sex: genes for color vision, blood clotting and muscle proteins, among others. The Y is small and carries only about 100 protein-coding genes, including *SRY*, a gene that triggers development of testes in the embryo.

Inheritance of the sex chromosomes is simple. A mother always passes on an X. A father passes on either his X (the child is XX, typically female) or his Y (the child is XY, typically male), each with probability $\tfrac12$. So:

- a son always gets his X from his mother and his Y from his father;
- a daughter gets one X from each parent, and always gets her father's only X.

## X-linked genes

A gene on the X chromosome is **[[X-linked]]** (more generally, sex-linked). Males have only one X, so they have only one allele of every X-linked gene. Whatever allele that X carries is expressed, dominant or recessive, because there is no second copy to mask it. Females have two copies, so for a recessive X-linked trait they behave like any other gene: they need two recessive alleles to show it.

We write X-linked alleles as superscripts on the X: $X^B$ (normal color vision, dominant) and $X^b$ (red-green color blindness, recessive). The Y carries no allele for this gene.

| Genotype | Phenotype |
|---|---|
| $X^BX^B$ | female, normal vision |
| $X^BX^b$ | female, normal vision, **[[carrier]]** |
| $X^bX^b$ | female, color-blind |
| $X^BY$ | male, normal vision |
| $X^bY$ | male, color-blind |

A carrier is an individual who has one copy of a recessive allele but does not show the trait; she can pass the allele on. (The word is also used for heterozygotes of autosomal recessive conditions.)

This is why recessive X-linked traits are much more common in males. A male needs only one copy of the allele; a female needs two. If a fraction $q$ of X chromosomes carry the allele, about $q$ of males are affected but only about $q^2$ of females. Red-green color blindness affects roughly 8% of men of Northern European ancestry but only about 0.5% of women, close to $0.08^2 = 0.0064$.

## Morgan's white-eyed fly

The first gene ever tied to a specific chromosome was X-linked. In 1910 Thomas Hunt Morgan, breeding fruit flies (*Drosophila*), found a single male with white eyes instead of the normal red. He crossed it with a red-eyed female. All the F1 had red eyes, so white was recessive. In the F2, he saw the expected 3 red : 1 white, with a twist: every white-eyed fly was male.

Morgan explained this by putting the eye-color gene on the X chromosome (fruit flies use XX/XY like humans). The original male was $X^wY$; the female was $X^WX^W$. The F1 females were $X^WX^w$ and the F1 males $X^WY$. In the F2, sons get their single X from their carrier mother, so half are white-eyed, while every daughter gets the father's $X^W$ and has red eyes. This was the first strong evidence for the chromosome theory of inheritance: genes are located on chromosomes.

### Example 1

A woman who is a carrier for hemophilia A ($X^HX^h$) and a man without hemophilia ($X^HY$) have children. Find the probability that (a) a son has hemophilia, (b) a daughter has hemophilia, and (c) a child of theirs, sex not yet known, is a son with hemophilia.

| | $X^H$ | $Y$ |
|---|---|---|
| $X^H$ | $X^HX^H$ | $X^HY$ |
| $X^h$ | $X^HX^h$ | $X^hY$ |

(a) Sons are the right column: $X^HY$ and $X^hY$, so $P(\text{affected} \mid \text{son}) = \tfrac12$.

(b) Daughters (left column) all get $X^H$ from their father: none are affected, though half are carriers.

(c) Among all four equally likely boxes, one is $X^hY$: $\tfrac14$. Equivalently, $P(\text{son}) \times P(\text{affected} \mid \text{son}) = \tfrac12 \times \tfrac12 = \tfrac14$.

Be careful to read which question is asked: "the probability that a son is affected" ($\tfrac12$) is not "the probability that a child is an affected son" ($\tfrac14$).

### Example 2

A color-blind man ($X^bY$) and a woman homozygous for normal vision ($X^BX^B$) have children. What fraction of their sons and daughters are color-blind?

Every son gets his X from his mother: $X^B$. No sons are color-blind, and the father's allele can never reach a son. Every daughter gets the father's $X^b$ and a mother's $X^B$: all daughters are carriers ($X^BX^b$) with normal vision. The trait then tends to reappear in the daughters' sons, skipping a generation through carrier females.

## Pedigrees

Geneticists can't arrange human matings, so they work backward from family histories drawn as a **[[pedigree]]**, a chart of a family's relationships showing who has a trait. The standard symbols:

- square = male, circle = female;
- filled symbol = has the trait; open symbol = does not;
- a dot inside or a half-filled symbol = known carrier (not always shown);
- a horizontal line joining a male and a female = a mating; a vertical line down from it leads to their children, drawn left to right in birth order;
- generations are labeled with Roman numerals (I, II, III).

```shape
{"x": [-1.5, 6], "y": [0.8, 5], "polygons": [{"points": [[0.5, 3.5], [1.5, 3.5], [1.5, 4.5], [0.5, 4.5]]}, {"points": [[0, 1.5], [1, 1.5], [1, 2.5], [0, 2.5]], "fill": true}, {"points": [[4, 1.5], [5, 1.5], [5, 2.5], [4, 2.5]]}], "circles": [{"center": [4, 4], "r": 0.5}, {"center": [4, 4], "r": 0.12, "fill": true}, {"center": [2.5, 2], "r": 0.5}], "segments": [{"from": [1.5, 4], "to": [3.5, 4]}, {"from": [2.5, 4], "to": [2.5, 2.9]}, {"from": [0.5, 2.9], "to": [4.5, 2.9]}, {"from": [0.5, 2.9], "to": [0.5, 2.5]}, {"from": [2.5, 2.9], "to": [2.5, 2.5]}, {"from": [4.5, 2.9], "to": [4.5, 2.5]}], "labels": [{"at": [-1, 4], "text": "I"}, {"at": [-1, 2], "text": "II"}], "caption": "An X-linked recessive pattern: an unaffected father and a carrier mother (dot) have an affected son, an unaffected daughter and an unaffected son"}
```

The main inheritance patterns leave recognizable signatures:

| Pattern | Clues in a pedigree |
|---|---|
| Autosomal recessive | Often skips generations; two unaffected parents can have an affected child; males and females affected about equally |
| Autosomal dominant | Every affected person has at least one affected parent; does not skip generations; two affected parents can have an unaffected child; both sexes affected |
| X-linked recessive | Many more affected males than females; affected sons usually have unaffected (carrier) mothers; never passed from father to son |

Examples: cystic fibrosis and sickle-cell disease are autosomal recessive; Huntington's disease and achondroplasia are autosomal dominant; hemophilia A, Duchenne muscular dystrophy and red-green color blindness are X-linked recessive.

### Example 3

Two parents who do not have a condition have a daughter who does. What inheritance pattern does this show, and what is the probability that her unaffected brother is a carrier?

- Not dominant: a dominant trait in the daughter would require an affected parent.
- Not X-linked recessive: an affected daughter would need $X^aX^a$, with one $X^a$ from her father, and he would then be affected.
- So it is autosomal recessive, and both parents must be carriers, Aa × Aa.

The brother is unaffected, so he is AA or Aa, not aa. Among the Punnett boxes that are not aa, 1 is AA and 2 are Aa. So his probability of being a carrier is $\tfrac23$, not $\tfrac12$. Knowing he is unaffected removes the aa box from consideration.

Sorting out a pedigree this way, by asking which patterns are impossible, is usually faster than trying to prove the right one directly.

## Common mistakes

- Giving a male two alleles for an X-linked gene, or writing an allele on the Y.
- Saying a son inherited an X-linked trait from his father. Sons get their X from their mother.
- Mixing up "probability a son is affected" (out of sons only) and "probability a child is an affected son" (out of all children).
- Assuming X-linked traits never appear in females. A female is affected if she gets a recessive allele from both her carrier mother and her affected father.
- In pedigrees, deciding "dominant" because a trait is in many people. Look for the deciding clues: a trait skipping a generation, or two unaffected parents with an affected child, rules dominance out.

## Key points

- Humans have 22 pairs of autosomes and one pair of sex chromosomes (XX or XY in most people).
- Males have one allele of each X-linked gene, so a recessive X-linked allele always shows in a male.
- Sons get their X from their mother; fathers give their X to every daughter and never to a son.
- Carrier mother × unaffected father: half the sons affected, half the daughters carriers, no affected daughters.
- Pedigrees use squares, circles, and filled symbols; rule out patterns using the clues for autosomal recessive, autosomal dominant and X-linked recessive inheritance.

lessons.title: Chromosomes, karyotypes, and chi-square
lessons.body:
Lesson 20 linked a gene to a chromosome. This lesson zooms out to whole chromosomes: how biologists look at a full set, what happens when a cell ends up with too many or too few, and what that means for health. It closes the module with a tool you will need whenever you test a genetic prediction against real data: the chi-square test, which tells you whether a difference between observed and expected counts is small enough to be chance.

## Karyotypes

A **[[karyotype]]** is an organized picture of all the chromosomes in one cell, arranged in pairs by size, centromere position and banding pattern. To make one, a lab grows cells (often white blood cells), adds a chemical that stops division in metaphase, when chromosomes are most condensed, then spreads, stains and photographs them. The stain gives each chromosome a characteristic pattern of light and dark bands, so each pair can be identified.

A typical human karyotype has 46 chromosomes: 22 pairs of autosomes, numbered 1 to 22 from roughly largest to smallest, and the sex chromosomes, XX or XY. It is written as 46,XX or 46,XY. Karyotypes can reveal an extra or missing chromosome and large structural changes such as a missing or moved piece; small changes inside a single gene need DNA methods (module 6).

## Nondisjunction and aneuploidy

Lesson 16 introduced nondisjunction: in meiosis, a homologous pair (anaphase I) or a pair of sister chromatids (anaphase II) occasionally fails to separate, so both copies go to one daughter cell and none to the other. As a reminder of the two cases:

- Nondisjunction in meiosis I: all four gametes are abnormal. Two have an extra chromosome (n + 1 = 24 in humans) and two lack one (n − 1 = 22).
- Nondisjunction in meiosis II: two gametes are normal, one is n + 1 and one is n − 1.

If an abnormal gamete is fertilized by a normal one, the zygote has 47 or 45 chromosomes. Having an abnormal number of one or more chromosomes is **[[aneuploidy]]**. Three copies of a chromosome is a trisomy; one copy (where there should be two) is a monosomy.

Most aneuploidies of autosomes are not compatible with development and end in early miscarriage. A few are seen in people:

| Karyotype | Condition | About how common |
|---|---|---|
| 47,+21 (trisomy 21) | Down syndrome: intellectual disability of varying degree, characteristic facial features, higher risk of heart defects | about 1 in 650 to 700 births |
| 47,+18 or 47,+13 | Trisomy 18 (Edwards) or 13 (Patau): severe developmental effects; most affected infants live less than a year | rare |
| 45,X | Turner syndrome: short stature, ovaries that don't develop typically | about 1 in 2,000 to 2,500 female births |
| 47,XXY | Klinefelter syndrome: often taller, reduced fertility; many people are never diagnosed | about 1 in 500 to 1,000 male births |

The risk of trisomy 21 rises with the age of the egg-producing parent, because human egg cells stay paused partway through meiosis I from before birth until ovulation, sometimes for 40 years or more. Sex-chromosome aneuploidies tend to have milder effects than autosomal ones; in females one X is largely inactivated in each cell, which buffers changes in X number, and the Y carries few genes.

Not every case of Down syndrome is a simple trisomy. In a few percent of cases, extra chromosome 21 material is attached to another chromosome (a translocation).

### Example 1

A sperm cell formed after nondisjunction of the sex chromosomes in meiosis I fertilizes a normal egg (23,X). What karyotypes can the zygote have?

In meiosis I the X and Y fail to separate, so the gametes are either 24,XY (both sex chromosomes) or 22 with no sex chromosome.

- 24,XY sperm + 23,X egg → 47,XXY (Klinefelter syndrome).
- 22 sperm (no sex chromosome) + 23,X egg → 45,X (Turner syndrome).

If nondisjunction happened instead in meiosis II, in the X-carrying cell, sperm with 24,XX and with 22 (no sex chromosome) would form, giving 47,XXX or 45,X.

## Changes in chromosome structure and number of sets

Pieces of chromosomes can also break and rejoin wrongly:

- deletion: a segment is lost (for example, cri-du-chat syndrome, a deletion on chromosome 5);
- duplication: a segment is repeated;
- inversion: a segment is flipped end to end;
- translocation: a segment moves to a different, non-homologous chromosome.

Some organisms have whole extra sets of chromosomes, called polyploidy. It is usually lethal in animals but common in plants: bread wheat has six sets (hexaploid), and many cultivated strawberries have eight. Polyploid plants are often larger, and polyploidy has produced many new plant species.

## Testing a prediction: the chi-square test

Back to counting offspring. Mendel's F2 for seed shape was 5474 round : 1850 wrinkled, not exactly 3 : 1. Is that close enough? Chance alone always produces some deviation, as with coin flips. The **[[chi-square test]]** measures how far observed counts are from the counts a hypothesis predicts and tells you whether that gap is reasonably explained by chance.

The steps:

1. State the hypothesis being tested (the null hypothesis), for example "the offspring follow a 3 : 1 ratio." It always predicts specific numbers.
2. Compute the expected count $E$ for each category: total × predicted fraction.
3. For each category compute $\dfrac{(O - E)^2}{E}$, where $O$ is the observed count, and add them:
$$\chi^2 = \sum \frac{(O - E)^2}{E}$$
4. Find the degrees of freedom: number of categories − 1.
5. Compare $\chi^2$ with the critical value for that number of degrees of freedom at $p = 0.05$.

| Degrees of freedom | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Critical value ($p = 0.05$) | 3.84 | 5.99 | 7.81 | 9.49 |

- If $\chi^2$ is less than the critical value, the deviation is small enough to be chance. We fail to reject the hypothesis: the data are consistent with it.
- If $\chi^2$ is greater than or equal to the critical value, a deviation this large would happen by chance less than 5% of the time if the hypothesis were true. We reject the hypothesis and look for another explanation.

Why square the differences? So that positive and negative deviations both count, and big ones count more. Why divide by $E$? A difference of 10 is huge if you expected 20, trivial if you expected 2000. And always use counts, never percentages: the test depends on sample size.

```plot
{"x": [0, 14], "y": [0, 0.27], "xLabel": "chi-square value", "yLabel": "probability density", "functions": [{"f": "chi2pdf(x, 3)", "label": "df = 3"}], "shade": [{"f": "chi2pdf(x, 3)", "from": 7.81, "to": 14}], "segments": [{"from": [7.81, 0], "to": [7.81, 0.2], "dashed": true}], "labels": [{"at": [9.5, 0.05], "text": "5% of area"}], "caption": "If the hypothesis is true, chi-square values beyond 7.81 (df = 3) happen only 5% of the time"}
```

### Example 2

Test Mendel's seed-shape data (5474 round, 1850 wrinkled) against a 3 : 1 ratio.

Total: 7324. Expected: round $\tfrac34 \times 7324 = 5493$; wrinkled $\tfrac14 \times 7324 = 1831$.

| | O | E | O − E | (O − E)² / E |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Round | 5474 | 5493 | −19 | 0.066 |
| Wrinkled | 1850 | 1831 | 19 | 0.197 |

$\chi^2 = 0.066 + 0.197 = 0.26$. There are 2 categories, so df = 1 and the critical value is 3.84. Since $0.26 < 3.84$, we fail to reject: the data fit 3 : 1 well.

### Example 3

Test Mendel's dihybrid data (315, 108, 101, 32) against 9 : 3 : 3 : 1.

Total: 556. Expected: $\tfrac{9}{16} \times 556 = 312.75$, $\tfrac{3}{16} \times 556 = 104.25$ (twice), $\tfrac{1}{16} \times 556 = 34.75$.

$$\chi^2 = \frac{2.25^2}{312.75} + \frac{3.75^2}{104.25} + \frac{(-3.25)^2}{104.25} + \frac{(-2.75)^2}{34.75} = 0.016 + 0.135 + 0.101 + 0.218 = 0.47$$

Four categories, df = 3, critical value 7.81. $0.47 < 7.81$: fail to reject. The data are consistent with independent assortment.

### Example 4

A student test-crosses a heterozygous fruit fly and expects 1 : 1. Of 200 offspring, 128 show the dominant trait and 72 the recessive trait. Is this consistent with 1 : 1?

Expected: 100 and 100. $\chi^2 = \dfrac{28^2}{100} + \dfrac{(-28)^2}{100} = 7.84 + 7.84 = 15.68$. With df = 1, the critical value is 3.84, and $15.68 > 3.84$, so we reject the 1 : 1 hypothesis. Something besides chance is going on: perhaps flies with the recessive phenotype survive less well, or the parent was not the genotype assumed. The test says that the data don't fit the hypothesis; it doesn't say why.

## Common mistakes

- Running chi-square on percentages or ratios instead of raw counts.
- Using the number of categories as the degrees of freedom; it is categories − 1.
- Dividing by $O$ instead of $E$.
- Saying the test "proves" a hypothesis. Failing to reject means the data are consistent with it, not that it is certainly true.
- Confusing nondisjunction in meiosis I (all four gametes abnormal) with meiosis II (half of them normal).
- Thinking a karyotype can detect any genetic condition. It shows chromosome number and large structural changes, not single-gene alleles such as the one for cystic fibrosis.

## Key points

- A karyotype shows a cell's chromosomes in pairs; typical humans are 46,XX or 46,XY.
- Nondisjunction makes gametes with n + 1 or n − 1 chromosomes; the zygote is aneuploid (trisomy 21, 45,X, 47,XXY).
- Structural changes: deletion, duplication, inversion, translocation. Polyploidy (extra full sets) is common in plants.
- $\chi^2 = \sum (O - E)^2/E$ on counts; df = categories − 1.
- Critical values at $p = 0.05$: 3.84, 5.99, 7.81, 9.49 for df 1–4. Below: fail to reject; at or above: reject.

lessons.title: DNA structure and replication
lessons.body:
In the last module you followed genes through crosses and pedigrees without asking what a gene physically is. Mendel never knew; he only saw the ratios. This module opens the box. This lesson answers two questions: how do we know genes are made of DNA, and how does the shape of the DNA molecule let it be copied every time a cell divides?

## How biologists showed that genes are DNA

By the 1940s genes were known to sit on chromosomes, which are made of DNA and protein. Most biologists bet on protein: proteins use 20 different amino acids, while DNA has only four kinds of nucleotide, which seemed too simple to carry instructions. Three experiments changed their minds.

*Griffith, 1928.* Frederick Griffith worked with two strains of pneumonia bacteria. The S strain has a smooth sugar coat and kills mice; the R strain lacks the coat and is harmless. Heat-killed S bacteria were harmless too. But when he injected heat-killed S bacteria *mixed with* live R bacteria, the mice died, and live S bacteria came out of their blood. Something from the dead S cells had permanently changed the R cells, and the change was passed on to their descendants. Griffith called this transformation. He did not know what the "transforming principle" was.

*Avery, MacLeod and McCarty, 1944.* They purified extract from S cells and destroyed one kind of molecule at a time with enzymes before mixing it with R cells.

### Example 1

Here is the logic of the Avery experiment as a data table. Which molecule is the transforming principle?

| S-cell extract treated with | Live S cells appear? |
|---|---|
| Nothing | Yes |
| Protease (destroys protein) | Yes |
| RNase (destroys RNA) | Yes |
| DNase (destroys DNA) | No |

Reason through each row. Destroying protein did not stop transformation, so protein is not needed. The same holds for RNA. Only destroying DNA stopped it. The transforming principle is DNA. The untreated extract is the control: it shows transformation works at all.

*Hershey and Chase, 1952.* Some biologists still doubted, so Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase used a virus that infects bacteria (a bacteriophage). A phage is just protein wrapped around DNA, and it injects its genes into the bacterium. Protein contains sulfur but almost no phosphorus; DNA contains phosphorus but no sulfur. So they grew one batch of phages with radioactive sulfur (³⁵S, labeling protein) and another with radioactive phosphorus (³²P, labeling DNA). After infection, they shook the empty phage coats off in a blender and spun the bacteria down. The ³²P was found inside the bacteria; the ³⁵S stayed outside with the coats. The material that enters the cell and directs new phages is DNA.

## The structure of DNA

Recall from module 1 that DNA is a nucleic acid, a polymer of nucleotides. Each nucleotide has three parts: a phosphate group, the five-carbon sugar deoxyribose, and one of four nitrogen bases: adenine (A), thymine (T), guanine (G) and cytosine (C). A and G are purines, with a double ring; T and C are pyrimidines, with a single ring.

Nucleotides link into a strand through sugar–phosphate bonds, forming a backbone with the bases sticking out to one side. The two ends of a strand differ: one ends in a phosphate attached to the sugar's 5′ (five-prime) carbon, the other in the sugar's 3′ carbon. So every strand has a direction, written 5′ → 3′.

Two strands make the **[[double helix]]**, a twisted ladder. The sugar–phosphate backbones are the rails; pairs of bases are the rungs, held together by hydrogen bonds. The pairing follows strict rules, called **[[complementary base pairing]]**:

- A pairs with T (two hydrogen bonds);
- G pairs with C (three hydrogen bonds).

Each rung is one purine plus one pyrimidine, so every rung is the same width and the helix is a uniform 2 nm wide. The strands are **[[antiparallel]]**: they run in opposite directions, one 5′ → 3′ and its partner 3′ → 5′.

The model came together in 1953. Rosalind Franklin's X-ray photographs, taken at King's College London (where Maurice Wilkins also studied DNA), showed a helix of constant width with a repeating pattern every 3.4 nm. James Watson and Francis Crick, who saw her data without her knowledge, combined it with a key clue from chemistry, Chargaff's measurements, and built the model.

## Chargaff's rules

Erwin Chargaff measured the base composition of DNA from many species. He found two patterns, now called **[[Chargaff's rules]]**: in any double-stranded DNA, the amount of A equals the amount of T, and the amount of G equals the amount of C; but the proportion of A + T versus G + C varies from species to species. Base pairing explains the first rule at once: every A on one strand has a T across from it.

Human DNA is about 30% A, 30% T, 20% G and 20% C.

### Example 2

A sample of double-stranded DNA is 22% guanine. Find the percentages of the other three bases.

- G pairs with C, so C = 22%.
- G + C = 44%, so A + T = 100% − 44% = 56%.
- A = T, so each is 56% ÷ 2 = 28%.

Answer: A 28%, T 28%, G 22%, C 22%. Check: 28 + 28 + 22 + 22 = 100.

Chargaff's rules apply to the double helix as a whole, not to one strand. One strand can have far more A than T; its partner then has the extra T.

### Example 3

Write the strand complementary to 5′-ATGCCGTT-3′.

Pair each base in turn: A→T, T→A, G→C, C→G. Under the given strand, the partner bases are T A C G G C A A. Because the strands are antiparallel, the partner runs the other way, so its left end is 3′:

| Given strand | 5′- A T G C C G T T -3′ |
|---|---|
| Complement | 3′- T A C G G C A A -5′ |

If you are asked to write the complement in the usual 5′ → 3′ direction, read it from its 5′ end (the right): 5′-AACGGCAT-3′. Both descriptions are the same molecule. The safest habit is to write the complement directly under the original with its ends labeled.

## Replication is semiconservative

Watson and Crick noticed that base pairing suggests a copying method: separate the two strands, and each one is a template for building its partner. Each new double helix would then have one old strand and one new strand. This is **[[semiconservative replication]]**. Two other ideas were possible: conservative (the original helix stays intact and a wholly new one is made) and dispersive (old and new pieces mixed along both strands).

In 1958 Matthew Meselson and Franklin Stahl tested them. They grew bacteria for many generations on heavy nitrogen (¹⁵N), so all their DNA was heavy, then moved them to normal light nitrogen (¹⁴N) and let them divide. They spun DNA samples in a dense salt solution, where DNA settles in a band at its own density.

### Example 4

Predict the bands after one and two generations in light nitrogen if replication is semiconservative.

- Generation 0: all DNA is heavy/heavy: one heavy band.
- Generation 1: each helix has one old heavy strand and one new light strand: one band, halfway between heavy and light (hybrid). This alone rules out the conservative model, which would give separate heavy and light bands.
- Generation 2: the two strands of each hybrid separate. The heavy strand gets a light partner (hybrid); the light strand gets a light partner (light). Half the DNA is hybrid, half is light: two bands of equal amount.

That is exactly what Meselson and Stahl saw. The dispersive model predicts a single band that just drifts lighter each generation, so the two bands in generation 2 ruled it out too. In general, after $n$ generations the two original heavy strands sit in exactly two of the $2^n$ helices, so the hybrid fraction is $2/2^n$.

## The replication machinery

Copying is done by a team of enzymes:

1. Replication starts at specific sites called origins. A bacterial chromosome has one origin; a human chromosome has hundreds to thousands, so the work is split among many replication forks.
2. Helicase unwinds the helix, breaking the hydrogen bonds between bases and forming a Y-shaped replication fork.
3. Primase lays down a short RNA primer, because the main copying enzyme cannot start a strand from nothing.
4. **[[DNA polymerase]]** reads the template and adds matching nucleotides. It can only add to the 3′ end of a growing strand, so new DNA is always built 5′ → 3′.
5. Because the two template strands are antiparallel, one new strand (the leading strand) is built continuously toward the fork. The other (the lagging strand) must be built in short pieces, working away from the fork each time a new stretch opens up. These pieces are **[[Okazaki fragments]]**, named for Reiji and Tsuneko Okazaki, who found them in the 1960s.
6. The RNA primers are replaced with DNA, and DNA ligase seals the gaps between fragments.

DNA polymerase also proofreads: it backs up and removes a wrongly paired base. With proofreading and later repair, the final error rate is roughly one mistake per billion bases copied. Errors that slip through are mutations, a topic in lesson 24.

## Common mistakes

- Pairing A with G or C with T. The pairs are always A–T and G–C (purine with pyrimidine).
- Applying Chargaff's rules to one strand. A = T and G = C hold for double-stranded DNA, not for a single strand or for RNA.
- Forgetting that A + T and G + C both add to 100%. If G is 22%, A is not 78%; G and C together are 44%, leaving 56% to split between A and T.
- Ignoring direction. The complement of a 5′ → 3′ strand runs 3′ → 5′; label the ends.
- Thinking the lagging strand is made in the 3′ → 5′ direction. Every new strand grows 5′ → 3′; the lagging strand is made in fragments precisely because of that rule.
- Saying Meselson and Stahl's first generation ruled out the dispersive model. Generation 1 rules out conservative; generation 2 rules out dispersive.

## Key points

- Griffith found transformation; Avery's enzyme tests identified DNA as the transforming principle; Hershey and Chase showed phage DNA, not protein, enters the cell.
- DNA is a double helix of two antiparallel strands with sugar–phosphate backbones and base pairs A–T and G–C.
- Chargaff's rules: in double-stranded DNA, A = T and G = C; the A + T to G + C ratio differs between species.
- Replication is semiconservative: each new helix keeps one old strand (Meselson–Stahl, 1958).
- Helicase unwinds, primase primes, DNA polymerase builds 5′ → 3′ (leading strand continuous, lagging strand in Okazaki fragments), ligase joins, and proofreading keeps errors near one per billion bases.

lessons.title: From gene to protein
lessons.body:
The last lesson showed how DNA is copied. But a gene is not useful just sitting in the nucleus being copied; it has to *do* something. Almost everything a gene does, it does through a protein: an enzyme, a channel, a hormone receptor, a structural fiber. This lesson follows the path from a stretch of DNA to a finished protein, and explains how a four-letter alphabet spells out sequences of 20 amino acids.

## The central dogma

Francis Crick summed up the flow of genetic information in 1958 as the **[[central dogma]]**: DNA → RNA → protein. Information is copied from DNA into RNA by **[[transcription]]**, and the RNA's message is decoded into a chain of amino acids by **[[translation]]**. Using a gene's information to make its product is called gene expression.

There are exceptions to the simple arrow. Retroviruses such as HIV copy RNA back into DNA, and many genes make RNA molecules that are never translated but do jobs of their own. Still, the main traffic of information goes DNA → RNA → protein, and it never goes from protein back to nucleic acid.

Why use an RNA middleman at all? In eukaryotes the DNA stays in the nucleus, while ribosomes work in the cytoplasm. A gene can be transcribed into many RNA copies, each translated many times, so one gene can make thousands of protein molecules quickly while the master copy stays protected.

## RNA is not DNA

RNA is a nucleic acid too, but it differs from DNA in three ways:

| | DNA | RNA |
|---|---|---|
| Sugar | deoxyribose | ribose |
| Bases | A, T, G, C | A, U, G, C (uracil replaces thymine) |
| Strands | usually two (double helix) | usually one |

Uracil pairs with adenine, just as thymine does. Three kinds of RNA do the main work of protein synthesis:

- **[[mRNA]]** (messenger RNA) carries a gene's sequence to the ribosome.
- **[[tRNA]]** (transfer RNA) brings amino acids to the ribosome; each tRNA carries one specific amino acid.
- **[[rRNA]]** (ribosomal RNA) makes up much of the ribosome and catalyzes the bonds between amino acids.

## Transcription

Transcription copies one gene, not a whole chromosome, and it uses only one of the two DNA strands as a pattern.

1. *Initiation.* The enzyme **[[RNA polymerase]]** binds to a **[[promoter]]**, a DNA sequence just upstream of the gene that marks where to start and which strand to read. It unwinds a short stretch of the helix.
2. *Elongation.* RNA polymerase moves along the template strand, adding RNA nucleotides that pair with the template bases (A with U, T with A, G with C, C with G). Like DNA polymerase, it builds 5′ → 3′, so it reads the template 3′ → 5′. Unlike DNA polymerase, it needs no primer.
3. *Termination.* At a terminator sequence the polymerase releases the RNA and the DNA rewinds.

The DNA strand that is read is the template strand. The other strand is called the coding strand, because its sequence matches the mRNA (with T in place of U).

In eukaryotes the new RNA is processed before it leaves the nucleus. A protective cap is added to its 5′ end and a tail of many A's to its 3′ end. Most genes also contain **[[introns]]**, stretches that are cut out, and **[[exons]]**, the stretches that are spliced together and expressed. Splicing can join exons in different combinations, which is one reason humans make far more kinds of protein than their roughly 20,000 protein-coding genes.

### Example 1

A DNA template strand reads 3′-TACGGATCC-5′. Write the mRNA.

Pair each template base with its RNA partner: T→A, A→U, C→G, G→C, G→C, A→U, T→A, C→G, C→G. The mRNA is antiparallel to the template, so its left end is 5′:

5′-AUGCCUAGG-3′.

Check with the coding strand: it would be 5′-ATGCCTAGG-3′, the same as the mRNA with T for U. A common error is to write the DNA complement (ATGCCTAGG) and forget that RNA uses U.

## The genetic code

Four bases cannot code for 20 amino acids one at a time, or even two at a time ($4^2 = 16$). Three at a time gives $4^3 = 64$ combinations, enough with some to spare. Each group of three mRNA bases is a **[[codon]]**. In 1961 Marshall Nirenberg and Heinrich Matthaei cracked the first word: they added an artificial mRNA made only of U's (UUUUUU…) to a cell-free extract, and it made a protein made only of phenylalanine. So UUU means Phe. Within five years all 64 codons were assigned.

| First base | Second U | Second C | Second A | Second G | Third base |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| U | UUU Phe | UCU Ser | UAU Tyr | UGU Cys | U |
|  | UUC Phe | UCC Ser | UAC Tyr | UGC Cys | C |
|  | UUA Leu | UCA Ser | UAA Stop | UGA Stop | A |
|  | UUG Leu | UCG Ser | UAG Stop | UGG Trp | G |
| C | CUU Leu | CCU Pro | CAU His | CGU Arg | U |
|  | CUC Leu | CCC Pro | CAC His | CGC Arg | C |
|  | CUA Leu | CCA Pro | CAA Gln | CGA Arg | A |
|  | CUG Leu | CCG Pro | CAG Gln | CGG Arg | G |
| A | AUU Ile | ACU Thr | AAU Asn | AGU Ser | U |
|  | AUC Ile | ACC Thr | AAC Asn | AGC Ser | C |
|  | AUA Ile | ACA Thr | AAA Lys | AGA Arg | A |
|  | AUG Met | ACG Thr | AAG Lys | AGG Arg | G |
| G | GUU Val | GCU Ala | GAU Asp | GGU Gly | U |
|  | GUC Val | GCC Ala | GAC Asp | GGC Gly | C |
|  | GUA Val | GCA Ala | GAA Glu | GGA Gly | A |
|  | GUG Val | GCG Ala | GAG Glu | GGG Gly | G |

To read the table, find the first base in the left column, the second base in the column headings, and the third base on the right. The code has four features worth knowing:

- *Start and stop.* AUG codes for methionine (Met) and is also the start codon where translation begins. UAA, UAG and UGA are stop codons: no tRNA matches them, and they end translation.
- *Redundant.* 61 codons code for 20 amino acids, so most amino acids have several codons (Leu has six). The extra codons usually differ in the third base, so many third-base changes don't change the protein.
- *Unambiguous.* Each codon means exactly one thing.
- *Nearly universal.* Bacteria, plants and people read codons almost the same way, which is strong evidence that all life shares a common ancestor, and the reason a human gene can be expressed in bacteria (lesson 25).

## Translation

Translation happens on ribosomes. Each tRNA has, at one end, an **[[anticodon]]**: three bases that pair with an mRNA codon. At the other end it carries the amino acid that codon specifies. The tRNA is the adapter that connects the nucleic acid language to the protein language.

1. *Initiation.* The small ribosomal subunit attaches to the mRNA near its 5′ end and slides to the first AUG. A tRNA with anticodon UAC, carrying Met, pairs with it, and the large subunit joins. The AUG sets the reading frame: from here the mRNA is read in non-overlapping groups of three.
2. *Elongation.* The next tRNA whose anticodon matches the next codon enters the ribosome. The rRNA joins its amino acid to the growing chain with a peptide bond. The ribosome shifts one codon along the mRNA (toward the 3′ end), the empty tRNA leaves to be reloaded, and the cycle repeats.
3. *Termination.* When a stop codon enters the ribosome, a release factor (a protein, not a tRNA) binds, the finished chain is let go, and the ribosome comes apart.

The new chain then folds into its three-dimensional shape, sometimes helped by other proteins, and may be modified or sent to the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus you met in module 2.

### Example 2

Translate the mRNA 5′-GCAUGUUUGGCAAAUGAUC-3′.

- Find the start codon. Scanning from the 5′ end, the first AUG begins at the third base: GC AUG UUU…, so the reading frame starts there and the GC before it is not translated.
- Split into codons from AUG: AUG | UUU | GGC | AAA | UGA | UC.
- Look up each: AUG = Met, UUU = Phe, GGC = Gly, AAA = Lys, UGA = Stop.

The polypeptide is Met–Phe–Gly–Lys: four amino acids. The stop codon adds nothing, and the bases after it are not read.

### Example 3

A tRNA has the anticodon 3′-AAG-5′. Which amino acid does it carry?

The anticodon pairs with the codon, so the codon is the complement: A pairs with U, A with U, G with C, giving 5′-UUC-3′. From the table, UUC codes for Phe. Don't look up the anticodon itself in the table; the table is written in codons.

## Common mistakes

- Writing T in an mRNA. RNA uses U; the mRNA matches the coding strand, not the template strand.
- Translating from the first base instead of the first AUG.
- Looking up anticodons or DNA triplets in the codon table. The table lists mRNA codons.
- Counting the stop codon as an amino acid. A coding region of $n$ codons, start to stop, makes $n - 1$ amino acids.
- Saying ribosomes are made of protein only. rRNA forms the core and catalyzes peptide bonds.
- Thinking each gene makes exactly one protein. Alternative splicing lets one gene make several.

## Key points

- Central dogma: DNA → (transcription) → RNA → (translation) → protein.
- RNA has ribose, uracil instead of thymine, and is usually single-stranded; mRNA, tRNA and rRNA work together to make proteins.
- RNA polymerase starts at a promoter and builds an RNA complementary to the template strand. Eukaryotic RNA gets a cap and tail, and its introns are removed.
- The genetic code uses triplet codons: 64 codons, AUG = start (Met), three stops, redundant, unambiguous and nearly universal.
- tRNA anticodons pair with codons; the ribosome links amino acids in codon order from AUG to the stop codon.

lessons.title: Gene regulation and mutation
lessons.body:
Your skin cells and your nerve cells carry the same DNA, copied from the same fertilized egg. Yet one makes keratin and the other makes neurotransmitter receptors. The last lesson showed how a gene becomes a protein; this lesson asks when it does. Cells constantly decide which genes to express, and that control is what makes cell types different. The second half of the lesson looks at what happens when the DNA sequence itself changes.

## Why cells regulate genes

Making RNA and protein costs energy and raw materials. A bacterium that made every one of its roughly 4,000 proteins all the time would waste resources on enzymes it has no use for. A multicellular organism has a different problem: hundreds of cell types must each express the right set of genes, at the right time in development, in the right amount. Most regulation happens at the first step, transcription, because it is cheapest to not start making something you don't need.

## The lac operon: a switch in bacteria

The first gene switch to be understood was found by François Jacob and Jacques Monod in the bacterium *E. coli*, work that earned a Nobel Prize in 1965. *E. coli* prefers glucose, but it can live on lactose (milk sugar) if it has to. To use lactose it needs enzymes, including one that splits lactose into glucose and galactose. Those enzymes are made only when lactose is around.

In bacteria, genes that work together are often grouped into an **[[operon]]**: a cluster of genes controlled by a single promoter and transcribed together as one mRNA. The lac operon has:

- a promoter, where RNA polymerase binds;
- an operator, a short DNA sequence overlapping the promoter that acts as the on/off switch;
- three genes for lactose-handling enzymes, transcribed together.

A separate gene, always on, makes a **[[repressor]]** protein that binds the operator.
