questions.explanation: Two ATP release 61 kJ/mol, which is less than 70, so the total would still be uphill (+9 kJ/mol). Three ATP release 91.5 kJ/mol, giving −21.5 kJ/mol overall. Four would work but is not the smallest number.

questions.stem: Your body holds only about 50 g of ATP at any moment, yet it uses roughly its own body mass of ATP every day. Which explains this?
choices: Most ATP is stored in fat cells and released when needed.
ATP is constantly regenerated from ADP and phosphate.
ATP is absorbed directly from food in large amounts.
Each ATP molecule can be hydrolyzed many times without changing.
questions.explanation: ATP is a currency, not a store. Each molecule is hydrolyzed to ADP and recharged over and over, many times a day. Long-term energy is stored as fat and glycogen, not ATP. Once hydrolyzed, ATP is ADP until it is recharged.

questions.stem: In the reaction NAD⁺ + 2 electrons + H⁺ → NADH, the NAD⁺ is
choices: oxidized, because it gains electrons
reduced, because it loses electrons
oxidized, because it loses electrons
reduced, because it gains electrons
questions.explanation: Reduction is gain of electrons (OIL RIG: oxidation is loss, reduction is gain). NAD⁺ picks up two electrons and becomes NADH, the reduced, electron-carrying form. The molecule that gave up the electrons was oxidized.

questions.stem: Why do cells break glucose down in many small steps instead of one big reaction?
choices: So energy is released in small amounts that can be captured as ATP instead of lost as heat
Because a one-step reaction would release less total energy
Because a one-step reaction would create energy and break the first law
So that glucose can be broken down without any enzymes
questions.explanation: The total energy released is the same either way (a flame releases the same amount). Small steps let the cell trap the energy in usable packets (ATP, NADH) rather than releasing it all at once as heat. Each step needs its own enzyme, and no reaction creates energy.

questions.stem: Which are the raw materials (reactants) of photosynthesis?
choices: Glucose and oxygen
Oxygen and water
Carbon dioxide and water
Carbon dioxide and glucose
questions.explanation: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + light → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂. Glucose and oxygen are the products; they are the reactants of cellular respiration, which is why the two processes are often called reverses of each other.

questions.stem: Algae are given water whose oxygen atoms are the heavy isotope ¹⁸O, with ordinary CO₂. The O₂ gas they release contains ¹⁸O. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: The oxygen gas released in photosynthesis comes from carbon dioxide.
The oxygen gas comes equally from water and carbon dioxide.
The oxygen in glucose comes from water.
The oxygen gas released in photosynthesis comes from water.
questions.explanation: Only the water was labeled, and the label showed up in the O₂, so the O₂ comes from splitting water (Ruben and Kamen, 1941). The reverse experiment, labeling CO₂, gave unlabeled O₂. This experiment says nothing about glucose, whose oxygen actually comes from CO₂.

questions.stem: Van Helmont's willow gained about 164 pounds in five years while the soil lost only about 2 ounces. Where did most of the tree's added dry mass actually come from?
choices: Water absorbed by the roots
Carbon dioxide taken from the air
Minerals absorbed from the soil
Sunlight converted into matter
questions.explanation: Most of a plant's dry mass is carbon compounds built from CO₂ fixed in the Calvin cycle. Van Helmont credited the water, because he never measured the air. The soil loss shows minerals contribute very little, and light supplies energy, not matter.

questions.stem: In Priestley's experiments, a mouse in a sealed jar with a sprig of mint in the light survived much longer than a mouse in a sealed jar alone. The best explanation is that the mint
choices: released oxygen that the mouse used
absorbed oxygen that would have harmed the mouse
released carbon dioxide that the mouse needed
absorbed heat from the mouse's body
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis releases O₂, which the mouse uses in cellular respiration, and also takes up the CO₂ the mouse exhales. The mouse needs oxygen, not carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: Most leaves look green because chlorophyll
choices: absorbs green light more strongly than any other color
gives off green light when it is struck by sunlight
absorbs little green light and reflects it
absorbs green light and uses it most efficiently
questions.explanation: The color you see is the light that is not absorbed. Chlorophyll absorbs mostly blue-violet and red light, so green is reflected and transmitted to your eye.

questions.stem: Engelmann lit a strand of alga with a spectrum of colors. Oxygen-seeking bacteria gathered mostly along the parts lit by blue and red light. What did this show?
choices: Photosynthesis releases oxygen fastest in blue and red light.
The bacteria are attracted to blue and red light.
Green light drives photosynthesis fastest.
The alga has chlorophyll only in the blue- and red-lit sections.
questions.explanation: The bacteria were an oxygen detector: they crowded where O₂ was being released, so the rate of photosynthesis (the action spectrum) peaks in blue and red, matching chlorophyll's absorption. The bacteria respond to oxygen, not light, and chlorophyll runs along the whole strand.

questions.stem: Where in a chloroplast do the light-dependent reactions take place?
choices: In the stroma
In the outer chloroplast membrane
In the cytoplasm outside the chloroplast
In the thylakoid membranes
questions.explanation: Chlorophyll, the photosystems, the electron transport chain and ATP synthase are all in the thylakoid membranes. The stroma is where the Calvin cycle runs.

questions.stem: Which products of the light-dependent reactions are used to power the Calvin cycle?
choices: Oxygen and glucose
Carbon dioxide and water
ATP and NADPH
ADP and NADP⁺
questions.explanation: The light reactions charge up ATP and NADPH; the Calvin cycle spends them to reduce CO₂ to sugar and returns ADP and NADP⁺ to be recharged. O₂ is a by-product that leaves the leaf.

questions.stem: To make 2 molecules of glucose, how many CO₂, ATP, and NADPH does the Calvin cycle use?
choices: 6 CO₂, 18 ATP, 12 NADPH
12 CO₂, 36 ATP, 24 NADPH
12 CO₂, 24 ATP, 36 NADPH
2 CO₂, 6 ATP, 4 NADPH
questions.explanation: One glucose (6 carbons) needs 6 CO₂, 18 ATP and 12 NADPH, so two glucose need 12 CO₂, 36 ATP and 24 NADPH. The first choice is the amount for one glucose; the third swaps ATP and NADPH.

questions.stem: An Elodea sprig releases 36 bubbles of oxygen in 3 minutes. What is the rate of photosynthesis?
choices: 108 bubbles per minute
12 bubbles per minute
33 bubbles per minute
3 bubbles per minute
questions.explanation: Rate = bubbles ÷ time = 36 ÷ 3 = 12 bubbles per minute. Multiplying gives 108, subtracting gives 33.

questions.stem: A plant's rate of photosynthesis rises with light intensity and then levels off at a plateau. On the plateau, which change is most likely to increase the rate?
choices: Raising the light intensity further
Lowering the temperature to 5 °C
Removing some of the plant's leaves
Raising the carbon dioxide concentration
questions.explanation: On the plateau, light is no longer the limiting factor, so more light does nothing. Some other factor, often CO₂, is now limiting; raising it raises the plateau. Cold slows the Calvin cycle enzymes, and fewer leaves means less photosynthesis.

questions.stem: A plant is moved from bright light into darkness. Within seconds, the Calvin cycle slows to a stop. Why?
choices: Calvin cycle enzymes need to absorb light directly.
Carbon dioxide cannot enter leaves in the dark.
It runs out of the ATP and NADPH made by the light reactions.
Rubisco is destroyed as soon as light is removed.
questions.explanation: The Calvin cycle does not use light itself, but it depends on the ATP and NADPH that only the light reactions make. Once those run out, it stops. This is why "light-independent" is more accurate than "dark reactions."

questions.stem: In a eukaryotic cell, where do glycolysis, the Krebs cycle, and the electron transport chain take place, in that order?
choices: Cytoplasm; mitochondrial matrix; inner mitochondrial membrane
Mitochondrial matrix; cytoplasm; outer mitochondrial membrane
Cytoplasm; inner mitochondrial membrane; mitochondrial matrix
Inner mitochondrial membrane; mitochondrial matrix; cytoplasm
questions.explanation: Glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm, before pyruvate enters the mitochondrion. The Krebs cycle runs in the matrix, and the electron transport chain is built into the folded inner membrane (cristae), where the H⁺ gradient forms.

questions.stem: What is the net yield of glycolysis from one molecule of glucose?
choices: 2 ATP, 2 NADH, and 2 pyruvate
4 ATP, 2 NADH, and 2 pyruvate
2 ATP, 6 CO₂, and 2 pyruvate
30 ATP, 10 NADH, and 2 pyruvate
questions.explanation: Glycolysis makes 4 ATP but spends 2 in its investment phase, so the net is 2 ATP, plus 2 NADH and 2 pyruvate. No CO₂ is released in glycolysis; that happens in the mitochondrion. About 30 ATP is the total for all of respiration.

questions.stem: What is the role of oxygen in aerobic respiration?
choices: It combines with carbon from glucose to form carbon dioxide.
It splits glucose into two pyruvate molecules in glycolysis.
It becomes part of the ATP molecules made by ATP synthase.
It accepts electrons at the end of the electron transport chain, forming water.
questions.explanation: Oxygen is the final electron acceptor; it combines with electrons and H⁺ to make water, keeping the chain flowing. The CO₂ comes from the carbon in glucose during pyruvate oxidation and the Krebs cycle, and glycolysis needs no oxygen at all.

questions.stem: A person breathes oxygen gas labeled with the isotope ¹⁸O. In which product of respiration does the label appear?
choices: Carbon dioxide
Water
Glucose
ATP
questions.explanation: Inhaled O₂ accepts electrons at the end of the electron transport chain and becomes water. The oxygen atoms in exhaled CO₂ come from glucose and water, not from the O₂ you breathe, a common misconception.

questions.stem: Cyanide blocks the last protein of the electron transport chain, so electrons cannot be passed to oxygen. What is the most direct effect?
choices: Glycolysis stops immediately because it requires oxygen.
The Krebs cycle speeds up and makes extra ATP to compensate.
Oxygen use and ATP production by chemiosmosis both stop.
The cell starts producing more carbon dioxide.
questions.explanation: With the chain blocked, no H⁺ is pumped and no O₂ is used, so oxidative phosphorylation stops, and the cell loses most of its ATP supply. Glycolysis does not need oxygen, and the Krebs cycle soon stops too, because NADH cannot unload and NAD⁺ runs out.

questions.stem: Using about 2.5 ATP per NADH and 1.5 ATP per FADH₂, how many ATP are made from 10 NADH, 2 FADH₂, and 4 ATP made directly?
questions.explanation: 10 × 2.5 = 25, 2 × 1.5 = 3, and 25 + 3 + 4 = 32. Using the older values of 3 and 2 gives 30 + 4 + 4 = 38; 25 counts only the NADH; 29 forgets the 3 ATP from FADH₂.

questions.stem: Older textbooks say one glucose yields 36 to 38 ATP; current estimates are about 30 to 32. Why the difference?
choices: Cells today make less ATP than cells did when the books were written.
Older figures forgot to count the ATP made in glycolysis.
Older figures assumed 3 ATP per NADH and 2 per FADH₂; measurements show fewer.
Older figures included ATP made by photosynthesis.
questions.explanation: The difference comes from the conversion factors. The link between electron transport and ATP synthase is an H⁺ gradient, and measurements give about 2.5 and 1.5 ATP per NADH and FADH₂, not 3 and 2. Including glycolysis was never the issue, and cells have not changed.

questions.stem: What is the main function of fermentation?
choices: To regenerate NAD⁺ so that glycolysis can continue making ATP
To make about 30 extra ATP when oxygen is absent
To produce oxygen for the electron transport chain
To turn lactate into glucose for the Krebs cycle
questions.explanation: Without oxygen, NADH cannot unload in the electron transport chain and NAD⁺ runs out, which would stop glycolysis. Fermentation passes NADH's electrons to pyruvate, regenerating NAD⁺. It makes no ATP itself; all 2 ATP per glucose come from glycolysis.

questions.stem: Bread dough rises because the yeast in it
choices: release oxygen during photosynthesis
release carbon dioxide during alcoholic fermentation
release lactic acid gas during lactic acid fermentation
release water vapor during the Krebs cycle
questions.explanation: Alcoholic fermentation converts pyruvate to ethanol and CO₂; the CO₂ bubbles make the dough rise (the ethanol evaporates during baking). Yeast are fungi and cannot photosynthesize, and lactate is not a gas.

questions.stem: A culture of cells needs 300 ATP. Without oxygen (2 ATP per glucose), how many glucose molecules must it use?
questions.explanation: 300 ÷ 2 = 150 glucose. With oxygen, about 300 ÷ 30 = 10 would be enough. 600 multiplies instead of dividing; 15 is the ratio between the two methods.

questions.stem: How many grams of CO₂ are produced when 90 g of glucose is completely oxidized? (Glucose = 180 g/mol; CO₂ = 44 g/mol.)
questions.explanation: 90 g is 0.5 mol of glucose. Each mole makes 6 mol CO₂, so 3 mol × 44 g/mol = 132 g. 264 g is the amount from a full mole (180 g); 44 g is the mass of just one mole of CO₂; 90 g assumes the CO₂ weighs the same as the glucose.

questions.stem: A potted plant is kept in a sealed, dark container. The CO₂ level inside steadily rises. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: Plants photosynthesize faster in the dark.
Plants respire only when they cannot photosynthesize.
Plant cells carry out cellular respiration.
The plant is fixing CO₂ through the Calvin cycle.
questions.explanation: Rising CO₂ in the dark means the plant is releasing it by respiration. Plant cells respire all the time, day and night; in light, photosynthesis usually outpaces respiration so the plant takes up CO₂ overall. The data cannot show respiration stops in light, and fixing CO₂ would lower the level.

questions.stem: A day or two after a hard workout, your muscles ache. What is the best current explanation?
choices: Tiny injuries to muscle fibers and the repair process that follows
Lactic acid that stays in the muscles for several days
Muscles running out of ATP until the next meal
Muscle cells switching to alcoholic fermentation
questions.explanation: Lactate made during hard exercise is cleared from muscle within about an hour, so it cannot explain soreness days later. Delayed soreness comes from small injuries to muscle fibers and inflammation during repair. Human muscle cells use lactic acid fermentation, never alcoholic fermentation.

questions.stem: During which phase of the cell cycle is the DNA replicated?
choices: Prophase
G1 phase
Anaphase
S phase
questions.explanation: DNA is copied in the S (synthesis) phase of interphase, before mitosis begins. By prophase the chromosomes already consist of two sister chromatids. G1 is growth before copying; anaphase is when the copies separate.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes interphase?
choices: The cell rests and carries out almost no activity until it divides.
The nucleus divides and the chromosomes separate.
The cell grows, carries out its normal functions, and replicates its DNA.
The cytoplasm divides to form two daughter cells.
questions.explanation: Interphase (G1, S, G2) is the busiest part of the cycle: growth, normal work, and DNA replication. Calling it a resting phase is a common misconception. Dividing the nucleus is mitosis, and dividing the cytoplasm is cytokinesis.

questions.stem: A cell has 12 chromosomes in G1. How many chromosomes and chromatids does it have in G2?
choices: 24 chromosomes and 24 chromatids
12 chromosomes and 24 chromatids
12 chromosomes and 12 chromatids
6 chromosomes and 12 chromatids
questions.explanation: After S phase each chromosome has two sister chromatids joined at one centromere. It is still one chromosome, so the count stays 12, with 24 chromatids. Counting chromatids as chromosomes gives 24; halving is what meiosis does, not interphase.

questions.stem: A human body cell (46 chromosomes) is in anaphase of mitosis. How many chromosomes are in the whole cell at this moment?
questions.explanation: In anaphase the 46 pairs of sister chromatids separate, and each chromatid now counts as a chromosome: 92 in the cell, 46 moving to each pole. After cytokinesis each daughter cell has 46.

questions.stem: Chromosomes are lined up along the middle of the cell, each attached to spindle fibers from both poles. Which stage is this?
choices: Prophase
Anaphase
Telophase
Metaphase
questions.explanation: Lining up at the middle (the metaphase plate) defines metaphase. In prophase the chromosomes are still condensing, in anaphase the chromatids are moving apart, and in telophase they have reached the poles.

questions.stem: Which sequence lists the stages of mitosis in order?
choices: Metaphase, prophase, anaphase, telophase
Prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase
Prophase, anaphase, metaphase, telophase
Interphase, prophase, telophase, anaphase
questions.explanation: Chromosomes condense (prophase), line up (metaphase), separate (anaphase), and arrive at the poles as new nuclei form (telophase). Interphase is not part of mitosis.

questions.stem: Why do plant cells form a cell plate during cytokinesis instead of a cleavage furrow?
choices: Plant cells do not have a cell membrane to pinch.
Plant cells divide only by binary fission.
Their rigid cell wall prevents the cell from pinching in two.
The cell plate is needed to separate the sister chromatids.
questions.explanation: A plant cell is enclosed by a stiff wall, so it builds a new wall from the middle outward instead of pinching. Plant cells do have membranes, binary fission is the prokaryote process, and the chromatids are already separated in anaphase.

questions.stem: In a root tip sample of 300 cells, 24 are in some stage of mitosis. What is the mitotic index?
questions.explanation: Mitotic index = 24 ÷ 300 × 100% = 8%. Dividing by the 276 non-dividing cells gives 8.7%; 92% is the share in interphase; 24% treats the count as a percent.

questions.stem: In an unsynchronized sample of 400 cells, 20 are in metaphase. The full cell cycle takes 20 hours. About how long does metaphase last?
choices: 20 minutes
5 minutes
60 minutes
6 hours
questions.explanation: The fraction of cells in a stage equals the fraction of time spent in it: 20 ÷ 400 = 0.05, and 0.05 × 20 h = 1 h = 60 minutes.

questions.stem: Compared with the parent cell, the two daughter cells produced by mitosis are
choices: genetically identical, with the same number of chromosomes
genetically identical, with half the number of chromosomes
genetically different, with the same number of chromosomes
genetically different, with half the number of chromosomes
questions.explanation: Mitosis gives each daughter cell one copy of every chromosome, so they match the parent in number and genes (apart from rare copying errors). Halving the number and creating genetic differences are features of meiosis.

questions.stem: A graph of DNA content per cell shows the amount rising steadily from 1 unit to 2 units over several hours, then staying at 2 until it suddenly drops back to 1. The rising section corresponds to
choices: G1 phase
S phase
Anaphase
Cytokinesis
questions.explanation: DNA content doubles gradually as it is replicated in S phase. G1 holds steady at 1 unit, and the sudden drop back to 1 is cell division (cytokinesis), when the DNA is split between two cells.

questions.stem: In onion roots, the mitotic index is 15% in the region just behind the tip and 2% in a region farther back. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: Cells near the tip spend more time in interphase.
Cells farther back have more chromosomes.
Mitosis takes longer in cells farther back.
Cells near the tip are dividing much more actively.
questions.explanation: A higher mitotic index means a larger share of cells are dividing, as expected in the growth zone near a root tip. More time in interphase would lower the index. The index says nothing about chromosome number, and a slower mitosis would raise the index, not lower it.

questions.stem: What does the spindle (metaphase) checkpoint check before allowing anaphase to begin?
choices: That the cell has grown large enough to divide
That the DNA has been replicated
That every chromosome is attached to spindle fibers from both poles
That growth factors are present outside the cell
questions.explanation: The spindle checkpoint delays anaphase until all chromosomes are correctly attached, so each daughter gets one copy of each. Cell size and growth factors are checked at G1, and completion of DNA replication at G2.

questions.stem: When a cell in S phase was fused with a cell in G1, the G1 nucleus began replicating its DNA early. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: DNA can be copied only when two nuclei share one cell.
The cytoplasm of the S-phase cell contains signals that trigger DNA replication.
The G1 nucleus had already finished G1 before the fusion.
Cell fusion damages DNA, which triggers replication.
questions.explanation: The G1 nucleus was pushed into S phase ahead of schedule by something in the S-phase cell, pointing to chemical signals in the cytoplasm (later identified as cyclin–CDK complexes). Single-nucleus cells copy DNA normally, and damage halts the cycle rather than speeding it up.

questions.stem: How do cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) behave during the cell cycle?
choices: CDK levels rise and fall; cyclins stay constant and are always active.
Both are made only during mitosis and destroyed during interphase.
Cyclins are made once in the life of a cell and never broken down.
Cyclin levels rise and fall; CDKs stay fairly constant but are active only when bound to cyclin.
questions.explanation: Cyclins are made and destroyed each cycle (hence the name). CDKs are present all the time but act only when a cyclin binds; destroying the cyclin switches the CDK off. This rise and fall times the transitions of the cycle.

questions.stem: A mutation leaves the RAS protein, which relays "divide" signals from growth factors, permanently switched on. This mutation has changed
choices: a proto-oncogene into an oncogene
a tumor suppressor gene into an oncogene
an oncogene into a proto-oncogene
a proto-oncogene into a tumor suppressor gene
questions.explanation: RAS is a normal gas-pedal gene (a proto-oncogene). An overactive, stuck-on version is an oncogene, and one mutated copy is enough. Tumor suppressor genes are brakes, and cancer involves their loss, not their creation.

questions.stem: Cells that have lost both working copies of the p53 gene are exposed to DNA-damaging radiation. What is the most likely result, compared with normal cells?
choices: The cells repair their DNA faster than normal cells.
The cells stop dividing permanently and enter G0.
Damaged cells keep dividing and pass on mutations instead of stopping or undergoing apoptosis.
The cells are unaffected because p53 only works during mitosis.
questions.explanation: p53 halts the cycle at G1 when DNA is damaged and triggers apoptosis if repair fails. Without it, damaged cells keep dividing and mutations accumulate, which is why p53 is mutated in about half of human cancers.

questions.stem: Children with inherited retinoblastoma often develop tumors in both eyes at a young age. Knudson's two-hit explanation is that these children
choices: inherit one damaged copy of a tumor suppressor gene, so a single new mutation in a cell is enough
inherit two damaged copies of an oncogene, so no new mutations are needed
inherit an oncogene that only becomes active in the eyes
are exposed to more ultraviolet light than other children
questions.explanation: Both copies of the RB tumor suppressor gene must be lost. Inherited cases start with one bad copy in every cell, so one more hit in any retinal cell is enough, making tumors earlier and more numerous. Non-inherited cases need two hits in the same cell.

questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes a malignant tumor from a benign tumor?
choices: Its cells divide more than normal cells.
It forms a mass of abnormal cells.
It begins from a single abnormal cell.
Its cells can invade nearby tissue and spread to other parts of the body.
questions.explanation: Both kinds of tumor are masses of abnormally dividing cells that started from one cell. Only malignant tumors invade and metastasize, and metastasis causes most cancer deaths.

questions.stem: Starting from one cell, about how many cells are there after 20 doublings?
choices: About 1 million
About 1 billion
questions.explanation: 2²⁰ = 1,048,576, about a million. Since 2¹⁰ ≈ 1000, 20 doublings give about 1000 × 1000. 40 is 2 × 20 (adding instead of multiplying), and about a billion takes 30 doublings.

questions.stem: Tumor cells in a dish increase from 500 to 8,000 in 48 hours. What is their doubling time?
choices: 12 hours
16 hours
3 hours
6 hours
questions.explanation: 8000 ÷ 500 = 16 = 2⁴, so there were 4 doublings, and 48 ÷ 4 = 12 hours. Using 16 as the number of doublings gives 3 hours; 16 hours assumes 3 doublings.

questions.stem: Why does the risk of most cancers increase with age?
choices: Older cells stop having checkpoints entirely.
Cancer is caused by a single mutation that appears at a set age.
Several mutations must build up in the same cell line, and that takes time.
Older people have more cells, so each cell divides faster.
questions.explanation: Most cancers need multiple mutations in proto-oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes, so the chance that one cell has collected enough rises the longer we live. A single mutation is almost never enough, and checkpoints do not simply switch off with age.

questions.stem: Which statement about stem cells is correct?
choices: Adult stem cells are pluripotent, while embryonic stem cells are multipotent.
Embryonic stem cells are pluripotent, while most adult stem cells are multipotent.
Stem cells cannot divide; they only differentiate.
Induced pluripotent stem cells are taken directly from early embryos.
questions.explanation: Embryonic stem cells can become any body cell type (pluripotent); adult stem cells, such as blood stem cells, make a limited range (multipotent). Stem cells self-renew by dividing. iPSCs are reprogrammed body cells, such as skin cells, which is why they avoid using embryos.

questions.stem: Chemotherapy often causes hair loss and damage to the lining of the gut. Why?
choices: Cancer cells move into the hair follicles and gut during treatment.
The drugs act only on cells in G0.
Hair and gut cells are the source of most cancers.
Many chemotherapy drugs target rapidly dividing cells, including normal ones.
questions.explanation: Hair follicles and the gut lining divide rapidly, like cancer cells, so drugs that attack dividing cells harm them too. Cells in G0 are not dividing, so they are largely spared.

questions.stem: Mature nerve cells in the brain almost never divide. In which part of the cell cycle do they remain?
choices: S phase
G2
G0
Metaphase
questions.explanation: Cells that leave the cycle after G1 and stop dividing are in G0. They are fully active, just not dividing. S, G2 and metaphase are all stages on the way to division.

questions.stem: Human body cells have 46 chromosomes. How many chromosomes does a normal human egg cell have?
questions.explanation: Gametes are haploid: n = 23, one from each homologous pair. Fertilization restores 2n = 46. 22 is the number of autosomes in a gamete, leaving out the sex chromosome.

questions.stem: How do homologous chromosomes differ from sister chromatids?
choices: Homologs are identical copies; sister chromatids come from different parents.
Homologs carry different genes; sister chromatids carry the same genes.
There is no difference; the terms mean the same thing.
Homologs come from different parents and may carry different versions of genes; sister chromatids are identical copies.
questions.explanation: One homolog came from each parent; they carry the same genes in the same order but possibly different versions. Sister chromatids are made by copying one chromosome in S phase, so they are identical (before crossing over).

questions.stem: What separates during anaphase I of meiosis?
choices: Sister chromatids, while homologous chromosomes stay together
Homologous chromosomes, while sister chromatids stay together
Both homologous chromosomes and sister chromatids
Nothing; the cell divides without separating chromosomes
questions.explanation: Anaphase I pulls homologs to opposite poles; sister chromatids stay joined until anaphase II. This is what halves the chromosome number, and it is the key difference from mitosis, where sister chromatids separate.

questions.stem: During which stage does crossing over occur?
choices: Prophase I
Metaphase II
Anaphase I
Telophase II
questions.explanation: Crossing over happens when homologs are paired closely along their length, which is in prophase I. By anaphase I they are already separating, and in meiosis II homologs are no longer together.

questions.stem: A species has 2n = 10. Ignoring crossing over, how many genetically different gametes can independent assortment produce?
questions.explanation: There are n = 5 pairs, each able to line up 2 ways: 2⁵ = 32. 10 is 2 × 5 (multiplying instead of raising 2 to the 5th power); 25 is 5²; 1024 is 2¹⁰, using 2n instead of n.

questions.stem: A fruit fly has 2n = 8. Ignoring crossing over, how many different chromosome combinations are possible in a zygote produced by two flies?
questions.explanation: Each parent can make 2⁴ = 16 kinds of gametes, and any egg can meet any sperm: 16 × 16 = 256. 16 counts gametes from one parent only; 64 is 8 × 8 (using 2n = 8 as the number of gamete types), and 32 adds 16 + 16 instead of multiplying.

questions.stem: A cell with 2n = 20 completes meiosis I. What does each resulting cell contain?
choices: 10 chromosomes, each made of 1 chromatid
10 chromosomes, each made of 2 chromatids
20 chromosomes, each made of 2 chromatids
20 chromosomes, each made of 1 chromatid
questions.explanation: Meiosis I separates homologs, halving the number to 10, but the sister chromatids stay together until meiosis II. There is no DNA replication between the two divisions, so the gametes end up with 10 single-chromatid chromosomes.

questions.stem: One homologous pair fails to separate in meiosis I, but meiosis II is normal. What are the four gametes?
choices: Two with an extra chromosome (n + 1) and two missing one (n − 1)
Two normal, one n + 1, and one n − 1
All four normal
Four with an extra chromosome (n + 1)
questions.explanation: Both homologs go to one cell in meiosis I, so that cell's two products each get an extra copy and the other cell's two products each lack it. Nondisjunction in meiosis II instead gives two normal gametes, one n + 1 and one n − 1.

questions.stem: Which is true of meiosis but not of mitosis?
choices: Sister chromatids separate at an anaphase.
The DNA is replicated beforehand, during S phase.
A spindle moves the chromosomes.
Homologous chromosomes pair up and exchange segments.
questions.explanation: Pairing of homologs (synapsis) and crossing over happen only in prophase I of meiosis. Sister chromatids separate in mitosis and in meiosis II, DNA replicates before both, and both use a spindle.

questions.stem: Van Beneden found that in a roundworm, the egg nucleus and sperm nucleus each contributed 2 chromosomes and the fertilized egg had 4. What did this support?
choices: Sperm contribute more chromosomes than eggs.
Chromosome number doubles in every generation.
Gametes carry half the chromosome number of body cells.
Only the egg passes chromosomes to the offspring.
questions.explanation: Each gamete brought half of the zygote's number, and the two halves added up to the body-cell number. This pointed to a reduction division (meiosis) that keeps the chromosome number constant across generations.

questions.stem: Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) usually results from
choices: crossing over between chromosome 21 and its homolog
nondisjunction, producing a gamete with an extra chromosome 21
a mutation in a single gene on chromosome 21
a gamete that is missing chromosome 21
questions.explanation: If chromosome 21 fails to separate in meiosis, a gamete gets two copies; after fertilization the zygote has three (47 chromosomes). Crossing over is normal and does not change chromosome number, and a missing chromosome would give 45, not 47.

questions.stem: How does meiosis in females differ from meiosis in males?
choices: Females make four eggs per meiosis; males make one sperm.
Females skip meiosis II, so eggs are diploid.
Only males use crossing over during meiosis.
Females make one egg and small polar bodies per meiosis; males make four sperm.
questions.explanation: Unequal division of the cytoplasm gives one large egg (keeping stored nutrients) plus polar bodies that break down, while each male meiosis gives four sperm. Both sexes complete both divisions, and crossing over happens in both.

questions.stem: Mendel crossed true-breeding purple-flowered peas with true-breeding white-flowered peas. Every F1 plant was purple, yet about one quarter of the F2 plants were white. What best explains this?
choices: The F1 plants carried the white allele, but it was masked by the dominant purple allele
The white allele was destroyed in the F1 and re-created by mutation in the F2
The purple and white factors blended in the F1 and separated again in the F2
Environmental conditions in the F2 year turned some purple plants white
questions.explanation: The F1 plants were Pp: the p allele was present but hidden because P is dominant. When two Pp plants were crossed, pp offspring appeared in about 1/4 of the F2. Mutation is far too rare to give a steady 1/4. Blending would make the F1 an intermediate color and could not bring back pure white.

questions.stem: In pea plants, purple flowers (P) are dominant to white (p). Two Pp plants are crossed. What fraction of the offspring are expected to have white flowers?
questions.explanation: Each parent gives p with probability 1/2, and a white plant (pp) needs p from both: $\tfrac12 \times \tfrac12 = \tfrac14$. 3/4 is the purple fraction; 1/2 is the heterozygous fraction; 1/16 belongs to a two-gene cross.

questions.stem: What is the expected genotype ratio among the offspring of Aa × Aa?
choices: 3 AA : 1 aa
1 AA : 1 aa
1 AA : 1 Aa : 2 aa
1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa
questions.explanation: The Punnett square has four equal boxes: AA, Aa, aA and aa, so 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa. The 3 : 1 ratio is the phenotype ratio (AA and Aa look the same), not the genotype ratio.

questions.stem: A tall pea plant (T is dominant to t for dwarf) is crossed with a dwarf plant. Of 60 offspring, 31 are tall and 29 are dwarf. What is the genotype of the tall parent?
choices: TT
tt
Tt
It cannot be determined from a test cross
questions.explanation: This is a test cross: the dwarf parent (tt) gives only t. Dwarf offspring (tt) must have received t from the tall parent as well, so it is Tt, and Tt × tt predicts 1 tall : 1 dwarf, matching 31 : 29. A TT parent would give only tall offspring; a tt parent would not be tall.

questions.stem: What kinds of gametes does an Aa individual produce?
choices: Every gamete carries both A and a
Half carry AA and half carry aa
Half carry A and half carry a
All carry A, because A is dominant
questions.explanation: By the law of segregation, the two alleles separate into different gametes, each gamete gets one allele, and the two types are equally common. A gamete never carries two alleles of the same gene. Dominance affects the phenotype, not which allele gets into a gamete.

questions.stem: Which pair of pea plants have the same phenotype but different genotypes? (Purple, P, is dominant to white, p.)
choices: PP and pp
Pp and pp
pp and pp
PP and Pp
questions.explanation: PP and Pp both have purple flowers because one P allele is enough. PP and pp, and Pp and pp, differ in phenotype (purple vs white). Two pp plants have the same genotype.

questions.stem: Which statement about dominant alleles is correct?
choices: A dominant allele is always the most common allele in a population
A dominant allele shows its effect even in a heterozygote
A dominant allele is always better for survival
A dominant allele is passed to offspring more often than a recessive one
questions.explanation: Dominant only describes how alleles interact in a heterozygote. It says nothing about frequency (the dominant allele for Huntington's disease is rare), benefit, or how often it is inherited: a heterozygote passes each allele with probability 1/2.

questions.stem: What event in meiosis is the physical basis of Mendel's law of segregation?
choices: Homologous chromosomes separating in anaphase I
DNA replicating during the S phase
Sister chromatids separating in mitosis
Crossing over between homologous chromosomes in prophase I
questions.explanation: The two alleles of a gene sit on the two homologous chromosomes, and homologs go to opposite poles in anaphase I, so each gamete gets one allele. Replication copies alleles rather than separating them, mitosis doesn't make gametes, and crossing over swaps segments between homologs but doesn't separate the allele pair.

questions.stem: Mendel's F2 plants for stem length were 787 tall and 277 dwarf. What does this result suggest about the F1 plants that were crossed to produce them?
choices: They were TT × tt
Both were heterozygous, Tt × Tt
They were Tt × tt
They were TT × Tt
questions.explanation: 787/277 is about 2.84 : 1, close to the 3 : 1 expected from Tt × Tt. Tt × tt gives 1 : 1, TT × tt and TT × Tt give only tall offspring.

questions.stem: In the offspring of Pp × Pp, what fraction of the purple-flowered plants are heterozygous?
questions.explanation: Purple plants fill 3 of the 4 Punnett boxes (PP, Pp, Pp), and 2 of those 3 are Pp, so 2/3. The answer 1/2 is the fraction of all offspring that are Pp; here the white plants are excluded.

questions.stem: Two Aa parents have three children, all with the dominant phenotype. What is the probability that their fourth child has the recessive phenotype?
questions.explanation: Each fertilization is independent, so the earlier children don't change the odds: P(aa) = 1/4 for every child. Expecting the recessive child to be "due" is the gambler's fallacy; 1/256 is the chance that all four children are aa.

questions.stem: In guinea pigs, black fur (B) is dominant to white (b). A Bb guinea pig is crossed with a bb guinea pig, and 120 offspring are produced over several litters. About how many are expected to be white?
questions.explanation: Bb × bb gives 1/2 Bb (black) and 1/2 bb (white), so expect $\tfrac12 \times 120 = 60$ white. 30 uses 1/4 (as if it were Bb × Bb); 90 is the 3/4 dominant fraction of that cross.

questions.stem: Which gametes can an AaBb individual produce, assuming the two genes assort independently?
choices: Aa and Bb, each 1/2 of the gametes
Only AB and ab, each 1/2 of the gametes
AA, BB, aa and bb, each 1/4 of the gametes
AB, Ab, aB and ab, each 1/4 of the gametes
questions.explanation: Each gamete gets one allele of each gene. A or a (1/2 each) combines independently with B or b (1/2 each), giving four types at $\tfrac12 \times \tfrac12 = \tfrac14$. Aa or AA would put two alleles of one gene in a gamete; only AB and ab would mean the genes are completely linked.

questions.stem: Round (R) is dominant to wrinkled (r) and yellow (Y) is dominant to green (y). In the cross RrYy × RrYy, what fraction of offspring have round, green seeds?
questions.explanation: Gene by gene: P(round) = 3/4 from Rr × Rr, P(green) = 1/4 from Yy × Yy. Product rule: $\tfrac34 \times \tfrac14 = \tfrac{3}{16}$. 9/16 is round and yellow; 1/16 is wrinkled and green.

questions.stem: Mendel's RrYy × RrYy cross gave 315 round-yellow, 108 round-green, 101 wrinkled-yellow and 32 wrinkled-green seeds. Which conclusion do these data support?
choices: The two genes are always inherited together as a unit
The seed-shape and seed-color genes assort independently
The traits blend together in the offspring
Alleles of the seed-color gene do not segregate
questions.explanation: All four combinations appear, close to 9 : 3 : 3 : 1, including the new combinations round-green and wrinkled-yellow. If the genes traveled together, only the parental types would appear (3 : 1). The traits come back in pure form, so there is no blending, and each gene alone still shows 3 : 1, so segregation holds.

questions.stem: In the cross AaBbCc × AaBbCc (three unlinked genes), what is the probability of an aabbcc offspring?
questions.explanation: Each gene gives the homozygous recessive genotype with probability 1/4, and the genes are independent, so $\left(\tfrac14\right)^3 = \tfrac{1}{64}$. 1/8 uses 1/2 per gene (the chance of one recessive allele from one parent).

questions.stem: An RrYy plant is test-crossed with an rryy plant. What phenotype ratio is expected in the offspring?
questions.explanation: RrYy makes RY, Ry, rY and ry gametes equally; rryy adds only ry. Each gamete type from the heterozygote therefore produces its own phenotype, in equal numbers: 1 : 1 : 1 : 1. 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 is for two double heterozygotes.

questions.stem: What is the probability that an offspring of Aa × Aa is homozygous (either AA or aa)?
questions.explanation: AA and aa are mutually exclusive outcomes, so use the sum rule: $\tfrac14 + \tfrac14 = \tfrac12$. Multiplying them (1/16) is the product-rule mistake; "either … or" adds.

questions.stem: How many genetically different kinds of gametes can an individual with genotype AaBBCcDd produce, if all four genes are unlinked?
questions.explanation: Only heterozygous genes double the number of gamete types: A/a, C/c and D/d are heterozygous and BB always gives B, so $2^3 = 8$. 16 would treat BB as heterozygous.

questions.stem: Two parents are carriers (Aa) of a recessive condition. If they have two children, what is the probability that exactly one child has the condition?
questions.explanation: Affected then unaffected: $\tfrac14 \times \tfrac34 = \tfrac{3}{16}$. Unaffected then affected: also 3/16. These orders are mutually exclusive, so add: $\tfrac{6}{16} = \tfrac38$. Stopping at 3/16 counts only one order.

questions.stem: In the cross AaBbCc × aabbCc (unlinked genes, complete dominance), what fraction of offspring show the dominant phenotype for all three genes?
questions.explanation: Aa × aa: dominant phenotype 1/2. Bb × bb: 1/2. Cc × Cc: 3/4. Product: $\tfrac12 \times \tfrac12 \times \tfrac34 = \tfrac{3}{16}$. 27/64 would be correct for AaBbCc × AaBbCc, not for this cross.

questions.stem: Which event in meiosis explains Mendel's law of independent assortment?
choices: Sister chromatids separate at anaphase II
DNA is copied before meiosis begins
Each pair of homologous chromosomes lines up at metaphase I independently of the other pairs
The cytoplasm divides at the end of telophase II
questions.explanation: Whether the chromosome with R goes to the same pole as the chromosome with Y or the one with y depends on how the two pairs happen to orient at metaphase I, and each pair orients at random. The other events occur in meiosis but don't determine which alleles of different genes end up together.

questions.stem: A test cross AaBb × aabb gives mostly AaBb and aabb offspring and only a few Aabb and aaBb offspring. What is the best explanation?
choices: Genes A and B are close together on the same chromosome
A and B show incomplete dominance
The genes assort independently
Nondisjunction occurred in every meiosis
questions.explanation: Independent assortment predicts 1 : 1 : 1 : 1. An excess of the parental combinations means the alleles A and B (and a and b) tend to stay together: the genes are linked. The rare recombinant offspring come from crossing over between them. Incomplete dominance changes phenotypes, not how alleles are packaged.

questions.stem: Round (R) is dominant to wrinkled and yellow (Y) is dominant to green. In the cross RrYy × Rryy, what fraction of offspring have round, yellow seeds?
questions.explanation: Rr × Rr gives round 3/4; Yy × yy gives yellow 1/2. Product: $\tfrac34 \times \tfrac12 = \tfrac38$. 9/16 assumes a 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 cross, but one parent is yy.

questions.stem: Red snapdragons crossed with white snapdragons give all pink offspring. If two of the pink plants are crossed, what phenotype ratio is expected?
choices: 3 pink : 1 white
All pink
1 red : 2 pink : 1 white
3 red : 1 white
questions.explanation: Pink is the heterozygote $C^RC^W$. Crossing two heterozygotes gives 1 $C^RC^R$ : 2 $C^RC^W$ : 1 $C^WC^W$, and with incomplete dominance each genotype has its own color. 3 : 1 would apply only if one allele were fully dominant; all pink is what blending would predict.

questions.stem: A red bull and a white cow produce a roan calf whose coat is a mixture of individual red hairs and individual white hairs. This is an example of
choices: codominance
incomplete dominance
epistasis
polygenic inheritance
questions.explanation: Both alleles are fully expressed side by side: each hair is pure red or pure white. Incomplete dominance would give hairs of an intermediate color. Epistasis involves two genes, and polygenic traits vary continuously.

questions.stem: A woman with type A blood and a man with type B blood have a child with type O blood. What are the parents' genotypes?
choices: Mother $I^AI^A$, father $I^BI^B$
Mother $I^Ai$, father $I^Bi$
Mother $I^Ai$, father $I^BI^B$
Mother $ii$, father $ii$
questions.explanation: A type O child is $ii$ and must have received $i$ from each parent, so both parents carry $i$: $I^Ai$ and $I^Bi$. Parents who are $ii$ would themselves be type O.

questions.stem: A parent with type AB blood ($I^AI^B$) and a parent with type O blood ($ii$) have children. Which blood types are possible among their children?
choices: AB and O only
A, B, AB and O
A, B and O
A and B only
questions.explanation: The AB parent gives $I^A$ or $I^B$; the O parent gives only $i$. Children are $I^Ai$ (type A) or $I^Bi$ (type B), each with probability 1/2. Neither AB (needs both $I^A$ and $I^B$) nor O (needs two $i$ alleles) is possible.

questions.stem: With the three ABO alleles $I^A$, $I^B$ and $i$, how many different genotypes are possible?
questions.explanation: Three homozygotes ($I^AI^A$, $I^BI^B$, $ii$) plus three heterozygotes ($I^AI^B$, $I^Ai$, $I^Bi$) make 6. Four is the number of blood types (phenotypes), because $I^AI^A$ and $I^Ai$ both give type A and $I^BI^B$ and $I^Bi$ both give type B.

questions.stem: Why can type O red blood cells be transfused into a patient with type A blood?
choices: Type O blood contains no antibodies at all
Type O red cells carry the A antigen, which matches the patient
Type O red cells carry neither the A nor the B antigen, so the patient's anti-B antibodies have nothing to attack
The $i$ allele is dominant to $I^A$
questions.explanation: The danger in a transfusion is the patient's antibodies attacking antigens on donor red cells. A type A patient has anti-B antibodies, and type O cells have no A or B antigen. Type O plasma actually contains both anti-A and anti-B antibodies, and $i$ is recessive.

questions.stem: A child has type O blood and the mother has type A. Which man could NOT be the child's biological father, judging by ABO type alone?
choices: A man with type AB
A man with type A
A man with type B
A man with type O
questions.explanation: The child is $ii$ and needs an $i$ allele from the father. A type AB man is $I^AI^B$ and has no $i$ to give. Men with type A or B may be $I^Ai$ or $I^Bi$, and a type O man is $ii$. Blood type can exclude a man but never prove he is the father.

questions.stem: Human adult height varies continuously and forms a bell-shaped distribution. What is the best explanation?
choices: One gene with two alleles shows complete dominance
One gene with many alleles is codominant
Height is determined by the environment alone
Many genes each add a small effect, and the environment adds further variation
questions.explanation: Height is polygenic: many genes with small additive effects produce many genotype classes, and nutrition and health blur them into a smooth curve. A single gene with complete dominance would give two distinct classes.

questions.stem: In a model where three unlinked genes each have an additive allele (A, B, C), what fraction of the offspring of AaBbCc × AaBbCc carry exactly three additive alleles?
questions.explanation: The six allele positions each get an additive allele with probability 1/2, so the count follows the 1 : 6 : 15 : 20 : 15 : 6 : 1 pattern out of 64. Exactly three: $\tfrac{20}{64} = \tfrac{5}{16}$. 1/64 is the fraction with all six (or none).

questions.stem: A single allele causes sickle-shaped red blood cells, anemia, episodes of pain and organ damage, and in carriers some resistance to malaria. One gene affecting many traits is called
choices: epistasis
codominance
polygenic inheritance
pleiotropy
questions.explanation: Pleiotropy means one gene influences several traits. Epistasis is one gene masking another gene; polygenic inheritance is the opposite situation, many genes affecting one trait.

questions.stem: In Labrador retrievers, B (black) is dominant to b (chocolate), but any dog that is ee is yellow regardless of its B gene. Two BbEe dogs are mated. What fraction of their puppies are expected to be yellow?
questions.explanation: A puppy is yellow whenever it is ee, which has probability 1/4 from Ee × Ee, whatever the B genotype. The full ratio is 9 black : 3 chocolate : 4 yellow. 3/16 is the chocolate fraction ($\tfrac14$ bb × $\tfrac34$ not ee).

questions.stem: Himalayan rabbits are white with dark ears, nose and paws. If a patch of white back fur is shaved and the skin kept cold with an ice pack, the fur grows back dark. What is the best conclusion?
choices: Cold temperatures cause a mutation in the fur-color gene
The pigment enzyme works only at low temperature, so the environment affects the phenotype
Dark fur is a polygenic trait
The dark allele is dominant only on the ears and paws
questions.explanation: The rabbit's genotype didn't change; the same genes produced dark fur where the skin was cooler. This shows an environmental effect on gene expression. A mutation would not appear reliably wherever cold is applied.

questions.stem: Why are X-linked recessive conditions such as hemophilia A much more common in males than in females?
choices: The Y chromosome carries a dominant allele that causes the condition
Males inherit their X chromosome from their father
Recessive alleles are dominant in males
Males have one X chromosome, so a single recessive allele is expressed
questions.explanation: A male has only one copy of each X-linked gene, so whatever allele it carries shows. A female needs a recessive allele on both X chromosomes. Males inherit their X from their mother, and the Y carries no allele for these genes.

questions.stem: A woman who is a carrier for hemophilia A ($X^HX^h$) and a man without hemophilia ($X^HY$) have a son. What is the probability that the son has hemophilia?
questions.explanation: A son gets Y from his father and one of his mother's X chromosomes, $X^H$ or $X^h$, with equal probability, so 1/2. The answer 1/4 is the probability that a child of unknown sex is an affected son.

questions.stem: A color-blind man ($X^bY$) and a woman who is homozygous for normal vision ($X^BX^B$) have children. Which describes their daughters?
choices: All are carriers with normal vision
All are color-blind
Half are color-blind and half are carriers
Half are carriers and half are $X^BX^B$
questions.explanation: Every daughter receives her father's only X, $X^b$, and an $X^B$ from her mother, so all are $X^BX^b$: normal vision, carriers. None can be color-blind, because the mother has no $X^b$ to give.

questions.stem: A man with an X-linked recessive condition has a son. Why can't the son inherit the condition from his father?
choices: The allele is recessive, so it is masked in all sons
A father passes his Y chromosome, not his X, to every son
X-linked alleles are passed only to daughters by mothers
Sons inherit both sex chromosomes from their mother
questions.explanation: A child is male because he got his father's Y, so his single X came from his mother. The father's X goes to every daughter instead. Sons get only one sex chromosome from their mother, not both.

questions.stem: In a pedigree, two parents who do not have a condition have a daughter who does. Which inheritance pattern fits?
choices: Autosomal dominant
Autosomal recessive
X-linked recessive
Y-linked
questions.explanation: A dominant condition would require an affected parent. An X-linked recessive daughter needs an $X^a$ from her father, who would then be affected. Y-linked traits never appear in daughters. So both parents are carriers of an autosomal recessive allele.

questions.stem: Two unaffected carrier parents (Aa × Aa) have a child with an autosomal recessive condition and also an unaffected son. What is the probability that this unaffected son is a carrier?
questions.explanation: The son is not aa, so only three Punnett boxes remain possible: AA, Aa, aA. Two of the three are carriers: 2/3. The value 1/2 is the carrier probability for a child whose phenotype is not yet known.

questions.stem: In a standard pedigree, what does a filled-in square represent?
choices: A female who has the trait
A male who is a carrier
A male who does not have the trait
A male who has the trait
questions.explanation: Squares are males and circles females; a filled symbol means the person has the trait. Carriers, when shown, are marked with a dot or a half-filled symbol, and an open square is an unaffected male.

questions.stem: Morgan crossed a white-eyed male fruit fly with a red-eyed female. The F1 were all red-eyed, and in the F2 every white-eyed fly was male. What did he conclude?
choices: The eye-color gene is on the X chromosome
White eyes are dominant in males
The eye-color gene is on the Y chromosome
Eye color is a polygenic trait
questions.explanation: F2 sons get their only X from their carrier mother, so half are white-eyed, while daughters all get the father's red-eye X. A Y-linked gene would pass from father to all sons and appear in the F1 males. The all-red F1 shows white is recessive.

questions.stem: A color-blind woman ($X^bX^b$) and a man with normal vision ($X^BY$) have a son. What is the probability that he is color-blind?
questions.explanation: A son's X comes from his mother, and every X she has carries $b$. So every son is $X^bY$ and color-blind. (Every daughter is an $X^BX^b$ carrier.)

questions.stem: In a family, two parents who both have a condition have a child who does not. Which inheritance pattern is consistent with this?
choices: Autosomal recessive
X-linked recessive
Y-linked
Autosomal dominant
questions.explanation: Two affected parents can each be Aa for a dominant condition and have an aa child. For an autosomal recessive condition, two aa parents can only have aa children; for X-linked recessive, an affected mother and father give only affected children. A Y-linked trait can't affect the mother.

questions.stem: About 8% of men in a population are red-green color-blind. If the same fraction of X chromosomes carry the allele, about what percentage of women would you expect to be color-blind?
questions.explanation: A man is affected if his one X carries the allele (probability 0.08). A woman needs it on both X chromosomes: $0.08 \times 0.08 = 0.0064 = 0.64\%$. That is why the condition is much rarer in women.

questions.stem: How many autosomes are in a typical human body cell?
questions.explanation: A typical body cell has 46 chromosomes: 22 pairs of autosomes (44) and one pair of sex chromosomes. 46 counts the sex chromosomes too; 22 is the number of autosomal pairs; 23 is the number in a gamete.

questions.stem: If nondisjunction of one chromosome pair occurs in meiosis I, what are the four gametes like?
choices: All four are normal
Two have an extra chromosome and two are missing one
Two are normal, one has an extra chromosome and one is missing one
All four have an extra chromosome
questions.explanation: In meiosis I both homologs go to one cell, so that cell's two products are n + 1 and the other cell's two products are n − 1. Two normal gametes plus one n + 1 and one n − 1 is the result of nondisjunction in meiosis II.

questions.stem: How many chromosomes are in the body cells of a person with Down syndrome caused by trisomy 21?
questions.explanation: Trisomy means three copies of one chromosome instead of two, so 46 + 1 = 47. 45 would be a monosomy (as in 45,X); 69 would be a whole extra set of chromosomes (triploidy).

questions.stem: A sperm that carries both an X and a Y chromosome, after nondisjunction in meiosis I, fertilizes a normal egg. What is the karyotype of the zygote?
choices: 47,XXY
47,XYY
46,XY
questions.explanation: The egg adds 23 chromosomes including an X; the sperm has 24 including X and Y. Total: 47,XXY (Klinefelter syndrome). 45,X comes from a gamete with no sex chromosome; 47,XYY would need two Y chromosomes from the father (nondisjunction in meiosis II).

questions.stem: Which condition could NOT be detected from a standard karyotype?
choices: Down syndrome (trisomy 21)
Turner syndrome (45,X)
Cystic fibrosis, caused by a recessive allele of a single gene
A large deletion on chromosome 5
questions.explanation: A karyotype shows chromosome number and large structural changes. A cystic fibrosis allele is a small change within one gene that leaves the chromosome looking normal; it needs DNA testing.

questions.stem: A segment of chromosome 9 breaks off and becomes attached to chromosome 22. This structural change is
choices: a deletion
an inversion
a duplication
a translocation
questions.explanation: A translocation moves a segment to a non-homologous chromosome. A deletion loses a segment, an inversion flips one in place, and a duplication repeats one.

questions.stem: A chi-square test compares observed counts in four phenotype classes with a 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 prediction. How many degrees of freedom are there?
questions.explanation: Degrees of freedom = number of categories − 1 = 4 − 1 = 3. Using the number of categories (4) is the common mistake; 15 is 16 − 1, the ratio total minus one.

questions.stem: A cross is expected to give 3 : 1. Of 120 offspring, 84 show the dominant trait and 36 the recessive trait. What is $\chi^2$?
questions.explanation: Expected: 90 and 30. $\chi^2 = \dfrac{(84-90)^2}{90} + \dfrac{(36-30)^2}{30} = 0.40 + 1.20 = 1.60$. Dividing by the observed counts instead gives 1.43; 0.40 is only the first term; 3.84 is the critical value, not the statistic.

questions.stem: A test cross expected to give 1 : 1 yields $\chi^2 = 5.2$. Using $p = 0.05$, what should you conclude?
choices: Fail to reject, because 5.2 is less than the critical value 5.99
Reject the 1 : 1 hypothesis, because 5.2 is greater than the critical value 3.84 for df = 1
The data prove the 1 : 1 hypothesis is true
Fail to reject, because $\chi^2$ is positive
questions.explanation: Two categories give df = 1, critical value 3.84. Since $5.2 \ge 3.84$, a deviation this large would happen by chance less than 5% of the time, so reject. 5.99 is the critical value for df = 2. A chi-square test never proves a hypothesis.

questions.stem: Why must a chi-square test use raw counts rather than percentages?
choices: Percentages can't be squared
Percentages always add to 100, which makes $\chi^2$ zero
The test depends on sample size, and percentages hide how many individuals were counted
Expected values can only be whole numbers
questions.explanation: A 55% : 45% split is unremarkable among 20 offspring but very unlikely by chance among 2000. Counts carry that sample-size information; percentages discard it. Expected counts can be non-integers (e.g. 312.75).

questions.stem: The risk of trisomy 21 rises with the age of the egg-producing parent. What is the main reason?
choices: Egg cells stay paused partway through meiosis I for years or decades, which raises the chance of nondisjunction
Older parents produce more eggs per cycle
Chromosome 21 is copied more often in older people
Sperm cells cannot undergo nondisjunction
questions.explanation: Human oocytes begin meiosis I before birth and pause until ovulation, so an egg released at 40 has been paused for about 40 years; errors in separating chromosomes become more likely. Nondisjunction also occurs in sperm formation, but it accounts for a smaller share of trisomy 21.

questions.stem: In the Avery, MacLeod and McCarty experiment, extract from heat-killed S bacteria was treated with different enzymes before being mixed with live R bacteria. Which result identified DNA as the transforming principle?
choices: Transformation stopped after protease treatment but still happened after DNase treatment.
Transformation happened with every enzyme treatment.
Transformation still happened after protease or RNase treatment, but not after DNase treatment.
Transformation stopped after every enzyme treatment.
questions.explanation: Destroying a molecule that is needed should stop transformation. Only DNase (which destroys DNA) stopped it, so DNA is required; protein and RNA are not. If transformation stopped with every enzyme, or with none, no single molecule could be singled out.

questions.stem: Hershey and Chase labeled one batch of bacteriophages with radioactive sulfur and another with radioactive phosphorus. Why these two elements?
choices: Sulfur is found in DNA but not protein, and phosphorus is found in protein but not DNA.
Sulfur is found in protein but not DNA, and phosphorus is found in DNA but hardly at all in protein.
Both elements are found only in DNA, so they label it twice.
Both elements are found only in the bacterial cell, not in the virus.
questions.explanation: The point was to label the two candidate molecules separately. Proteins contain sulfur (in some amino acids) and almost no phosphorus; DNA has phosphorus in every nucleotide's phosphate group and no sulfur. Swapping them reverses the chemistry.

questions.stem: In the Hershey–Chase experiment, after infection and blending, where was most of the radioactive phosphorus found, and what did that show?
choices: In the empty phage coats, showing that protein carries the genetic instructions
Inside the bacteria, showing that phage protein enters the cell
Inside the bacteria, showing that phage DNA enters the cell and carries the genetic instructions
Spread evenly between the coats and the bacteria, showing that both molecules are genetic material
questions.explanation: Phosphorus labels DNA. It went into the bacteria, while the sulfur-labeled protein stayed outside with the coats. The material that enters and directs new phages is DNA.

questions.stem: A sample of double-stranded DNA is 18% cytosine. What percentage is adenine?
questions.explanation: C pairs with G, so G = 18% and G + C = 36%. That leaves 100 − 36 = 64% for A + T, and A = T, so A = 32%. 18% wrongly assumes A equals C; 64% forgets to split A + T in half; 82% is just 100 − 18.

questions.stem: One strand of a DNA molecule is 5′-GGATCA-3′. What is the complementary strand, written with its ends labeled?
choices: 3′-CCTAGT-5′
5′-CCTAGT-3′
3′-GGATCA-5′
3′-CCUAGU-5′
questions.explanation: Pair each base (G–C, A–T): C C T A G T. The strands are antiparallel, so the partner written under the original runs 3′ to 5′. Labeling it 5′ to 3′ ignores antiparallel orientation; repeating the original bases is not complementary; U appears only in RNA.

questions.stem: Why is the DNA double helix the same width (about 2 nm) along its whole length?
choices: Every base pair joins a two-ring purine with a one-ring pyrimidine.
Every base pair joins two purines.
Hydrogen bonds pull the backbones to a fixed distance regardless of the bases.
The sugar–phosphate backbone is on the inside of the helix.
questions.explanation: A–T and G–C each pair a double-ring base (A or G) with a single-ring base (T or C), so every rung is the same length. Two purines would make a wider rung. The backbones are on the outside, and hydrogen bonds alone don't fix the width.

questions.stem: Meselson and Stahl grew bacteria on heavy nitrogen (15N), then moved them to light nitrogen (14N). After one generation all the DNA formed a single band of intermediate density. Which model did this result rule out?
choices: Semiconservative replication
Dispersive replication
Conservative replication
No model; the result fits all three
questions.explanation: Conservative replication would keep the original heavy helix intact and make a separate all-light helix: two bands, heavy and light. A single hybrid band rules it out. Both semiconservative and dispersive replication predict one intermediate band after one generation; the second generation (half hybrid, half light) ruled out dispersive.

questions.stem: In the Meselson–Stahl experiment, what fraction of the DNA is hybrid (one heavy, one light strand) after 3 generations in light nitrogen?
questions.explanation: After $n$ generations there are $2^n$ helices from each original one, and the two original heavy strands sit in exactly two of them. With $n = 3$: $2/8 = 1/4$ hybrid, $3/4$ light. 1/2 is the answer after 2 generations; 3/4 is the light fraction.

questions.stem: Why is the lagging strand made in short Okazaki fragments?
choices: The lagging strand is copied by RNA polymerase, which makes only short pieces.
Helicase can unwind only short stretches of the lagging strand.
The lagging strand is built 3′ to 5′, which is slower.
DNA polymerase can add nucleotides only to a 3′ end, so the strand that runs the other way must be built in pieces away from the fork.
questions.explanation: All new DNA grows 5′ to 3′. The two template strands are antiparallel, so on one of them the new strand must grow away from the fork; it is made in fragments as the fork opens and later joined by ligase. No strand is built 3′ to 5′, and DNA polymerase, not RNA polymerase, does the copying.

questions.stem: Match the enzyme to its job in replication: which enzyme joins Okazaki fragments into one continuous strand?
choices: Helicase
Primase
DNA polymerase
DNA ligase
questions.explanation: Ligase seals the gaps in the backbone between fragments. Helicase unwinds the helix, primase makes the RNA primers, and DNA polymerase adds the nucleotides.

questions.stem: A student says Chargaff's rules mean that a single DNA strand must have equal amounts of A and T. Why is this wrong?
choices: The rules apply only to RNA.
The rules describe double-stranded DNA: each A on one strand is matched by a T on the other strand, not on the same strand.
The rules say A equals G, not A equals T.
The rules apply only to human DNA.
questions.explanation: A = T holds for the double helix because of base pairing between strands. One strand can be rich in A as long as its partner is equally rich in T. Chargaff found the rules in many species; they don't apply to RNA, which is usually single-stranded.

questions.stem: A DNA template strand reads 3′-TACGGT-5′. What mRNA is transcribed from it?
choices: 5′-AUGCCA-3′
5′-ATGCCA-3′
5′-UACGGU-3′
5′-ACCGUA-3′
questions.explanation: Pair each template base with an RNA base: T→A, A→U, C→G, G→C, G→C, T→A, giving AUGCCA. ATGCCA is the DNA complement (RNA uses U, not T). UACGGU copies the template with U for T. ACCGUA reverses the correct sequence.

questions.stem: Where does RNA polymerase first bind to begin transcribing a gene?
choices: The promoter
The start codon
The operator
The ribosome
questions.explanation: RNA polymerase binds the promoter, a DNA sequence just upstream of the gene. The start codon (AUG) is where translation starts, on the mRNA. The operator is a repressor-binding site in bacterial operons.

questions.stem: A eukaryotic pre-mRNA has four exons and three introns. What happens to it before it leaves the nucleus?
choices: The introns are removed, the exons are joined, and a cap and a tail are added.
The exons are removed and the introns are joined.
Nothing; mRNA is translated inside the nucleus.
The introns are translated into a separate protein.
questions.explanation: Introns are cut out and exons are spliced together (exons are the parts that are expressed). The 5′ cap and 3′ tail protect the mRNA. Translation happens in the cytoplasm.

questions.stem: Translate the mRNA 5′-CCAUGGCUUGGUAGCA-3′ using the codon table, starting at the first AUG.
choices: Pro–Trp–Leu–Gly–Ser
Met–Ala–Trp–Stop–Gln
Tyr–Arg–Thr
Met–Ala–Trp
questions.explanation: The first AUG follows CC. Read from there: AUG (Met), GCU (Ala), UGG (Trp), UAG (Stop). The stop codon ends translation and adds nothing, so the chain is Met–Ala–Trp. Reading from the first base gives a different frame; Tyr–Arg–Thr comes from looking up the complementary triplets instead of the codons.

questions.stem: Why must codons be at least three bases long?
choices: Two-base codons give only 16 combinations, too few for 20 amino acids; three bases give 64.
Ribosomes are exactly three bases wide.
There are three kinds of RNA.
Each amino acid contains three nitrogen atoms.
questions.explanation: With four bases, $4^2 = 16$ two-letter words can't name 20 amino acids, but $4^3 = 64$ three-letter words can, with extras (which is why the code is redundant).

questions.stem: A tRNA has the anticodon 3′-UAC-5′. Which codon does it pair with, and which amino acid does it carry?
choices: AUG, methionine
UAC, tyrosine
AUG, tyrosine
CAU, histidine
questions.explanation: The anticodon pairs with the codon: U–A, A–U, C–G gives 5′-AUG-3′, which codes for Met. Looking up UAC in the table is the classic error (the table lists codons, not anticodons). CAU is the anticodon read 5′ to 3′ and then looked up as if it were a codon.

questions.stem: The mRNA coding region of a gene, from the start codon through the stop codon, is 900 nucleotides long. How many amino acids are in the polypeptide?
questions.explanation: 900 ÷ 3 = 300 codons, one of which is the stop codon, which codes for no amino acid. So 299 amino acids. 300 counts the stop codon; 900 treats each nucleotide as an amino acid.

questions.stem: What ends translation when a ribosome reaches a stop codon?
choices: A tRNA carrying a stop amino acid pairs with the codon.
RNA polymerase falls off the mRNA.
The ribosome runs out of ATP.
A release factor protein binds the stop codon and frees the polypeptide.
questions.explanation: No tRNA matches UAA, UAG or UGA. A release factor binds instead, the chain is released, and the ribosome comes apart. RNA polymerase works in transcription, not translation.

questions.stem: A human insulin gene placed in bacteria makes working human insulin. Which feature of the genetic code makes this possible?
choices: It is redundant.
It is nearly universal.
It has three stop codons.
It is read in overlapping triplets.
questions.explanation: Bacteria read codons the same way human cells do, so a human gene's codons specify the same amino acids. Redundancy (several codons per amino acid) is true but doesn't explain it. The code is not read in overlapping triplets.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares RNA with DNA?
choices: RNA contains deoxyribose and thymine and is usually double-stranded.
RNA contains ribose and thymine and is usually double-stranded.
RNA contains ribose and uracil and is usually single-stranded.
RNA contains deoxyribose and uracil and is usually single-stranded.
questions.explanation: RNA's sugar is ribose (DNA's is deoxyribose), uracil replaces thymine, and most RNA molecules are a single strand.

questions.stem: Which molecule actually catalyzes the peptide bonds between amino acids in a ribosome?
choices: mRNA
tRNA
rRNA
DNA polymerase
questions.explanation: The core of the ribosome is ribosomal RNA, and the rRNA itself forms peptide bonds. mRNA carries the code and tRNA delivers amino acids; DNA polymerase copies DNA.

questions.stem: In the lac operon of E. coli, what happens when lactose is present?
choices: Lactose binds the operator and blocks RNA polymerase.
Lactose binds the promoter and attracts the repressor.
The repressor binds lactose and stays on the operator more tightly.
Lactose binds the repressor, which changes shape and releases the operator, so the genes are transcribed.
questions.explanation: The repressor normally sits on the operator and blocks transcription. A form of lactose binds the repressor, changing its shape so it lets go of the DNA. Lactose never binds the DNA itself.

questions.stem: A mutant E. coli strain makes a repressor that cannot bind to the operator. How are its lac genes expressed?
choices: Off, whether or not lactose is present
On, whether or not lactose is present
On only when lactose is present, as normal
On only when lactose is absent
questions.explanation: With no working repressor on the operator, nothing blocks RNA polymerase, so transcription runs all the time. A repressor that cannot release (for example, one that can't bind lactose) would instead keep the genes off.

questions.stem: A nerve cell and a skin cell from the same person make very different proteins. What is the best explanation?
choices: They contain different genes.
Nerve cells have lost the genes for skin proteins.
They express different genes from the same DNA, controlled by different transcription factors.
Skin cells have extra chromosomes.
questions.explanation: Nearly all body cells carry the same genome. Cell types differ in which genes are switched on, set largely by combinations of transcription factors and by how tightly DNA is packed.

questions.stem: Which describes an epigenetic change?
choices: A base substitution changes a codon.
A chromosome segment is deleted.
A plasmid carrying a new gene enters a bacterium.
Methyl groups added to DNA silence a gene, and the pattern is copied when the cell divides.
questions.explanation: Epigenetic changes alter gene activity without changing the DNA sequence, through tags such as DNA methylation or histone modification that can be passed to daughter cells. The other choices all change the DNA sequence or add new DNA.

questions.stem: A codon in an mRNA changes from GAA to GAG. What type of mutation is this?
choices: Missense
Silent
Nonsense
Frameshift
questions.explanation: GAA and GAG both code for glutamic acid (Glu), so the protein is unchanged: silent. A missense mutation would change the amino acid, a nonsense mutation would create a stop codon, and a frameshift needs an insertion or deletion.

questions.stem: The mRNA 5′-AUG GCA UGG AAA UAA-3′ codes for Met–Ala–Trp–Lys. A mutation changes UGG to UGA. What is the result?
choices: A nonsense mutation: the protein is Met–Ala only.
A missense mutation: Trp is replaced by Arg.
A silent mutation: the protein is unchanged.
A frameshift: every amino acid after Ala changes.
questions.explanation: UGA is a stop codon, so translation ends after Ala and the protein is cut short: a nonsense mutation. One base was substituted, not inserted or deleted, so the frame is unchanged.

questions.stem: One base is deleted near the start of a gene's coding region. Why is this usually more harmful than a single-base substitution?
choices: It always creates a stop codon at the site of the deletion.
It removes exactly one amino acid.
It changes the DNA in every cell of the body.
It shifts the reading frame, changing every codon after it and often creating an early stop codon.
questions.explanation: Codons are read in fixed groups of three from AUG, so losing one base regroups every later base. A substitution affects at most one codon. Removing exactly one amino acid requires deleting three bases.

questions.stem: The most common cystic fibrosis mutation deletes three bases from the gene. What effect does this have on the reading frame?
choices: It shifts the frame, changing every amino acid after the deletion.
It changes one amino acid to a stop codon.
None; one amino acid is missing but the rest of the sequence is read in the normal frame.
It doubles the length of the protein.
questions.explanation: Three bases are one codon, so the frame is kept. The protein lacks one phenylalanine but is otherwise normal in sequence (though it misfolds). Only insertions or deletions that are not multiples of three cause frameshifts.

questions.stem: A mutation occurs in a skin cell on a man's arm after years of sun exposure. Can it be passed to his children?
choices: Yes, because all mutations are inherited.
No, because it is a somatic mutation, not in a cell that makes sperm.
Yes, but only to his sons.
No, because ultraviolet light cannot cause mutations.
questions.explanation: Only germline mutations (in cells that make eggs or sperm) reach the next generation. A somatic mutation is passed only to that cell's descendants in the body, though it may contribute to skin cancer. UV light is a well-known mutagen.

questions.stem: Sickle cell disease results from codon 6 of a hemoglobin gene changing from GAG to GUG. Using the codon table, what kind of mutation is this?
choices: Silent: both codons code for Glu
Missense: Glu is replaced by Val
Nonsense: GUG is a stop codon
Frameshift: a base was inserted
questions.explanation: GAG codes for Glu and GUG for Val, so one amino acid changes: missense. GUG is not a stop codon, and the change is a substitution (one base swapped), not an insertion.

questions.stem: A PCR reaction starts with 10 copies of a target sequence. Assuming perfect doubling, how many copies are present after 10 cycles?
questions.explanation: $N = N_0 \times 2^n = 10 \times 2^{10} = 10 \times 1024 = 10{,}240$. 200 uses $N_0 \times 2n$ (adding instead of doubling); 1,024 forgets the starting 10 copies; 100 is $10 \times 10$.

questions.stem: Why does PCR use a DNA polymerase from bacteria that live in hot springs?
choices: Hot-spring polymerase copies RNA instead of DNA.
It works only at room temperature, which keeps the primers attached.
Each cycle heats the mixture to about 95 °C to separate the strands, which would destroy most enzymes.
It needs no primers.
questions.explanation: The denaturing step near 95 °C would ruin an ordinary enzyme every cycle. Taq polymerase survives it, so it can be added once. It still needs primers and copies DNA.

questions.stem: Put the three temperature steps of one PCR cycle in order.
choices: Anneal primers, denature, extend
Extend, denature, anneal primers
Denature, extend, anneal primers
Denature (about 95 °C), anneal primers (about 50–65 °C), extend (about 72 °C)
questions.explanation: The strands must first separate (denature) so the primers can bind (anneal) to single strands; only then can the polymerase extend from the primers.

questions.stem: DNA fragments of 300, 1,200 and 5,000 base pairs are run on the same gel. Which travels farthest from the well, and toward which electrode?
choices: The 5,000 bp fragment, toward the positive electrode
The 300 bp fragment, toward the negative electrode
The 300 bp fragment, toward the positive electrode
The 5,000 bp fragment, toward the negative electrode
questions.explanation: DNA's phosphate backbone is negatively charged, so it moves toward the positive electrode. Smaller fragments slip through the gel more easily and travel farthest.
