questions.stem: On a gel, ladder bands of 2,000 bp and 1,000 bp are 44 mm and 50 mm from the wells. An unknown band is at 47 mm. Which estimate is best?
choices: Exactly 1,500 bp
About 2,500 bp
About 1,400 bp
About 700 bp
questions.explanation: The band lies between the 1,000 and 2,000 bp bands, so its size is between them. Distance is linear in the logarithm of size, so halfway in distance is the geometric middle, $\sqrt{1000 \times 2000} \approx 1{,}414$ bp, not the arithmetic middle of 1,500. 2,500 and 700 lie outside the bracketing bands.

questions.stem: A linear DNA molecule 8,000 bp long has restriction sites at positions 2,000 and 5,000. What fragment sizes are produced?
questions.explanation: Two cuts in a linear molecule make three pieces: 0 to 2,000 (2,000 bp), 2,000 to 5,000 (3,000 bp), and 5,000 to 8,000 (3,000 bp). They add up to 8,000. Listing the cut positions as sizes is the usual error; two pieces would come from a circle.

questions.stem: To make human insulin in bacteria, why are the plasmid and the insulin gene cut with the same restriction enzyme?
choices: So the bacteria will be killed by the antibiotic
So the insulin gene is copied by PCR
So the plasmid becomes linear and stays that way
So their sticky ends are complementary and can pair before ligase seals them
questions.explanation: The same enzyme leaves matching single-stranded tails on both pieces. They base-pair, and DNA ligase joins the backbones to make recombinant DNA. The antibiotic step selects bacteria that took up a plasmid; it is meant to kill those that didn't.

questions.stem: Bacteria are mixed with recombinant plasmids carrying an antibiotic-resistance gene and then grown on a plate containing that antibiotic. What grows?
choices: Only bacteria that did not take up a plasmid
Only bacteria that took up a plasmid
All the bacteria
No bacteria
questions.explanation: The resistance gene travels on the plasmid, so only bacteria carrying a plasmid survive the antibiotic. This step selects the transformed cells from the many that took up nothing.

questions.stem: At one STR region, crime-scene DNA has alleles with 8 and 11 repeats. Suspect 1 has 8 and 11; suspect 2 has 8 and 10. What can be concluded from this region alone?
choices: Suspect 1 is definitely the source.
Suspect 2 is excluded; suspect 1 is not excluded but is not identified by one region.
Both suspects are excluded.
Neither suspect can be excluded.
questions.explanation: Suspect 2 has a 10-repeat allele that is not in the evidence, so suspect 2 cannot be the source. Suspect 1 matches, but many people share any one pair of alleles; labs compare about 20 regions before calling a match.

questions.stem: How does CRISPR-Cas9 find the gene it cuts?
choices: A guide RNA designed to match the target sequence base-pairs with it.
Cas9 recognizes a fixed six-base palindrome, like a restriction enzyme.
It cuts at random and the right cuts are selected later.
It binds the gene's promoter by recognizing RNA polymerase.
questions.explanation: The guide RNA is the targeting part: change its sequence and Cas9 cuts a different gene. A restriction enzyme, by contrast, always cuts the same fixed site.

questions.stem: A bone sample contains 1/16 of the carbon-14 found in living tissue. The half-life of carbon-14 is 5,730 years. About how old is the bone?
choices: 91,680 years
22,920 years
45,840 years
11,460 years
questions.explanation: $\tfrac{1}{16} = \left(\tfrac12\right)^4$, so 4 half-lives have passed: $4 \times 5{,}730 = 22{,}920$ years. 91,680 multiplies by 16 instead of using 4 half-lives; 45,840 uses 8 half-lives (taking 1/16 as 16 ÷ 2); 11,460 is 2 half-lives.

questions.stem: Why can't carbon-14 be used to date a 70-million-year-old dinosaur fossil?
choices: Dinosaurs did not contain carbon.
After so many half-lives, essentially no carbon-14 would be left to measure.
Carbon-14 decays faster in older rocks.
Carbon-14 is only found in volcanic rock.
questions.explanation: 70 million years is over 12,000 half-lives of carbon-14, so the amount left would be immeasurably small; carbon-14 works to about 50,000 years. Dinosaur fossils are dated with long-lived isotopes in nearby volcanic layers. Decay rates don't depend on the age of the rock.

questions.stem: The forelimbs of a human, a bat, a whale and a cat have the same set of bones arranged in the same pattern, though they are used for different tasks. These are
choices: analogous structures, evidence of a common ancestor
homologous structures, evidence of a common ancestor
vestigial structures with no function
analogous structures that evolved separately
questions.explanation: Same underlying structure, different jobs: that is homology, explained by inheritance from a shared ancestor. Analogous structures do similar jobs with different structures. These limbs are fully functional, so they are not vestigial.

questions.stem: A bird's wing and a butterfly's wing both allow flight, but one is a modified forelimb with bones and the other is a thin outgrowth of the body wall. What are they an example of?
choices: Analogous structures produced by convergent evolution
Homologous structures inherited from a winged ancestor
Vestigial structures
Transitional fossils
questions.explanation: Similar function but different structure and origin means analogous. The common ancestor of birds and insects had no wings; flight evolved separately in each line.

questions.stem: Some whales have small hip bones embedded in their bodies, not attached to any legs. What is the best description?
choices: Vestigial structures inherited from four-legged ancestors
Analogous structures
Structures that the whale grew because it needed them
Evidence that whales are fish
questions.explanation: Reduced remnants of structures that were functional in ancestors are vestigial. Fossil whales show a series from four-legged land mammals to fully aquatic forms, consistent with these bones being leftovers.

questions.stem: Before 2004, fish fossils were known from rocks about 385 million years old and four-legged animals from rocks about 365 million years old. Where were researchers most likely to find a fish–tetrapod transitional fossil?
choices: In deep-ocean rocks about 500 million years old
In any rock younger than 300 million years
In shallow freshwater rocks about 375 million years old
In rocks older than 400 million years
questions.explanation: A transition should lie between the ages of the two groups and in the environment where early tetrapods lived. That prediction led to Tiktaalik, found in about 375-million-year-old rocks on Ellesmere Island. Rocks much older or younger would be the wrong time.

questions.stem: Cytochrome c differs from the human version by 0 amino acids in chimpanzees, 13 in chickens and 21 in tuna. Which conclusion do these data support?
choices: Tuna evolved from chickens.
Humans share a more recent common ancestor with chickens than with tuna.
Chimpanzees and humans are the same species.
Cytochrome c has not changed since the first cells.
questions.explanation: Fewer differences mean less time since two lines split. Chickens differ by fewer amino acids than tuna, so the human–chicken split is more recent. Identical cytochrome c doesn't make two species the same (they differ in many other genes), and no living species evolved from another living species.

questions.stem: Species on the Galápagos Islands most closely resemble species from which place?
choices: Islands with a similar climate on the other side of the world
The nearby South American mainland
Africa
Europe, where Darwin lived
questions.explanation: Biogeography shows island species resemble those on the nearest mainland, the source of their ancestors, not species in similar climates far away. That pattern makes sense if species descend from colonists.

questions.stem: A volcanic ash layer contains 1/4 of its original potassium-40 (half-life 1.25 billion years). A fossil lies in the rock layer directly below the ash. What can be said about the fossil's age?
choices: It is at least 2.5 billion years old.
It is at most 2.5 billion years old.
It is exactly 1.25 billion years old.
It is about 5 billion years old.
questions.explanation: 1/4 remaining means 2 half-lives: $2 \times 1.25 = 2.5$ billion years. Lower layers are older, so the fossil is at least that old. 1.25 billion is one half-life (1/2 remaining); 5 billion uses 4 half-lives.

questions.stem: Which statement about humans and chimpanzees is accurate?
choices: Humans evolved from modern chimpanzees.
They share a common ancestor that lived roughly 6 to 8 million years ago.
Chimpanzees evolved from humans.
They have no ancestors in common.
questions.explanation: Both are living species that descend from a shared ancestor; neither evolved from the other. Both lines have been evolving for the same length of time since the split.

questions.stem: Why is the near-universal genetic code considered evidence for evolution?
choices: It shows that all organisms have the same genes.
It proves that the code can never change.
It is most simply explained if all life inherited the code from a common ancestor.
It shows that bacteria evolved from humans.
questions.explanation: Many different codes would work chemically, yet almost all life uses the same one, which points to a single origin. Organisms share the code, not all their genes, and minor variant codes do exist.

questions.stem: Which set of conditions is enough for natural selection to change a population?
choices: Variation in a trait, inheritance of that trait, and differences in reproductive success linked to it
A changing environment and individuals that try to adapt
A large population with no variation
Variation caused only by the environment, such as muscles built by exercise
questions.explanation: Selection needs heritable variation that affects survival or reproduction. Effort doesn't change genes, a population with no variation has nothing to select, and traits acquired during life (like gym muscles) aren't inherited.

questions.stem: In evolutionary terms, which individual has the highest fitness?
choices: A small, weak bird that raises 8 offspring that survive to breed
A large, strong bird that lives 15 years but raises 2 offspring
The fastest bird, which raises no offspring
A bird that lives longest without breeding
questions.explanation: Fitness is reproductive success relative to others: the number of offspring contributed to the next generation. Size, strength, speed and lifespan matter only if they lead to more offspring.

questions.stem: In the Lederbergs' replica-plating experiment, colonies that grew on antibiotic plates were traced back to the original plate, which had never been exposed to the antibiotic. Those original colonies were already resistant. What does this show?
choices: The antibiotic caused the resistance mutations.
Bacteria become resistant because they need to survive.
Resistance is not inherited.
Resistance mutations arose randomly before exposure; the antibiotic selected them.
questions.explanation: The original colonies were resistant without ever meeting the antibiotic, so the mutations came first and the antibiotic only revealed and favored them. Mutation is random with respect to need.

questions.stem: A moth population has 500 light and 500 dark moths. On sooty bark, 30% of light moths and 60% of dark moths survive. What percent of the survivors are dark?
choices: About 66.7%
questions.explanation: Survivors: light $500 \times 0.30 = 150$, dark $500 \times 0.60 = 300$. Dark fraction $= 300/450 \approx 66.7\%$. 50% is the starting share; 60% is the dark survival rate, not the share of survivors; 90% adds the two rates.

questions.stem: During the 1977 drought on Daphne Major, mostly large, hard seeds remained. Medium ground finch survivors had deeper beaks than those that died. What happened to the next generation?
choices: Its average beak depth was unchanged, because selection acts only on individuals.
Its average beak depth was larger, because beak depth is heritable.
Its beaks were smaller, because birds ate less.
Every bird developed a deeper beak by cracking hard seeds.
questions.explanation: Deeper-beaked birds survived and bred, and beak depth is inherited, so the average in the offspring generation rose. Individual birds didn't change their beaks by use; the population's makeup changed.

questions.stem: Human birth weight historically had the highest survival near the average, with lower survival for very small and very large babies. What type of selection is this?
choices: Directional selection
Disruptive selection
Stabilizing selection
Artificial selection
questions.explanation: Favoring the middle and removing both extremes is stabilizing selection: the average stays and the spread narrows. Directional selection would shift the average; disruptive would favor both extremes.

questions.stem: In a finch population, birds with small bills eat soft seeds well and birds with large bills crack hard seeds well, but intermediate bills do neither well. Over time, what pattern of selection is expected?
choices: Disruptive selection, favoring both extremes
Stabilizing selection, favoring intermediate bills
Directional selection toward small bills
No selection, because all bills are used
questions.explanation: When both extremes do better than the middle, selection is disruptive and can split the distribution into two peaks, as in the black-bellied seedcracker.

questions.stem: Cabbage, broccoli, kale and Brussels sprouts were all bred from one species of wild cabbage. This is an example of
choices: natural selection
genetic drift
artificial selection
convergent evolution
questions.explanation: People chose which plants to breed for leaves, buds, flowers or stems: artificial selection. In natural selection, the environment does the choosing through survival and reproduction.

questions.stem: Lamarck proposed that giraffes got long necks by stretching to reach leaves and passing the longer necks to their young. Why is this rejected?
choices: Changes acquired during an animal's life are not written into its DNA, so they are not inherited.
Giraffes do not eat leaves.
Neck length is not variable in giraffes.
Natural selection cannot act on body size.
questions.explanation: Stretching doesn't change the genes in eggs or sperm. The accepted explanation is that giraffes with heritably longer necks left more offspring.

questions.stem: Which statement about natural selection is correct?
choices: Individuals evolve during their lifetimes to fit the environment.
Selection produces the mutations a population needs.
Selection plans ahead for future environments.
Individuals are selected, but populations evolve.
questions.explanation: Selection acts on individuals (who survives and reproduces), and the result is a change in the population over generations. It has no foresight and doesn't create mutations; it sorts existing variation.

questions.stem: In a population in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, 9% of individuals show a recessive trait. What is the frequency of heterozygous carriers?
A population of 500 has 180 AA, 240 Aa and 80 aa individuals. What is the frequency of allele A?
questions.explanation: Gene copies: $2 \times 500 = 1{,}000$. Copies of A: $2(180) + 240 = 600$. $p = 600/1000 = 0.6$. 0.36 is the AA genotype frequency; 0.48 is the Aa frequency; 0.4 is $q$.

questions.stem: A recessive disorder affects 1 in 10,000 people. Assuming Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, about what fraction of people are carriers?
choices: About 1 in 100
About 1 in 5,000
About 1 in 50
About 1 in 10,000
questions.explanation: $q^2 = 1/10{,}000$, so $q = 1/100 = 0.01$ and $p = 0.99$. $2pq = 2(0.99)(0.01) \approx 0.02$, about 1 in 50. 1 in 100 is $q$, not $2pq$. Carriers are far more common than affected people.

questions.stem: Which is NOT one of the conditions for Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium?
choices: No natural selection
Random mating
The dominant allele must be more common than the recessive allele.
A very large population
questions.explanation: The conditions are no mutation, no gene flow, a very large population (no drift), random mating and no selection. Allele frequencies can be anything; equilibrium says they stay constant, not that dominant alleles are common.

questions.stem: With $p = 0.6$ and $q = 0.4$, a population of 1,000 is expected to have 480 heterozygotes under Hardy-Weinberg. A survey finds only 200. Which explanation best fits this shortage?
choices: Inbreeding or self-fertilization (nonrandom mating)
Random mating in a very large population
Gene flow that adds heterozygotes
A counting method that only finds homozygotes for A
questions.explanation: Too few heterozygotes and too many homozygotes is the signature of mating with relatives or self-fertilization. Random mating in a large population is the equilibrium case and would give about 480.

questions.stem: Northern elephant seals were hunted to a few dozen animals in the 1890s. Today there are over 200,000, but they have very little genetic variation. What explains the low variation?
choices: Gene flow from other seal species
Stabilizing selection on body size
The bottleneck effect
A high mutation rate
questions.explanation: The few survivors carried only a small, random sample of the original alleles, and the population regrew from them: a bottleneck, a form of genetic drift. Gene flow and mutation would add variation, not remove it.

questions.stem: A rare recessive form of dwarfism is much more common among the Old Order Amish of Lancaster County than in the general population. The best explanation is
choices: the founder effect
natural selection favoring the allele
gene flow into the community
a high mutation rate in the community
questions.explanation: The community descends from a small number of founders, at least one of whom happened to carry the allele, so it became more common by chance: the founder effect. Nothing suggests the allele is favored.

questions.stem: Why does genetic drift have a much larger effect in small populations than in large ones?
choices: Chance deviations from expected numbers are proportionally larger in small samples.
Small populations have higher mutation rates.
Natural selection is stronger in small populations.
Large populations have no random events.
questions.explanation: Like coin flips: 10 tosses can easily give 70% heads, but 10,000 tosses will be very close to 50%. Each generation is a sample of the parents' alleles, and small samples wander more.

questions.stem: Pollen carried by wind from one population of pines to another, distant population is an example of
choices: genetic drift
gene flow
mutation
the founder effect
questions.explanation: Moving alleles between populations (through migrating individuals or their gametes) is gene flow. It tends to make populations more alike.

questions.stem: Which mechanism of evolution consistently makes a population better adapted to its environment?
choices: Genetic drift
Gene flow
Natural selection
Mutation
questions.explanation: Only selection favors alleles because they improve survival and reproduction. Drift is random, gene flow depends on who migrates, and mutation is random with respect to need, though it supplies the raw variation.

questions.stem: Polydactyly (extra fingers) is caused by a dominant allele, yet it is rare. How can this be?
choices: Dominant alleles always become more common, so it must not really be dominant.
Dominance describes how an allele shows up in heterozygotes, not how common it is.
The allele is recessive in most people.
Hardy-Weinberg does not apply to humans.
questions.explanation: An allele can be dominant and still have a low frequency $p$. Hardy and Weinberg showed that dominant alleles do not automatically spread; frequencies stay constant unless something like selection or drift changes them.

questions.stem: Horses and donkeys can mate and produce mules, but mules are almost always sterile. Under the biological species concept, horses and donkeys are
choices: the same species, because they can mate
separate species, isolated by mechanical isolation
separate species, isolated by hybrid sterility
the same species, because mules are healthy
questions.explanation: The test is fertile offspring. Mules are sterile, a postzygotic barrier, so horses and donkeys are separate species. Mating can happen, so it is not mechanical isolation.

questions.stem: Two species of frogs live in the same ponds; one breeds in early spring and the other in early summer. What kind of barrier keeps them apart?
choices: Habitat isolation (prezygotic)
Hybrid inviability (postzygotic)
Gametic isolation (prezygotic)
Temporal isolation (prezygotic)
questions.explanation: Breeding at different times is temporal isolation, which acts before fertilization. They share a habitat, so it isn't habitat isolation, and no hybrids form, so postzygotic barriers don't come into play.

questions.stem: Sea urchins of two species release eggs and sperm into the same water, but sperm of one species can't bind to the other species' eggs. This is
choices: behavioral isolation
hybrid sterility
temporal isolation
gametic isolation
questions.explanation: Egg-surface proteins bind only sperm of the same species, so fertilization fails: gametic isolation, a prezygotic barrier. Behavior and timing are not the issue here.

questions.stem: When the Isthmus of Panama formed about 3 million years ago, populations of snapping shrimp were split into Caribbean and Pacific groups that have since become separate species. This is an example of
choices: sympatric speciation by polyploidy
gene flow
convergent evolution
allopatric speciation
questions.explanation: A geographic barrier split the populations and stopped gene flow; each side then evolved separately. That is allopatric speciation. Sympatric speciation happens without geographic separation.

questions.stem: An error in cell division doubles a plant's chromosome number. The new plant can't produce fertile offspring with its parent species but can reproduce with itself or other plants like it. What has happened?
choices: Allopatric speciation
Sympatric speciation by polyploidy
A bottleneck
Directional selection
questions.explanation: The polyploid is reproductively isolated from its parents in a single generation, in the same place. This is a common route to new plant species, with no geographic barrier needed.

questions.stem: Why is the biological species concept hard to apply to bacteria?
choices: Bacteria have no DNA.
Bacteria never evolve.
Bacteria reproduce asexually, so interbreeding can't be the test.
Bacteria all belong to one species.
questions.explanation: The concept is defined by interbreeding. Organisms that reproduce asexually, and fossils, are grouped instead by shared features or DNA sequences.

questions.stem: On a phylogenetic tree, how do you tell which of two species is more closely related to a third?
choices: Choose the species printed next to it at the tips.
Find which pair shares the most recent common ancestor (the node closest to the tips).
Choose the species that looks most similar.
Count how many tips separate them on the page.
questions.explanation: Relatedness is about the most recent shared ancestor. Tip order can change by rotating branches around nodes without changing the tree, and similar appearance can come from convergent evolution.

questions.stem: Using the vertebrate tree from the lesson (lamprey, shark, trout, frog, lizard, human), which group is a clade?
choices: Shark and frog
Frog, lizard and human
Trout and lizard
Lamprey, frog and human
questions.explanation: A clade is an ancestor and all its descendants. Frog, lizard and human are all the descendants of the four-limbed ancestor. The other groups each leave out some descendants of their common ancestor.

questions.stem: In a character table, which trait would help show which two of these three animals (frog, lizard and human) are most closely related?
choices: An amniotic egg, present in lizards and humans but not frogs
A backbone, which all three have
Four limbs, which all three have
Body size, which varies within each group
questions.explanation: A shared derived trait groups the species that inherited it from a common ancestor. The amniotic egg is shared by lizards and humans, marking them as a clade (the amniotes) that excludes frogs. A backbone and four limbs are shared by all three, so they can't separate them, and body size varies too much and can evolve repeatedly. A trait found in only one of the three, like hair in humans, marks that line but can't show which two are closest.

questions.stem: A student says the lamprey, which branches off first on a vertebrate tree, is "less evolved" than humans. What is wrong with this?
choices: Lampreys are actually the ancestors of humans.
Lampreys appeared after humans.
Nothing; early branches are less evolved.
The lamprey's lineage has been evolving for exactly as long as ours since the two split.
questions.explanation: All living groups at the tips have had the same amount of time to evolve since their common ancestor. Living lampreys are not our ancestors; ancestors sit at the nodes, not the tips.

questions.stem: About 15 to 18 species of Galápagos finches, with beaks suited to seeds, insects or cactus, descend from one ancestral species. This pattern is called
choices: a bottleneck
stabilizing selection
an adaptive radiation
gene flow
questions.explanation: One ancestor diversifying into many species, each adapted to a different way of life, is an adaptive radiation.

questions.stem: Genome studies of the Asgard archaea have changed how biologists picture the base of the tree of life. What do most recent analyses suggest?
choices: Eukaryotes descend from bacteria, and archaea branched off from eukaryotes later.
Archaea are eukaryotes that lost their nucleus.
Viruses form a fourth domain at the root of the tree.
Eukaryotes arose from within the archaea, from an archaeal cell that took in a bacterium.
questions.explanation: Asgard archaea carry many genes once thought unique to eukaryotes, and most analyses place eukaryotes on a branch growing out of the archaea, with the mitochondrion coming from an engulfed bacterium. Archaea have no nucleus and never did, archaea are not descended from eukaryotes, and viruses are not cells, so they are not placed in any domain.

questions.stem: If Earth's 4.54 billion years were compressed into 24 hours, about when would the Cambrian explosion (539 million years ago) occur?
choices: About 3 a.m.
About noon
About 11:59 p.m.
About 9 p.m.
questions.explanation: The time elapsed before the Cambrian is $4{,}540 - 539 = 4{,}001$ million years, and $24 \times 4001/4540 \approx 21.2$ hours, about 9 p.m. 3 a.m. comes from using 539/4540 of the day from midnight instead of time remaining.

questions.stem: In the Miller–Urey experiment, electric sparks passed through a mixture of gases and water produced amino acids. What did this show?
choices: Life arose from sparks in a single week.
The first cells contained DNA.
Oxygen was necessary for life to begin.
Some building blocks of life can form from simple chemicals without living things.
questions.explanation: The experiment made molecules, not cells, so it shows only that life's building blocks can form without life. Early Earth had almost no free oxygen; the experiment used no oxygen gas.

questions.stem: Why is the ability of RNA to act as a catalyst important for ideas about the origin of life?
choices: It proves that proteins came before nucleic acids.
RNA can store information and speed up reactions, so early life may have used RNA for both before DNA and proteins.
It shows that DNA is unnecessary in modern cells.
It means RNA can make energy from sunlight.
questions.explanation: The RNA world hypothesis rests on RNA doing both jobs (as rRNA still does when forming peptide bonds). It doesn't make DNA unnecessary today, and it suggests nucleic acids, not proteins, came first.

questions.stem: Put these events in order from oldest to most recent: (1) Great Oxidation Event, (2) first eukaryotes, (3) earliest widely accepted fossils of prokaryotes, (4) Cambrian explosion.
questions.explanation: Prokaryote fossils about 3.5 billion years ago; oxygen buildup about 2.4 billion; eukaryotes about 2 billion; Cambrian explosion about 539 million years ago.

questions.stem: Which observation supports the endosymbiotic origin of mitochondria?
choices: Mitochondria are found only in plant cells.
Mitochondria are made by the Golgi apparatus.
Mitochondria contain no ribosomes.
Mitochondria have their own circular DNA and divide by splitting, like bacteria.
questions.explanation: Their own circular DNA, bacterial-type ribosomes and division by splitting all point to descent from engulfed bacteria. Mitochondria are found in nearly all eukaryotes, including animals.

questions.stem: Which mass extinction was the largest, wiping out by most estimates 80 to 90 percent or more of marine species?
choices: End-Permian, about 252 million years ago
End-Cretaceous, about 66 million years ago
End-Ordovician, about 445 million years ago
End-Triassic, about 201 million years ago
questions.explanation: The end-Permian extinction, linked to massive volcanic eruptions in Siberia, was the worst. The end-Cretaceous, which ended the non-bird dinosaurs, is the best known but was smaller.

questions.stem: A thin clay layer rich in iridium is found worldwide at the boundary between rocks of the Cretaceous and the following period. What does it most strongly support?
choices: A large asteroid impact about 66 million years ago
A slow decline in sea level over millions of years
The first appearance of flowering plants
A global ice age 252 million years ago
questions.explanation: Iridium is rare in Earth's crust but common in asteroids. A worldwide layer at that boundary, plus the Chicxulub crater of the right age, points to an impact. The 252-million-year date belongs to the end-Permian.

questions.stem: Layers in a cliff, bottom to top: sandstone with trilobites, volcanic ash dated at 300 million years, shale with dinosaur bones. What can be said about the trilobite fossils?
choices: They are younger than 300 million years.
They are older than 300 million years.
They are exactly 300 million years old.
They are younger than the dinosaurs.
questions.explanation: By superposition, lower layers are older, so the trilobites predate the ash, and the dinosaurs postdate it. A fossil's age is usually a range bracketed by dated layers.

questions.stem: After the end-Cretaceous extinction, mammals diversified rapidly into many new forms, including whales, bats and grazers. This is best described as
choices: a mass extinction of mammals
a population bottleneck in dinosaurs
stabilizing selection on mammal size
an adaptive radiation into roles left empty
questions.explanation: Extinctions open ecological roles; surviving groups then diversify to fill them. Mammals had been mostly small for over 100 million years before this radiation.

questions.stem: Fossils of a snail lineage show almost no change for 3 million years, then a fairly quick shift (over tens of thousands of years) to a new form that stays stable again. Which model does this pattern match?
choices: Gradualism
Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium
Punctuated equilibrium
Endosymbiosis
questions.explanation: Long stability broken by relatively rapid change is punctuated equilibrium (Eldredge and Gould, 1972). Gradualism predicts slow, steady change throughout.

questions.stem: Why did oxygen-releasing photosynthesis by cyanobacteria matter so much for later life?
choices: It removed all carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.
It produced the first amino acids.
It caused the end-Cretaceous extinction.
The oxygen it built up made aerobic respiration possible, which yields much more ATP.
questions.explanation: Oxygen accumulated from about 2.4 billion years ago. Aerobic respiration gives about 30 ATP per glucose versus 2 from fermentation, which supports larger, more active organisms.

questions.stem: Which way of writing the scientific name of humans follows the capitalization rules of binomial nomenclature?
choices: Homo Sapiens
homo sapiens
HOMO sapiens
Homo sapiens
questions.explanation: The genus is capitalized and the specific epithet is always lowercase: Homo sapiens (italicized in print). Capitalizing the epithet is the most common slip; the genus is never lowercase or written in all capitals.

questions.stem: A wolf and a coyote are in the same genus, Canis. Which statement must be true?
choices: They are also the same species.
They are also in the same family, order, class, phylum, kingdom and domain.
They share no ranks above genus.
They must be able to interbreed and produce fertile offspring.
questions.explanation: Ranks are nested, so sharing a genus means sharing every rank above it (family Canidae, order Carnivora, and so on). It does not mean sharing the species rank below it, and interbreeding is not guaranteed by being in the same genus.

questions.stem: What evidence led Carl Woese to propose that archaea form a domain separate from bacteria?
choices: Differences in cell shape seen under a light microscope
Results of the Gram stain
Comparisons of ribosomal RNA sequences
Whether or not the cells have a nucleus
questions.explanation: Woese compared sequences of ribosomal RNA, a molecule all cells have. Archaea and bacteria both lack a nucleus and look alike under a microscope, which is exactly why they had been lumped together; the Gram stain separates groups of bacteria, not domains.

questions.stem: Which statement about archaea is supported by current evidence?
choices: They are a kind of bacteria that lives only in extreme environments.
They have a nucleus but no mitochondria.
In the machinery they use to copy DNA and make proteins, they resemble eukaryotes more than bacteria.
Many species cause disease in humans.
questions.explanation: Archaea are a separate domain whose RNA polymerase and other gene-expression machinery are eukaryote-like. They also live in soil, oceans and the human gut, not only in extreme places; they have no nucleus; and no archaea are known to cause human disease.

questions.stem: A culture starts with 500 bacteria that divide every 30 minutes. Assuming exponential growth, how many cells are there after 3 hours?
questions.explanation: 3 hours = 180 min, so $n = 180/30 = 6$ generations, and $N = 500 \times 2^{6} = 500 \times 64 = 32\,000$. Multiplying by 6 gives 3,000 (generations are doublings, not multiples); using 3 generations (the hours) gives 4,000; multiplying by 12 gives 6,000.

questions.stem: A bacterial population grows from 100 cells to 1,600 cells in 2 hours of exponential growth. What is its generation time?
choices: 7.5 minutes
30 minutes
20 minutes
60 minutes
questions.explanation: $1600/100 = 16 = 2^{4}$, so there were 4 generations in 120 minutes: $120/4 = 30$ minutes each. Dividing 120 by 16 (the fold increase) gives 7.5 minutes, which confuses the number of doublings with the fold change.

questions.stem: A water sample is diluted to $10^{-5}$, and 0.1 mL of the dilution is spread on a plate. 84 colonies grow. What was the concentration in the original sample?
choices: $8.4 \times 10^{7}$ CFU/mL
$8.4 \times 10^{6}$ CFU/mL
$8.4 \times 10^{2}$ CFU/mL
$8.4 \times 10^{-5}$ CFU/mL
questions.explanation: CFU/mL $= \dfrac{84}{10^{-5} \times 0.1} = 84 \times 10^{6} = 8.4 \times 10^{7}$. Forgetting that only 0.1 mL was plated gives $8.4 \times 10^{6}$; forgetting the dilution gives 840; multiplying by the dilution instead of dividing gives a tiny, impossible number.

questions.stem: A bacterial culture infected with a phage keeps growing normally for several days. After a dose of UV light, the cells burst within an hour. What best explains this?
choices: The phage was in the lysogenic cycle, and UV damage switched it into the lytic cycle.
The phage was in the lytic cycle the whole time, and UV light sped it up.
UV light killed the phage, so the bacteria burst from lack of nutrients.
The bacteria were resistant to the phage until UV light mutated them.
questions.explanation: Normal growth after infection means the viral DNA was integrated and copied along with the host chromosome (lysogenic). DNA damage from UV is a classic trigger that switches it to the lytic cycle, so new phages were made and the cells lysed. A lytic infection would have destroyed the culture within hours, not days.

questions.stem: Why are antibiotics ineffective against viral infections such as the flu?
choices: Viruses are too small for antibiotic molecules to reach.
Viruses hide inside the nucleus, where antibiotics cannot enter.
Every virus is already resistant to every antibiotic.
Viruses lack the cell walls, ribosomes and metabolism that antibiotics target.
questions.explanation: Antibiotics attack structures specific to bacteria, such as peptidoglycan walls and bacterial ribosomes. Viruses have none of these; they use the host cell's machinery. Resistance is not the reason, and size is not the problem.

questions.stem: A particular virus infects human liver cells but not skin cells. What is the most likely reason?
choices: Skin cells have cell walls that block viruses.
Liver cells lack DNA, so the virus can insert its own.
Viruses can only infect cells that are dividing rapidly.
Liver cells have surface receptor molecules that the virus can attach to, and skin cells do not.
questions.explanation: A virus attaches to specific receptor molecules on its host cell, so it infects only cell types that display them. Human cells have no cell walls, all of them contain DNA, and many viruses infect cells that are not dividing.

questions.stem: Bacteria in a flask grow exponentially for a while, then the population stops increasing. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The bacteria have reached their maximum generation time.
Binary fission can only happen a fixed number of times.
The bacteria have switched to sexual reproduction.
Nutrients are running out and waste products are building up.
questions.explanation: A closed flask has limited food, and wastes accumulate, so division slows until births balance deaths (the stationary phase). There's no built-in limit on the number of fissions, and bacteria don't reproduce sexually.

questions.stem: A textbook sorts life into three domains, but a recent research paper draws a tree with only two primary branches, Bacteria and Archaea. How can both be reasonable?
choices: The paper counts eukaryotes as bacteria because they have mitochondria.
Archaea have recently been shown to be a kind of bacteria.
The paper leaves out eukaryotes because many of them are multicellular.
On that tree eukaryotes sit inside the archaeal branch, but they are distinctive enough to keep as a domain.
questions.explanation: Genome studies place eukaryotes within the archaea (closest to the Asgard archaea), so a tree of descent has two primary branches; the three-domain system remains a useful classification because eukaryotes differ so much from both. Mitochondria came from a bacterium but the host was archaeal, archaea are not bacteria, and no tree of life leaves out eukaryotes.

questions.stem: Why do biologists say that protists are not a natural evolutionary group?
choices: Protists do not have a nucleus.
All protists are single-celled, unlike other eukaryotes.
Some protists are more closely related to plants, animals or fungi than to other protists.
Protists are not made of cells.
questions.explanation: A natural group contains an ancestor and all its descendants. DNA shows protists scattered across the eukaryote tree, with some closer to plants and others closer to animals and fungi, so the group is defined only by what it isn't. Protists are eukaryotes with nuclei, and some, like kelp, are multicellular.

questions.stem: A single-celled protist is covered in thousands of short, hair-like structures that beat in waves to move it. These structures are
choices: pseudopods
flagella
hyphae
cilia
questions.explanation: Many short, coordinated hair-like structures are cilia, as in Paramecium. Pseudopods are flowing extensions of cytoplasm (amoebas), flagella are few and long and whip-like, and hyphae are fungal filaments.

questions.stem: Malaria is caused by
choices: a virus carried by mosquitoes
a bacterium in contaminated water
a single-celled protist carried by mosquitoes
a fungus that grows in the lungs
questions.explanation: Malaria is caused by Plasmodium, a protist parasite spread by Anopheles mosquitoes. It multiplies in the liver and then in red blood cells. It is not a virus or a bacterium, though mosquitoes do carry some viral diseases.

questions.stem: The organism that caused the Irish potato famine grows in threads like a fungus, but it is classified as a protist. Which evidence supports that classification?
choices: Its cell walls contain cellulose rather than chitin, and its DNA groups it with diatoms and brown algae.
It grows in thread-like filaments.
It feeds by absorbing nutrients from its host.
It reproduces with spores.
questions.explanation: Phytophthora's cellulose walls and its DNA place it among protists. Threads, absorptive feeding and spores are exactly the features it shares with true fungi, so they can't separate it from them.

questions.stem: A student covers half of each of four dishes of Euglena with foil. After 30 minutes she counts cells in samples from each half: lit halves 410, 395, 430, 402; dark halves 90, 110, 85, 98. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: Euglena move toward light.
Light makes Euglena reproduce faster.
Euglena die in the dark.
Foil attracts Euglena.
questions.explanation: In every replicate, many more cells are in the lit half after only 30 minutes, too short for large changes from reproduction or death; the simplest explanation is movement toward light. Cells were counted in the covered half too, so foil did not attract them.

questions.stem: Roughly what share of all photosynthesis on Earth is carried out by phytoplankton in the oceans?
choices: About 1%
About 10%
Nearly all of it
About half
questions.explanation: Ocean phytoplankton (photosynthetic protists such as diatoms, plus cyanobacteria) do roughly half of global photosynthesis. Land plants do most of the rest, so 'nearly all' is wrong, and 1% or 10% badly underestimates the oceans.

questions.stem: Which set of features shows that a mushroom is not a plant?
choices: It grows from the ground and does not move.
It cannot photosynthesize, its cell walls contain chitin, and it stores glycogen.
Its cells have cell walls.
It reproduces by releasing spores.
questions.explanation: Fungi are heterotrophs with chitin walls that store glycogen, like animals. Growing in soil, staying put and having cell walls are shared with plants, and ferns and mosses also release spores, so those features can't distinguish them.

questions.stem: How does a fungus growing on rotting fruit get its food?
choices: It engulfs pieces of fruit into a gut and digests them.
It photosynthesizes using light passing through the fruit.
It absorbs whole proteins and starch without breaking them down.
It releases digestive enzymes into the fruit and absorbs the small molecules produced.
questions.explanation: Fungi digest outside their bodies: hyphae secrete enzymes and absorb the resulting sugars and amino acids. They have no gut and never photosynthesize, and large molecules must be broken down before they can be absorbed.

questions.stem: A mushroom popping up from a lawn is best described as
choices: the short-lived spore-producing structure of a much larger underground mycelium
the entire body of the fungus
a seed of the fungus
a single giant hypha
questions.explanation: The mushroom is a fruiting body. Most of the fungus is the mycelium of branching hyphae spreading through the soil. Fungi have spores, not seeds.

questions.stem: Pine seedlings grown in sterilized soil (no fungi) are smaller and contain less phosphorus than seedlings grown in soil with mycorrhizal fungi. What best explains the difference?
choices: Fungal hyphae extend the root system's reach and deliver minerals such as phosphate in exchange for sugars.
The fungi photosynthesize and give the seedlings extra sugar.
Sterilizing soil adds phosphorus that harms seedlings.
The fungi are parasites that make the seedlings grow faster to escape them.
questions.explanation: In a mycorrhizal partnership, the huge surface of the hyphae absorbs water and minerals such as phosphate for the plant, which pays in sugars. Fungi can't photosynthesize, and the result shows the fungi helping rather than harming.

questions.stem: On Fleming's 1928 plate, bacteria grew everywhere except in a clear zone around a Penicillium mold. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: The mold eats bacteria by engulfing them.
A substance spreading out from the mold kills or stops the growth of these bacteria.
The bacteria could not grow because the mold used up all the light.
The mold and bacteria are mutualists.
questions.explanation: The clear zone extends beyond the mold itself, so something diffusing out of the mold, not contact or engulfing, inhibited the bacteria. That substance was penicillin. Bacteria on a plate don't need light, and inhibiting one's partner is not mutualism.

questions.stem: Lichens are often the first organisms to grow on bare rock. A lichen is
choices: a partnership between a fungus and a photosynthetic alga or cyanobacterium
a type of moss
a single species of photosynthetic fungus
a colony of protists
questions.explanation: A lichen combines a fungus, which provides structure and absorbs minerals, with an alga or cyanobacterium that photosynthesizes. It is not a moss (a plant), and no fungus photosynthesizes.

questions.stem: Which group of plants has vascular tissue but does not produce seeds?
choices: Ferns
Mosses
Pine trees
Flowering plants
questions.explanation: Ferns have xylem and phloem but reproduce with spores. Mosses lack vascular tissue; pines (gymnosperms) and flowering plants (angiosperms) make seeds.

questions.stem: Why do mosses stay only a few centimeters tall?
choices: Their leaves cannot photosynthesize.
They cannot make seeds.
They lack vascular tissue, so water moves through them only by slow diffusion and capillary action.
Their cells have no cell walls.
questions.explanation: Without xylem, water can't be moved far, so mosses stay short and live in damp places. Mosses do photosynthesize and have cellulose walls; lacking seeds affects reproduction, not height (ferns lack seeds and grow tall).

questions.stem: In a fern, the large leafy plant you see in the forest is the
choices: haploid gametophyte
diploid sporophyte
haploid sporophyte
diploid gametophyte
questions.explanation: In ferns and seed plants the sporophyte, which is diploid and makes spores by meiosis, is the dominant stage. The gametophyte is haploid; in mosses it's the familiar green plant, but in ferns it's a tiny separate structure.

questions.stem: A strip of bark, including the phloem, is cut away in a ring around a tree trunk, leaving the xylem intact. What is the most likely long-term result?
choices: Water can no longer reach the leaves, so they wilt within hours.
Sugars build up above the cut and the roots eventually starve.
The roots fill with excess sugar.
Nothing, because sugars travel in the xylem.
questions.explanation: Phloem carries sugars from leaves (sources) down to roots (sinks). With the phloem ring gone, sugar collects above the cut and the roots slowly starve. The xylem is intact, so water still reaches the leaves.

questions.stem: In a potometer, the air bubble moves 36 mm in 4 minutes along a capillary with a cross-section of 0.50 mm². What is the rate of water uptake?
choices: 9.0 mm³/min
72 mm³/min
18 mm³/min
4.5 mm³/min
questions.explanation: Volume $= 0.50 \times 36 = 18$ mm³, so the rate is $18/4 = 4.5$ mm³/min. Using the distance alone gives 9.0 (forgot the area); 18 is the total volume, not a rate; 72 multiplies by the time instead of dividing.

questions.stem: Under which conditions would a well-watered plant transpire fastest?
choices: Cool, humid, still and bright
Warm, dry, windy and bright
Warm, humid, still and dark
Cool, dry, still and dark
questions.explanation: Transpiration is evaporation: heat, dry air and wind all speed it, and light opens the stomata. Humid, still air slows evaporation, and darkness closes stomata.

questions.stem: What supplies the energy that lifts water from the roots to the top of a tall tree?
choices: ATP spent by root cells pumping water upward
Contractions of the xylem walls
Evaporation of water from the leaves, driven by the sun
Sugar flowing down through the phloem
questions.explanation: In the cohesion-tension mechanism, evaporation (transpiration) pulls on continuous water columns held together by hydrogen bonds. The plant spends no ATP lifting water; xylem cells are dead and can't contract; phloem moves sugar, not the water column.

questions.stem: A leaf imprint is viewed at a magnification where the field of view is 0.50 mm in diameter. There are 39 stomata in the field. What is the stomatal density?
choices: About 199 per mm²
About 50 per mm²
About 78 per mm²
About 156 per mm²
questions.explanation: Area $= \pi r^2 = \pi(0.25)^2 \approx 0.196$ mm², so density $= 39/0.196 \approx 199$ per mm². Using 0.50 mm as the radius gives about 50; dividing by the diameter gives 78; dividing by the radius gives 156.

questions.stem: Darwin found that grass seedlings lit from one side bent toward the light, but not when their tips were covered with an opaque cap. They still bent when the cap was transparent. What does this show?
choices: Light acts directly on the cells that bend.
The tip detects the light, even though the bending happens lower down.
The cap blocked the hormone from entering the seedling.
Seedlings bend toward heat rather than light.
questions.explanation: The transparent cap is the control: covering the tip by itself doesn't stop bending; blocking light to the tip does. So the tip senses light and signals the region below, where bending happens. Shading only the lower part did not stop bending, which rules out light acting directly on the bending cells.

questions.stem: Frits Went placed agar blocks that had held seedling tips off-center on cut seedlings kept in the dark. The seedlings bent away from the side with the block. What did this show?
choices: Light is needed for seedlings to bend.
The signal from the tip is a chemical that can diffuse into agar and makes cells on that side grow more.
Agar itself is a plant hormone.
Cells under the block stopped growing.
questions.explanation: The tips' signal moved into the agar, so it must be a chemical (later named auxin). More auxin on one side made that side elongate more, bending the seedling away from it, even in darkness. A control block that never touched tips would rule out agar itself.

questions.stem: A tomato is botanically a fruit because it
choices: develops from the ovary of a flower and contains seeds
tastes sweet
develops from the anther
grows on a vine
questions.explanation: A fruit is a ripened ovary holding seeds; the ovules inside become the seeds. The anther makes pollen. Sweetness and growth habit have nothing to do with the botanical definition.

questions.stem: During a drought, a plant closes its stomata. What is the main cost of this response?
choices: The plant loses more water.
Less carbon dioxide enters the leaf, so photosynthesis slows.
The roots can no longer absorb minerals by diffusion.
Oxygen builds up and poisons the cells.
questions.explanation: Stomata let carbon dioxide in and water vapor out at the same time, so closing them saves water at the expense of carbon uptake and photosynthesis. Closing them reduces water loss rather than increasing it.

questions.stem: Which characteristic separates animals from fungi?
choices: Animals digest food inside their bodies and their cells lack walls.
Animals are heterotrophs.
Animals are eukaryotes.
Animals store energy as glycogen.
questions.explanation: Both animals and fungi are eukaryotic heterotrophs that store glycogen. Fungi digest food outside the body and have chitin cell walls; animals digest internally and have no cell walls.

questions.stem: Roughly what fraction of described animal species are invertebrates?
choices: About 5%
About 25%
About 50%
About 95%
questions.explanation: Invertebrates, dominated by insects and other arthropods, make up about 95% of described animal species. Vertebrates, though familiar, are a small minority.

questions.stem: Bilateral symmetry is closely linked to cephalization. Why?
choices: Bilateral animals cannot move, so they need a brain to catch food.
Radial animals have more sense organs than bilateral ones.
An animal that moves head-first benefits from sense organs and nerve cells concentrated at the front end.
Cephalization requires a shell to protect it.
questions.explanation: A bilateral body has a front end that meets new surroundings first, so concentrating senses and nerve cells there (cephalization) pays off. Radial animals such as jellyfish meet the world from all sides and lack a head.

questions.stem: Which animal has bilateral symmetry but no body cavity of any kind?
choices: An earthworm
A jellyfish
A flatworm
A crab
questions.explanation: Flatworms are bilateral with no body cavity between gut and body wall. Earthworms and crabs have a true coelom, and jellyfish are radially symmetric.

questions.stem: Which feature do all chordates have at some stage of their lives?
choices: A backbone
Four limbs
A notochord
Lungs
questions.explanation: All chordates have a notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord, pharyngeal slits and post-anal tail at some stage. Lancelets and sea squirts are chordates with no backbone, and fish have neither four limbs nor (in most) lungs.

questions.stem: Why was the evolution of the amniotic egg important?
choices: It allowed fish to breathe air.
It made animals endothermic.
It let vertebrates reproduce on land without needing water for their eggs.
It allowed fertilization to occur outside the body.
questions.explanation: The amnion and other membranes surround the embryo with its own fluid and handle gas exchange and wastes, so reptiles (including birds) and mammals could reproduce away from water. It is unrelated to air breathing and endothermy, and amniotic eggs are fertilized internally.

questions.stem: As a room is cooled from 25 °C to 5 °C, an animal's oxygen consumption at rest rises steadily. The animal is most likely
choices: an ectotherm whose metabolism speeds up in the cold
an ectotherm becoming more active to find warmth
an endotherm whose body temperature is falling with the air
an endotherm burning more fuel to hold its body temperature
questions.explanation: An endotherm keeps its body near a constant temperature, so in colder air it loses heat faster and must raise its metabolism, using more oxygen. An ectotherm's metabolism slows in the cold, and an endotherm's body temperature stays nearly constant.

questions.stem: Key: 1a. Jointed legs: go to 2. 1b. No jointed legs: go to 3. 2a. Eight legs: spider. 2b. Six legs: insect. 3a. Segmented body: earthworm. 3b. Unsegmented soft body with a shell: snail. An animal has no jointed legs and a soft, unsegmented body with a coiled shell. What is it?
choices: Earthworm
Snail
Insect
Spider
questions.explanation: Step 1b (no jointed legs) leads to 3, and 3b (unsegmented, shell) gives snail. Each step of a dichotomous key offers two mutually exclusive choices based on observable features.

questions.stem: A marine animal has tube feet and is radially symmetric as an adult, but its larvae are bilateral. In its embryo, the first opening becomes the anus. To which phylum does it belong?
choices: Cnidaria
Echinodermata
Mollusca
Arthropoda
questions.explanation: Tube feet, adult radial symmetry with bilateral larvae, and deuterostome development identify an echinoderm (like a sea star). Cnidarians are radial throughout and have no tube feet; mollusks and arthropods are protostomes.

questions.stem: Why are sea stars considered closer relatives of humans than insects are?
choices: Sea stars have a backbone.
Sea stars and humans both have radial symmetry as adults.
Sea stars and chordates are both deuterostomes, sharing a pattern of embryo development and DNA evidence of common ancestry.
Insects have no body cavity.
questions.explanation: Echinoderms and chordates are deuterostomes, a lineage confirmed by DNA. Sea stars have no backbone, humans are bilateral, and insects do have a coelom.

questions.stem: Where do birds fit on the vertebrate evolutionary tree?
choices: Within the reptiles, as descendants of feathered dinosaurs
On a separate branch closer to mammals than to reptiles
Within the amphibians
As the ancestors of all reptiles
questions.explanation: Birds descend from feathered theropod dinosaurs, so they sit inside the reptile branch; crocodiles are their closest living relatives. Birds and mammals are both endothermic, but they evolved it separately.

questions.stem: Why must a growing grasshopper molt?
choices: Its skin dries out every few days.
Molting removes parasites from its coelom.
Molting is how it reproduces asexually.
Its exoskeleton cannot grow, so it must be shed and replaced with a larger one.
questions.explanation: An arthropod's chitin exoskeleton is rigid and non-living, so it must be shed periodically for the animal to grow. Molting is not a form of reproduction.

questions.stem: Which of these is an example of negative feedback?
choices: Oxytocin strengthening contractions that release more oxytocin during childbirth
Activated platelets releasing chemicals that activate more platelets
Sweating when body temperature rises, which cools the body back toward 37 °C
Ripening fruit releasing ethylene that makes nearby fruit ripen and release more ethylene
questions.explanation: In negative feedback, the response reverses the change: sweating lowers a temperature that rose. The other three are positive feedback, where the response amplifies the change until an event (birth, a sealed wound, ripe fruit) ends it.

questions.stem: Why does the body rely on negative feedback, rather than positive feedback, to hold variables such as temperature steady?
choices: Negative feedback opposes any change, so it is self-correcting; positive feedback would push the variable further from its set point.
Positive feedback is too slow to respond to changes.
Negative feedback needs no sensors or effectors.
Positive feedback only works through hormones.
questions.explanation: Holding a set point requires a response that reverses deviations. Positive feedback amplifies them, which suits events that must be completed (childbirth, clotting) but would make a variable run away. Both kinds use sensors and effectors, and positive feedback can involve nerves as well as hormones.

questions.stem: A person steps out into freezing wind. Which pair of responses does the hypothalamus trigger to keep the core warm?
choices: Widening of skin blood vessels and sweating
Narrowing of skin blood vessels and shivering
Widening of skin blood vessels and shivering
Narrowing of skin blood vessels and sweating
questions.explanation: Vasoconstriction keeps warm blood away from the cold skin, reducing heat loss, and shivering muscles release heat. Vasodilation and sweating are the responses to overheating; mixing them with cold responses would work against each other.

questions.stem: After a meal, blood glucose is 150 mg/dL; the set point is 90 mg/dL. Suppose insulin action removes half of the excess above the set point every 30 minutes. What is the glucose level 1 hour later?
choices: 120 mg/dL
105 mg/dL
90 mg/dL
75 mg/dL
questions.explanation: The excess is $150 - 90 = 60$. After 30 min it is 30, after 60 min it is 15, so glucose is $90 + 15 = 105$ mg/dL. 120 is the value after only one interval; 90 assumes the excess disappears completely; 75 halves the whole glucose level instead of the excess.

questions.stem: A sensory neuron is stimulated first weakly (but above threshold) and then much more strongly. How do its action potentials differ?
choices: They are larger with the stronger stimulus.
They are the same size, but they fire more often with the stronger stimulus.
They travel faster with the stronger stimulus.
Only the weak stimulus produces action potentials.
questions.explanation: Action potentials are all-or-none: once threshold is reached, each impulse has the same size and speed. Stimulus strength is coded by how frequently they fire.

questions.stem: Repeating Helmholtz's experiment, a nerve is stimulated 60 mm from a muscle (twitch after 3.0 ms) and 15 mm from it (twitch after 1.5 ms). What is the conduction speed?
choices: 20 m/s
30 m/s
10 m/s
40 m/s
questions.explanation: Subtracting cancels the muscle's own delay: $\dfrac{60 - 15}{3.0 - 1.5} = \dfrac{45 \text{ mm}}{1.5 \text{ ms}} = 30$ mm/ms $= 30$ m/s. Using one trial alone (60/3.0 or 15/1.5) includes the muscle delay and gives 20 or 10; 60/1.5 mixes the trials.

questions.stem: Diseases that damage myelin slow nerve signals. Why does myelin normally speed conduction?
choices: It produces extra neurotransmitter.
It makes action potentials larger.
It pumps sodium ions into the axon.
It insulates the axon so the impulse jumps from gap to gap instead of traveling continuously.
questions.explanation: Myelin is a fatty insulating sheath with gaps; the action potential is regenerated only at the gaps, so it effectively jumps along the axon. It doesn't change the size of the impulse or release transmitters, and the ion pumps are in the neuron's own membrane.

questions.stem: What makes the inside of a neuron become positive during the rising phase of an action potential?
choices: Potassium ions rushing in through opened channels
Sodium ions being pumped out by the sodium-potassium pump
Sodium ions rushing in through opened channels
Neurotransmitter molecules entering the axon
questions.explanation: At threshold, sodium channels open and positive sodium ions flood in. Potassium then flows out (not in) to restore the negative inside. The pump maintains the resting gradients but is too slow to produce the spike.

questions.stem: A drug blocks the enzyme that breaks down acetylcholine at the synapses between nerves and muscles. What would you predict?
choices: Acetylcholine stays in the synapse and keeps stimulating the muscle, causing prolonged contraction.
The muscle can no longer receive any signal.
Nerve impulses stop traveling along the axon.
The muscle relaxes permanently because acetylcholine is used up.
questions.explanation: Normally the transmitter is broken down so each signal is brief. If it isn't removed, it keeps binding receptors and the muscle keeps being stimulated. Conduction along the axon itself is unaffected.

questions.stem: Bayliss and Starling cut all the nerves between the intestine and the pancreas, yet acid entering the intestine still made the pancreas release digestive juice. What did they conclude?
choices: The pancreas works without any signal at all.
The nerves had grown back during the experiment.
Acid travels from the intestine directly into the pancreas.
A chemical messenger carried in the blood links the two organs.
questions.explanation: With the nerves cut, the signal had to travel another way: through the blood. They extracted the messenger (secretin), the first hormone discovered. The response was triggered by acid in the intestine, so it wasn't spontaneous.

questions.stem: Several hours after a meal, blood glucose drops below the set point. Which response restores it?
choices: The pancreas releases glucagon, and the liver breaks down glycogen and releases glucose.
The pancreas releases insulin, and cells take up more glucose.
The pancreas releases glucagon, and muscle cells take up glucose from the blood.
The liver stores more glucose as glycogen.
questions.explanation: Low glucose triggers glucagon from the alpha cells, which makes the liver release glucose from its glycogen stores. Insulin and glycogen storage lower blood glucose, which would make the problem worse.

questions.stem: What is the underlying problem in type 1 diabetes?
choices: Cells stop responding to insulin even though plenty is made.
The pancreas makes too much glucagon.
The kidneys fail to remove glucose from the blood.
The immune system destroys the insulin-making beta cells, so little insulin is produced.
questions.explanation: Type 1 diabetes is autoimmune: beta cells are destroyed, so the body makes little or no insulin. Insulin resistance describes type 2 diabetes. Kidneys normally reabsorb glucose rather than remove it.

questions.stem: Blood leaving the right ventricle goes next to the
choices: body, through the aorta
left atrium, through a valve
lungs, through the pulmonary vein
lungs, through the pulmonary artery
questions.explanation: The right side of the heart pumps oxygen-poor blood to the lungs through the pulmonary artery. The aorta leaves the left ventricle; the pulmonary veins bring blood back from the lungs to the left atrium.

questions.stem: Which blood vessel carries oxygen-rich blood?
choices: The pulmonary vein
The pulmonary artery
The vena cava
A vein returning blood from the leg
questions.explanation: The pulmonary veins carry freshly oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium. Vessels are named for direction (arteries away from the heart, veins toward it), not oxygen content, so the pulmonary artery carries oxygen-poor blood.

questions.stem: During exercise, a student's heart rate is 80 beats per minute and the stroke volume is 75 mL. What is the cardiac output?
choices: 0.6 L/min
60 L/min
155 mL/min
6.0 L/min
questions.explanation: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume $= 80 \times 75 = 6000$ mL/min $= 6.0$ L/min. 0.6 and 60 are unit-conversion slips (1000 mL = 1 L); 155 adds the two numbers instead of multiplying.

questions.stem: William Harvey calculated that the heart pumps far more blood in a day than a person eats and drinks, or than the whole body contains. What did this show?
choices: The liver makes new blood very quickly.
Blood is mostly water absorbed from the air.
The same blood must circulate repeatedly instead of being made from food and used up.
Arteries and veins are not connected.
questions.explanation: Thousands of liters a day can't be made from food or held in the body, so the same blood must loop round. That contradicted Galen's idea of constant production and consumption, and it predicted connections between arteries and veins (capillaries), found later.

questions.stem: Why does exchange of oxygen and nutrients with tissues happen in capillaries rather than in arteries?
choices: Capillary walls are one cell thick, so substances diffuse across them quickly.
Capillaries have valves that push substances out.
Blood in capillaries is under the highest pressure.
Capillaries carry blood directly from the heart.
questions.explanation: Diffusion is fast only across short distances, and capillary walls are a single thin cell layer. Arteries have thick, muscular walls; valves are found in veins; pressure is highest in the large arteries.

questions.stem: What is the main signal that makes you breathe faster during exercise?
choices: Falling oxygen in the blood
Rising blood glucose
Falling body temperature
Rising carbon dioxide, which lowers blood pH
questions.explanation: Brainstem sensors respond mainly to carbon dioxide, which forms carbonic acid and lowers pH. Faster breathing removes it: negative feedback. Low oxygen matters only when it gets quite low.

questions.stem: What happens as you inhale?
choices: The lungs expand on their own, pulling the diaphragm upward.
The diaphragm contracts and flattens, chest volume increases, pressure in the lungs falls, and air flows in.
The diaphragm relaxes, increasing pressure in the lungs and drawing air in.
Air pressure in the lungs rises above outside air pressure.
questions.explanation: Contracting the diaphragm and rib muscles enlarges the chest; lower pressure inside means outside air pushes in. Lungs have no muscle of their own; a relaxing diaphragm and higher lung pressure push air out.

questions.stem: A person breathes 15 times per minute with a tidal volume of 600 mL. Dead space is 150 mL per breath. What is the alveolar ventilation?
choices: 9.0 L/min
2.25 L/min
6.75 L/min
0.45 L/min
questions.explanation: Alveolar ventilation $= (600 - 150) \times 15 = 6750$ mL/min $= 6.75$ L/min. 9.0 L/min is total minute ventilation (ignores dead space), 2.25 L/min is the dead-space ventilation, and 0.45 L is the useful air in a single breath, not per minute.

questions.stem: A resting person uses 0.30 L of oxygen per minute. About 20 kJ of energy is released per liter of oxygen. How much energy does the person use per hour?
choices: 360 kJ
6 kJ
18 kJ
questions.explanation: Per minute: $0.30 \times 20 = 6$ kJ. Per hour: $6 \times 60 = 360$ kJ. 6 kJ is per minute, 18 kJ multiplies 0.30 by 60 without the energy factor, and 8,640 kJ is the total for a whole day.

questions.stem: The kidneys of a person filter 170 L of fluid in a day and produce 1.7 L of urine. What percentage of the filtered water is reabsorbed?
questions.explanation: Reabsorbed $= 170 - 1.7 = 168.3$ L, and $168.3/170 = 0.99$, so 99%. 1% is the fraction that becomes urine; 90% and 10% are off by a factor of ten in the urine fraction.

questions.stem: Glucose is found in the fluid entering a nephron's tubule, but healthy urine contains almost no glucose. Why?
choices: Glucose is too large to be filtered.
Glucose is filtered at the glomerulus and then almost entirely reabsorbed into the blood along the tubule.
The bladder absorbs glucose from urine.
Glucose is converted to urea in the kidney.
questions.explanation: Filtration is nonselective for small molecules, so glucose enters the filtrate; carriers in the tubule then reclaim nearly all of it. Glucose is small enough to pass the filter, which is why it's in the filtrate. Urea comes from amino acids, not glucose.

questions.stem: After hours of hiking without water, a person's blood becomes more concentrated. What happens next?
choices: ADH release falls, and a large volume of dilute urine is made.
The kidneys stop filtering blood until the person drinks.
The pituitary releases more ADH, more water is reabsorbed, and a small volume of concentrated urine is made.
More water is secreted into the tubules to flush out salt.
questions.explanation: Concentrated blood is sensed by the hypothalamus; ADH makes the collecting ducts more permeable to water, so water returns to the blood: negative feedback. Less ADH is the response to drinking a lot. Filtration continues all the time.

questions.stem: Where does most chemical digestion and nearly all absorption of nutrients take place?
choices: The stomach
The large intestine
The esophagus
The small intestine
questions.explanation: Pancreatic enzymes and bile act in the small intestine, and its villi absorb the products. The stomach starts protein digestion but absorbs little; the large intestine mainly absorbs water; the esophagus only moves food.

questions.stem: What does bile do?
choices: It is an enzyme that digests fats into fatty acids.
It digests proteins in the stomach.
It breaks large fat droplets into tiny ones, giving lipase more surface to work on.
It neutralizes all the acid in the large intestine.
questions.explanation: Bile, made by the liver and stored in the gallbladder, emulsifies fat; it contains no enzymes. Lipase does the chemical digestion. Pepsin digests proteins in the stomach, and bicarbonate from the pancreas neutralizes acid in the small intestine.

questions.stem: Proteins in food are absorbed mainly in the form of
choices: fatty acids
amino acids
simple sugars
nucleotides
questions.explanation: Digestion hydrolyzes proteins (starting with pepsin in the stomach) into amino acids, which are absorbed in the small intestine. Fatty acids come from fats, sugars from carbohydrates, nucleotides from nucleic acids.

questions.stem: In celiac disease, an immune reaction to gluten flattens the villi of the small intestine. What would you predict?
choices: Faster absorption, because food passes more easily
No change in absorption, because villi only produce mucus
Less acid production in the stomach
Reduced absorption of nutrients, because the absorbing surface area is much smaller
questions.explanation: Villi multiply the surface area for absorption, so flattening them reduces nutrient uptake. They are absorbing structures, not mucus producers, and the stomach is unaffected.

questions.stem: A snack contains 30 g of carbohydrate, 10 g of protein and 12 g of fat. Using 4, 4 and 9 kcal per gram, what is its energy content?
choices: 268 kcal
208 kcal
468 kcal
52 kcal
questions.explanation: $30 \times 4 + 10 \times 4 + 12 \times 9 = 120 + 40 + 108 = 268$ kcal. Using 4 kcal/g for fat gives 208; using 9 kcal/g for everything gives 468; 52 is just the total mass in grams.

questions.stem: Spallanzani put meat in gastric juice at body temperature and saw it dissolve. Which control was needed to conclude that the juice itself digested the meat?
choices: Meat in gastric juice at a colder temperature
Gastric juice with no meat added
Meat in plain water at the same temperature for the same time
A larger piece of meat in gastric juice
questions.explanation: Only the juice should differ between the groups. Meat in water under identical conditions shows whether warmth and time alone break meat down. The other setups change different variables or have no meat to observe.

questions.stem: Which of these is part of adaptive immunity?
choices: Stomach acid killing swallowed bacteria
Antibodies made against one particular strain of virus
Inflammation around a splinter
Neutrophils engulfing any bacteria they meet
questions.explanation: Adaptive immunity is specific to one antigen and builds memory; antibodies are its hallmark. Stomach acid, inflammation and general phagocytes act against any invader and belong to innate immunity.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes an antigen from an antibody?
choices: An antigen is made by B cells; an antibody is found on the surface of bacteria.
Antigens and antibodies are two names for the same molecule.
An antigen is a foreign molecule the immune system recognizes; an antibody is a protein made by B cells that binds it.
An antigen is a type of white blood cell; an antibody is a type of virus.
questions.explanation: The antigen is the marker (often a surface protein of a pathogen); the antibody is the Y-shaped protein the body makes to bind that marker. Swapping the two (saying B cells make antigens) is a common mix-up.

questions.stem: A person's second exposure to an antigen produces antibodies within a few days at about ten times the level of the first exposure, which took about two weeks to peak. What explains this?
choices: Memory cells formed during the first response multiply quickly when the antigen returns.
Antibodies from the first exposure have been circulating at a high level ever since.
The antigen is weaker the second time.
Innate immunity learns to recognize the antigen.
questions.explanation: The first exposure leaves long-lived memory B and T cells, so the secondary response is faster and larger. Antibody levels fall after the primary response, the antigen hasn't changed, and memory is a feature of adaptive, not innate, immunity.

questions.stem: What does an mRNA vaccine deliver?
choices: A weakened form of the whole virus that multiplies slowly
Ready-made antibodies against the virus
Instructions that cells use for a short time to make one protein of the pathogen, which the immune system learns to recognize
Genes that become permanently part of the person's DNA
questions.explanation: The mRNA is translated in the cytoplasm into one viral protein (the antigen), then broken down within days; it never enters the nucleus and can't change DNA. Ready-made antibodies give short-term passive protection, not vaccination; live attenuated vaccines are a different type.

questions.stem: A disease has $R_0 = 5$. What fraction of the population must be immune to reach the herd immunity threshold?
questions.explanation: Threshold $= 1 - \tfrac{1}{R_0} = 1 - \tfrac15 = 0.80$, or 80%. 20% is $1/R_0$ itself; 95% is the kind of value needed for measles, whose $R_0$ is much higher.

questions.stem: HIV infects and destroys helper T cells. Why does this weaken the immune system so broadly?
choices: Helper T cells activate B cells and cytotoxic T cells, so both antibody and cell-killing responses fail.
Helper T cells are the only cells that make antibodies.
Helper T cells form the skin barrier.
Helper T cells are the main phagocytes.
questions.explanation: Helper T cells coordinate the adaptive response. Without them, B cells (which make antibodies) and cytotoxic T cells are poorly activated, leaving the body open to infections. Antibodies come from B cells, and phagocytes are innate cells.

questions.stem: In the food chain grass → rabbit → fox, what do the arrows show?
choices: The direction energy moves, from the food to the organism that eats it
Which organism hunts which, pointing from predator to prey
The order in which the organisms evolved
The direction in which matter is lost from the ecosystem
questions.explanation: Food-chain arrows point from the food to the eater, because they show energy (and matter) moving into the consumer. Reading them as "hunts" reverses them, the most common error. They say nothing about evolutionary order, and matter is recycled rather than lost.

questions.stem: The producers in a prairie store 80,000 kJ of energy per square meter per year. Using the ten percent rule, about how much energy reaches the secondary consumers?
choices: 800 kJ
80 kJ
8 kJ
questions.explanation: Secondary consumers are two transfers above producers: $80{,}000 \times 0.1 \times 0.1 = 800$ kJ. 8,000 kJ stops after one transfer (that is the primary consumers). 80 kJ takes three transfers, which counts levels instead of steps, and 8 kJ takes four.

questions.stem: A forest's plants capture 30,000 kJ per m² per year (gross primary productivity) and use 18,000 kJ per m² per year in their own cellular respiration. What is the net primary productivity?
choices: 48,000 kJ per m² per year
18,000 kJ per m² per year
12,000 kJ per m² per year
3,000 kJ per m² per year
questions.explanation: NPP = GPP − producer respiration = 30,000 − 18,000 = 12,000 kJ per m² per year. Adding gives 48,000, but respiration is a loss. 18,000 is the respiration itself. 3,000 is 10% of GPP, which confuses NPP with the ten percent rule between trophic levels.

questions.stem: Which ecological pyramid can never be inverted (wider at the top than at the bottom)?
choices: Pyramid of numbers
Pyramid of biomass
All three can be inverted in some ecosystems
Pyramid of energy
questions.explanation: Each trophic level gets its energy from the level below and loses some as heat, so a higher level can never carry more energy flow than the one feeding it. Numbers pyramids invert easily (one tree, thousands of caterpillars), and biomass pyramids can invert in the open ocean.

questions.stem: In some parts of the open ocean, the zooplankton present at a given moment weigh more than the phytoplankton they eat. How is this possible?
choices: Phytoplankton reproduce so quickly that they are eaten and replaced many times a year
Zooplankton are producers that make their own food
Energy flows from zooplankton back to phytoplankton
