Zooplankton get most of their energy directly from sunlight
questions.explanation: A biomass pyramid is a snapshot of what is present at one moment. Fast-reproducing phytoplankton have a small standing biomass but a large total production over the year, enough to feed a larger standing mass of zooplankton. Zooplankton are consumers, and energy never flows back down the food chain.

questions.stem: A rabbit eats 1,000 kJ of grass, but only about 100 kJ ends up as new rabbit tissue. Where does most of the rest go?
choices: It is destroyed during digestion
It is released as heat from the rabbit's cellular respiration, with some leaving in feces
It is stored as fat for the fox
It is returned to the grass as sunlight
questions.explanation: Most absorbed energy powers the rabbit's activity and body heat through cellular respiration and leaves as heat; undigested material leaves in feces and feeds decomposers. Energy is conserved, never destroyed. Fat is part of the 100 kJ of tissue, and energy does not return to plants as sunlight.

questions.stem: Which of these is an abiotic factor in a forest ecosystem?
choices: A fungus decomposing a log
The deer that browse on shrubs
The pH of the soil
Fallen leaves on the forest floor
questions.explanation: Soil pH is a nonliving physical and chemical condition. The fungus and deer are living. Fallen leaves are dead but came from living things, so they count as biotic material.

questions.stem: In Odum's Silver Springs study, the producers' gross production was about 20,810 kcal per m² per year and the herbivores' was about 3,368. About what percent of the producers' energy reached the herbivores?
questions.explanation: $3368 \div 20{,}810 \approx 0.16$, or about 16%, a bit above the typical 10%. 84% is the share that was not transferred. 6.2% comes from dividing the wrong way ($20{,}810 \div 3368 \approx 6.2$). 11% is the herbivore-to-carnivore transfer in the same study.

questions.stem: A grizzly bear eats berries in late summer and salmon (which eat smaller fish) in the fall. Which statement about the bear is correct?
choices: It feeds at more than one trophic level
It is a producer because it eats plants
It is only a primary consumer
It is a decomposer because it eats dead fish
questions.explanation: Eating berries makes the bear a primary consumer (level 2); eating salmon that eat other fish puts it at level 4 or higher. Omnivores often occupy several levels. Eating plants makes it a consumer, not a producer, and catching live fish is predation, not decomposition.

questions.stem: If all decomposers were removed from an ecosystem, what would happen over time?
choices: Producers would get more energy, because decomposers no longer take any
Nutrients would stay locked in dead material, and producers would run short of them
Nothing important, because decomposers are at the top of the food chain
Energy would begin to cycle instead of flowing through
questions.explanation: Decomposers break down dead organisms and wastes and release nutrients such as nitrogen and phosphorus for plants to reuse. Without them, nutrients pile up in dead material and plant growth would eventually stall. Producers get their energy from sunlight, not from decomposers, and energy never cycles.

questions.stem: A student clips, dries and weighs all plants in four 0.50 m² quadrats and gets a mean dry mass of 120 g per quadrat. What is the estimated biomass density?
choices: 60 g per m²
120 g per m²
240 g per m²
480 g per m²
questions.explanation: Divide the mean mass by the quadrat area: $120 \text{ g} \div 0.50 \text{ m}^2 = 240$ g per m². 60 multiplies by 0.50 instead of dividing. 120 ignores the quadrat size. 480 adds up all four quadrats without dividing by the area they cover (2.0 m²).

questions.stem: Which process removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and moves its carbon into food webs?
choices: Cellular respiration
Combustion of fossil fuels
Decomposition
Photosynthesis
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis builds CO₂ into sugars, the entry point of carbon into living things. Respiration, decomposition (which is respiration by decomposers) and combustion all release CO₂ to the air.

questions.stem: The Mauna Loa CO₂ record rises every year but also dips each Northern Hemisphere spring and summer. What best explains the summer dips?
choices: Photosynthesis by the large area of northern land plants increases during their growing season
People burn less fossil fuel in summer
Warm oceans absorb more CO₂ in summer
Volcanoes are less active in summer
questions.explanation: The Northern Hemisphere has most of the world's land plants. In its growing season, photosynthesis outpaces respiration and draws CO₂ down; in fall and winter, decay and respiration dominate. Fuel use does not fall enough to explain it, warm water actually holds less dissolved gas, and volcanoes have no seasons.

questions.stem: What happens in nitrogen fixation?
choices: Plants absorb nitrate from the soil through their roots
Bacteria convert nitrogen gas (N₂) into ammonia or ammonium
Bacteria convert nitrate back into nitrogen gas
Animals excrete nitrogen in urea
questions.explanation: Fixation turns unusable N₂ into ammonia/ammonium, mostly by bacteria (some in legume root nodules), plus lightning and the industrial Haber–Bosch process. Absorbing nitrate is assimilation, converting nitrate to N₂ is denitrification, and urea excretion is part of returning nitrogen through wastes.

questions.stem: Where is denitrification most likely to happen?
choices: In legume root nodules
In lightning strikes
In waterlogged, low-oxygen soil
In the leaves of plants during photosynthesis
questions.explanation: Denitrifying bacteria use nitrate in place of oxygen, so they are most active where oxygen is scarce, such as soggy soils and wetland sediments, releasing N₂ back to the air. Root nodules and lightning are sites of nitrogen fixation, the opposite process.

questions.stem: Fertilizer runoff reaches a bay, and fish later die in a large low-oxygen dead zone. What is the most direct cause of the low oxygen?
choices: Nitrate is poisonous to fish
Fertilizer reacts with oxygen in the water
Algae use up oxygen by photosynthesis
Decomposers breaking down the dead algae from blooms use up the oxygen
questions.explanation: Extra nitrogen fuels algal blooms. When the algae die, decomposers respire as they break them down and consume the dissolved oxygen. This is eutrophication. Photosynthesis releases oxygen rather than using it, and the fertilizer does not react with oxygen directly.

questions.stem: A population of 50 frogs grows by a factor of $\lambda = 1.2$ each year. Using $N_t = N_0\lambda^t$, about how many frogs are there after 3 years?
questions.explanation: $N_3 = 50 \times 1.2^3 = 50 \times 1.728 = 86.4 \approx 86$. 80 adds 20% of the original 50 each year (linear growth, $50 + 3 \times 10$). 180 multiplies by $1.2 \times 3$. 104 uses 4 years ($50 \times 1.2^4$).

questions.stem: A population follows logistic growth with $r = 0.5$ per year and $K = 1000$. How fast is it growing when $N = 250$?
choices: 125 individuals per year
About 94 individuals per year
About 31 individuals per year
375 individuals per year
questions.explanation: $\frac{dN}{dt} = rN\frac{K-N}{K} = 0.5 \times 250 \times \frac{750}{1000} = 93.75 \approx 94$. 125 is $rN$, the exponential rate that ignores $K$. 31 uses $N/K$ instead of $(K-N)/K$. 375 divides by $N$ instead of $K$, which leaves just $r(K-N)$.

questions.stem: For a population growing logistically toward carrying capacity $K$, at what population size is the number of individuals added per year greatest?
choices: Very small $N$, near 0
Just below $K$
Above $K$
questions.explanation: $dN/dt = rN(K-N)/K$ is a product of $N$ (small when the population is small) and $(K-N)$ (small near $K$); it peaks halfway, at $N = K/2$, the steepest part of the S-curve. Above $K$ the growth rate is negative.

questions.stem: Which of these is a density-independent factor?
choices: A disease that spreads faster when animals are crowded
Competition for nesting sites
Predators that focus on the most common prey
An early frost that kills 40% of the insects in an area whatever their number
questions.explanation: A frost kills the same fraction whether the population is large or small, so its effect does not depend on density. Disease, competition and predation all hit harder as density rises, so they are density-dependent.

questions.stem: Biologists catch and band 60 birds, then release them. A week later they catch 45 birds, and 9 have bands. What is the Lincoln–Petersen estimate of the population?
questions.explanation: $N = \frac{MC}{R} = \frac{60 \times 45}{9} = 300$. Check: 9 of 45 (20%) are banded, and 60 is 20% of 300. 2,700 forgets to divide by $R$. 405 is $45 \times 9$, and 7 inverts the formula; a population smaller than the 60 birds already banded is impossible.

questions.stem: Reindeer introduced to St. Matthew Island grew from 29 (1944) to about 6,000 (1963), overgrazed the slow-growing lichen, and crashed to 42 (1966) after a severe winter. Which conclusion do these data best support?
choices: Reindeer populations are limited only by predators
The population overshot the island's carrying capacity and damaged its own food supply
The population was growing logistically and stayed near $K$
Density-independent factors had no role in the crash
questions.explanation: The herd grew almost exponentially past what the lichen could sustain, then crashed, a classic overshoot. There were no predators, so predation cannot be the limit. A population that stays near $K$ does not crash by 99%. The severe winter (density-independent) triggered the crash after food shortage (density-dependent) set it up.

questions.stem: Barnacles attach to a whale's skin and filter food as the whale swims; the whale is neither helped nor harmed. What kind of interaction is this?
choices: Mutualism
Parasitism
Commensalism
Competition
questions.explanation: One species benefits and the other is unaffected (+/0): commensalism. Mutualism needs both to benefit, parasitism needs the host to be harmed, and competition harms both.

questions.stem: A sample contains 20 beetles: 5 each of four species. What is Simpson's diversity index, $D = 1 - \frac{\sum n(n-1)}{N(N-1)}$?
questions.explanation: $\sum n(n-1) = 4 \times (5 \times 4) = 80$ and $N(N-1) = 20 \times 19 = 380$, so $D = 1 - \frac{80}{380} = 0.79$. 0.21 forgets to subtract from 1. 0.75 uses $n^2/N^2$ (sampling with replacement) instead of the formula given, and 0.25 is just $1/4$.

questions.stem: Forest X has 100 trees: 25 each of four species. Forest Y has 100 trees: 85 of one species and 5 each of three others. Which statement is correct?
choices: Both have the same species richness, but X is more diverse because it is more even
Y is more diverse because it has more trees of its main species
They are equally diverse because both have four species
X is less diverse because no species dominates
questions.explanation: Both forests have four species (equal richness), but X spreads its trees evenly while Y is dominated by one species. Diversity indexes such as Simpson's count evenness as well as richness, so X scores higher. Treating richness as the whole of diversity is the mistake behind the third choice.

questions.stem: When Robert Paine removed the sea star Pisaster from a rocky shore, mussels took over and the number of species fell from 15 to 8. What does this show?
choices: Sea stars compete with mussels for sunlight
Pisaster is a keystone species that maintains diversity by keeping a dominant competitor in check
Mussels are parasites of other shore organisms
Removing a predator always increases diversity
questions.explanation: The predator kept mussels from monopolizing space, so its removal caused a large drop in species: the definition of a keystone species. Sea stars are predators of mussels, not competitors for light. The mussels outcompeted the others rather than parasitizing them, and the result shows the opposite of "removing a predator increases diversity."

questions.stem: A farm field is abandoned. Weeds appear the first year, then grasses and shrubs, then young pine trees after about 15 years. What is this?
choices: Primary succession, because the community is starting over
Competitive exclusion
Secondary succession, because soil was already present
Biomagnification
questions.explanation: Succession that begins where soil remains (after farming, fire or storms) is secondary succession, and it is fast because seeds and soil organisms are already there. Primary succession starts on bare rock or new ground with no soil.

questions.stem: A biome has very cold temperatures most of the year, permanently frozen ground below the surface, and low-growing mosses, lichens and shrubs but no trees. Which biome is it?
choices: Boreal forest
Desert
Temperate grassland
Tundra
questions.explanation: Permafrost and a treeless landscape of mosses, lichens and low shrubs define the tundra. The boreal forest is also cold but has dense conifers. Deserts are defined by low precipitation, and temperate grasslands have deep soils and warm summers.

questions.stem: Gause grew two Paramecium species separately and each thrived. Grown together on the same limited food, one species always died out. Which idea does this support?
choices: The competitive exclusion principle
Mutualism between the two species
The ten percent rule
Primary succession
questions.explanation: Two species using the same limited resource in the same place cannot coexist indefinitely; one outcompetes the other. That is competitive exclusion. Mutualism would help both species, and the ten percent rule and succession concern energy flow and community change over time.

questions.stem: According to the 2019 IPBES global assessment, what is the largest single driver of biodiversity loss on land?
choices: Invasive species
Habitat loss from changes in land use
Light pollution
Natural volcanic eruptions
questions.explanation: Converting forests, grasslands and wetlands to farms, cities and roads is the leading driver. Invasive species, climate change, pollution and overexploitation matter too, but rank behind land-use change on land. Volcanoes are natural and not a major cause of current losses.

questions.stem: In a lake, DDT measures 0.04 ppm in zooplankton and 10 ppm in fish-eating birds. By what factor is DDT more concentrated in the birds?
questions.explanation: $10 \div 0.04 = 250$. This is biomagnification: each predator eats many prey and stores the fat-soluble toxin. 0.004 divides the wrong way, and 25 and 2,500 are decimal-place slips.

questions.stem: Why do invasive species often spread so rapidly after being introduced to a new region?
choices: They have higher mutation rates than native species
They are always larger than native species
They are producers, which grow faster than consumers
They often lack the predators, parasites and competitors that limited them in their native range
questions.explanation: Freed from the enemies that kept them in check at home, introduced species can grow nearly exponentially, as the brown tree snake did on Guam. Invasives include animals and plants of every size, and nothing makes their mutation rates special.

questions.stem: Long-term fur records show snowshoe hare and lynx numbers both cycling about every 10 years. How do the peaks typically line up?
choices: Lynx peaks come shortly after hare peaks
Lynx peaks come shortly before hare peaks
The peaks happen in exactly the same year
The two cycles are unrelated
questions.explanation: Abundant hares feed more lynx, so lynx numbers rise after hares do; when hares crash, lynx follow. Predators cannot peak before their food supply has grown. Field experiments show food supply and predation together drive the hare cycle.

cards.back: Made of cells; metabolism (uses energy); homeostasis; responds to stimuli; grows and develops; reproduces; heritable DNA; populations evolve.

cards.front: Why is a flame or a growing crystal not alive?
cards.back: It shows one or two features (growth, energy release) but has no cells, metabolism, homeostasis or DNA. Life needs the whole set.
Keeping internal conditions stable despite outside changes, usually by negative feedback (e.g. sweating when hot).

cards.front: Levels of organization, smallest to largest
cards.back: atom → molecule → organelle → cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism → population → community → ecosystem → biosphere
Population: one species in an area. Community: all species in an area. Ecosystem: the community plus nonliving surroundings.
A new ability that arises from how parts interact at a higher level, e.g. a heart pumps but a single muscle cell cannot.
Independent: the one factor you change (x-axis). Dependent: what you measure (y-axis).
Control group: subjects without the treatment, used as a baseline. Controlled variables: conditions kept the same in all groups.
Individuals vary; more subjects and repeated trials make it less likely a difference is due to chance.
$\dfrac{\text{new} - \text{original}}{\text{original}} \times 100\%$ (negative = decrease)
Hypothesis: testable explanation of one observation. Theory: broad, well-tested explanation. Law: describes a pattern without explaining it.
Two variables changing together does not show one causes the other; a third variable may drive both. Controlled experiments test causation.
Carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, phosphorus, sulfur: about 98% of living mass.
Oxygen pulls shared electrons harder than hydrogen, and the molecule is bent: O end δ−, H ends δ+.

cards.front: Properties of water caused by hydrogen bonds
cards.back: Cohesion and surface tension, adhesion and capillary action, high specific heat, ice floats, excellent solvent for polar and ionic substances.
Cohesion: water attracted to water. Adhesion: water attracted to other substances.
$\text{pH} = -\log[\text{H}^+]$, so $[\text{H}^+] = 10^{-\text{pH}}$ mol/L

cards.front: A difference of 3 pH units means…
cards.back: A $10^3 = 1000$-fold difference in H⁺ concentration; the lower pH has more H⁺.
Resists pH change by taking up or releasing H⁺; blood is buffered near pH 7.4 by bicarbonate/carbonic acid.
Dehydration synthesis joins monomers and releases water; hydrolysis splits polymers and uses water.

cards.front: Water released when $n$ monomers form one chain
cards.back: $n - 1$ molecules (one per bond)

cards.front: Four classes of macromolecules and their monomers
cards.back: Carbohydrates: monosaccharides. Proteins: amino acids. Nucleic acids: nucleotides. Lipids: no true monomer (fats are glycerol + 3 fatty acids).
All glucose polymers. Starch: plant energy store. Glycogen: animal energy store. Cellulose: plant cell walls (different linkage, indigestible to humans).
Saturated: no C=C double bonds, straight chains, solid (butter). Unsaturated: double bonds kink the chains, liquid (oils).
Benedict's (heated): simple sugars → orange/brick-red. Iodine: starch → blue-black. Biuret: protein → violet. Paper spot or Sudan III: lipid.
Primary: amino acid sequence. Secondary: helices and sheets. Tertiary: 3-D fold of one chain. Quaternary: several chains together.
DNA: deoxyribose, A T G C, double-stranded, stores information. RNA: ribose, A U G C, usually single-stranded, helps make proteins.
They lower the activation energy; they are not used up and do not change the overall energy of the reaction.

cards.front: Effect of temperature on enzyme activity
cards.back: Rises to an optimum (≈37 °C for human enzymes), then falls steeply as the enzyme denatures. Cold slows enzymes but does not denature them.
Competitive: binds the active site; overcome by more substrate. Noncompetitive: binds elsewhere and changes shape; extra substrate does not help.
Biotic: living parts of an ecosystem (organisms, dead leaves, dung). Abiotic: nonliving conditions (light, temperature, water, pH, minerals).
Producers make their own food (photosynthesis or chemosynthesis). Consumers eat other organisms. Decomposers (bacteria, fungi) break down dead matter and return nutrients.

cards.front: Which way do food-chain arrows point?
cards.back: From the food to the eater: the direction energy moves (grass → rabbit means the rabbit eats the grass).
A food chain is one feeding path; a food web shows all the interlinked feeding relationships in a community.
NPP = GPP − producer respiration: the energy producers store as new biomass, available to consumers.
About 10% (roughly 1–20%) of the energy at one trophic level reaches the next. Energy at level $n$ above producers $= E_0 \times 0.1^n$.

cards.front: Why is so little energy passed up a trophic level?
cards.back: Not everything is eaten, not everything eaten is absorbed (feces), and most absorbed energy is used in cellular respiration and lost as heat.
Energy flows one way (sunlight in, heat out). Matter (carbon, nitrogen, water) cycles and is reused.

cards.front: Which ecological pyramid is always upright?
cards.back: The pyramid of energy. Pyramids of numbers (one tree, many insects) and biomass (open-ocean plankton) can be inverted.

cards.front: Why measure biomass as dry mass?
cards.back: Water content varies with weather and time of day, so drying gives a consistent measure of living material.

cards.front: Carbon cycle: processes that add vs remove atmospheric CO₂
cards.back: Remove: photosynthesis, dissolving in the ocean. Add: cellular respiration, decomposition, combustion of fuels, volcanoes.
About 280 ppm before 1750; about 424 ppm in 2024, mainly from burning fossil fuels.
N₂ → (fixation by bacteria) ammonium → (nitrification) nitrite → nitrate → absorbed by plants → animals → (decomposers) ammonium; denitrification returns nitrate to N₂.
Excess nutrients (fertilizer runoff) cause algal blooms; decomposers breaking down dead algae use up dissolved oxygen, creating dead zones.
$\Delta N = B - D + I - E$ (births − deaths + immigration − emigration).
Continuous: $dN/dt = rN$. Discrete (yearly): $N_t = N_0\lambda^t$. J-shaped curve.
$dN/dt = rN\dfrac{K-N}{K}$. S-shaped curve; fastest at $N = K/2$; levels off at $K$.
Dependent (stronger when crowded): competition, predation, disease, parasites. Independent (same regardless of density): frost, drought, flood, fire.
$N = \dfrac{M \times C}{R}$: $M$ marked first, $C$ caught second, $R$ marked in the second catch.
Marked animals mix evenly, marks are not lost, marking does not change catchability, and no births, deaths or migration between samples.
Mutualism +/+, commensalism +/0, parasitism +/−. (Predation is +/−, competition −/−.)
Two species cannot share the same niche in the same place indefinitely; one wins, or they partition resources (MacArthur's warblers).
A species with an effect far larger than its abundance. Paine removed the sea star Pisaster and species on the shore fell from 15 to 8.
Primary: starts with no soil (lava, retreating glacier), pioneers are lichens and mosses. Secondary: soil remains (after fire or farming), faster.

cards.front: What mainly determines which biome develops?
cards.back: Climate: temperature and precipitation.

cards.front: Tundra vs boreal forest vs desert
cards.back: Tundra: very cold, permafrost, no trees. Boreal forest: cold winters, conifers. Desert: under about 25 cm of rain a year.
$D = 1 - \dfrac{\sum n(n-1)}{N(N-1)}$. Near 0: one species dominates. Near 1: many evenly represented species.
Richness: number of species. Evenness: how equally individuals are spread among them. Diversity indexes combine both.
Habitat loss (largest), climate change, invasive species, pollution, overexploitation.
A persistent, fat-soluble toxin (such as DDT) becomes more concentrated at each higher trophic level.

cards.front: The three parts of the cell theory
cards.back: All living things are made of cells; the cell is the basic unit of structure and function; all cells come from preexisting cells.

cards.front: Who contributed what to cell theory
cards.back: Hooke (1665) named cells; Leeuwenhoek saw microbes; Schleiden (plants) and Schwann (animals) are made of cells; Virchow: every cell from a cell.
Boiled broth open to air via an S-shaped neck stayed sterile; breaking the neck let dust and microbes in. Microbes come from microbes, not spontaneous generation.
Ocular × objective (e.g. 10× × 40× = 400×)
Actual size = image size ÷ magnification (convert mm to µm: × 1000)

cards.front: Field of view at higher power
cards.back: Shrinks in proportion: new diameter = old diameter × (low mag ÷ high mag). Cell size ≈ field diameter ÷ number of cells across.
Magnification: how much bigger the image is. Resolution: smallest separation still seen as two points (≈ 0.2 µm light, ≈ 1 nm or better electron).
Light: living cells, color, ≈ 1000×. Electron: far higher resolution, but dead specimens in a vacuum. TEM: thin slices; SEM: surfaces.
Plasma membrane, cytoplasm, DNA, ribosomes
Prokaryote: no nucleus or membrane-bound organelles, DNA in nucleoid, 1–5 µm (bacteria, archaea). Eukaryote: nucleus and organelles, 10–100 µm (animals, plants, fungi, protists).
Bacteria, Archaea (both prokaryotic) and Eukarya; found by comparing ribosomal RNA (Woese, 1977; domains formally proposed 1990).
Virus: not a cell, DNA or RNA in a capsid, 20–300 nm, no ribosomes or metabolism, reproduces only in a host, not affected by antibiotics. Bacterium: a living cell, 1–5 µm.

cards.front: Why antibiotics don't treat viral infections
cards.back: They target bacterial structures (peptidoglycan walls, bacterial ribosomes) that viruses don't have.
Holds DNA; double envelope with pores; nucleolus makes ribosome parts.
Rough ER: ribosomes, makes proteins for export and membranes. Smooth ER: makes lipids, detoxifies (liver), stores calcium (muscle).
Ribosome on rough ER → ER → vesicle → Golgi apparatus → secretory vesicle → exocytosis (shown by Palade's pulse–chase experiments).
Membrane sac of digestive enzymes, acidic inside (≈ pH 5); digests food particles, bacteria and worn-out organelles.
Mitochondrion: cellular respiration, makes ATP (plants and animals). Chloroplast: photosynthesis, makes sugar (plants and algae).

cards.front: Plant cells have, animal cells lack
cards.back: Cell wall (cellulose), chloroplasts, large central vacuole
Mitochondria and chloroplasts have double membranes, their own circular DNA, bacteria-like ribosomes, divide by splitting, and have DNA most similar to particular bacteria.
Membrane = fluid phospholipid bilayer with a mosaic of proteins that move sideways (Frye–Edidin cell fusion experiment).
Small nonpolar molecules (O₂, CO₂). Water slowly (fast via aquaporins). Ions and large polar molecules need transport proteins.
Passive (diffusion, facilitated diffusion, osmosis): down the gradient, no energy. Active: against the gradient, needs ATP and a pump.
Water moves toward the higher solute concentration ("water follows solute").
Hypertonic: cell loses water (shrinks, plasmolysis). Hypotonic: cell gains water (animal cell may burst, plant cell turgid). Isotonic: no net change.
$\Psi = \Psi_s + \Psi_p$, with $\Psi_s = -iCRT$; water moves from higher to lower $\Psi$.
Active transport: each ATP moves 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in.

cards.front: SA:V of a cube of side $s$
cards.back: SA $= 6s^2$, $V = s^3$, so SA:V $= 6/s$; it falls as the cube grows.
Needs grow with volume but supply through the membrane grows only with surface area; diffusion is only fast over short distances.
A cell specializes by switching genes on and off; nearly all body cells have the same DNA (Gurdon's frog nuclear transfer).
Energy is converted from one form to another, never created or destroyed.
Every energy conversion loses some energy as unusable heat, so entropy increases; living things need a constant energy input.
Catabolism breaks molecules down and releases energy (respiration). Anabolism builds molecules and requires energy (protein synthesis, Calvin cycle).
Exergonic reactions release free energy and can proceed on their own; endergonic reactions absorb free energy and need an input, usually from ATP.
Adenine + ribose + three phosphate groups (adenosine triphosphate).
ATP + H₂O → ADP + Pᵢ + energy (about 30.5 kJ/mol under standard conditions).
Using ATP hydrolysis to drive an endergonic process, usually by transferring a phosphate group to another molecule; works if the total energy change is negative.
Catabolism recharges ADP + Pᵢ into ATP; cellular work spends ATP back to ADP. A cell holds little ATP and remakes it constantly.
Oxidation Is Loss of electrons; Reduction Is Gain. NAD⁺ is reduced to NADH.
NADH and FADH₂ carry electrons in respiration; NADPH carries them in photosynthesis.
6CO₂ + 6H₂O + light → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂
Autotrophs make their own food from inorganic materials (plants, algae). Heterotrophs eat other organisms (animals, fungi).
Water, split by photosystem II (shown with ¹⁸O by Ruben and Kamen, 1941).
Van Helmont (mass not from soil) → Priestley (plants restore air) → Ingenhousz (only in light) → Engelmann (action spectrum) → Ruben and Kamen (O₂ from water) → Calvin (carbon path, ¹⁴C).
Chlorophyll absorbs mostly blue-violet and red light and reflects green.
Absorption: how much light a pigment absorbs at each wavelength. Action: how fast photosynthesis runs at each wavelength.
Thylakoid membranes. In: light, H₂O, ADP, NADP⁺. Out: O₂, ATP, NADPH.
Stroma. Rubisco fixes CO₂; ATP and NADPH reduce it to G3P. Per glucose: 6 CO₂, 18 ATP, 12 NADPH.
Light intensity, CO₂ concentration, temperature; the scarcest one sets the rate.
C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy (about 30–32 ATP)

cards.front: Stages of aerobic respiration, in order
cards.back: Glycolysis (cytoplasm) → pyruvate oxidation and Krebs cycle (mitochondrial matrix) → electron transport chain and chemiosmosis (inner membrane).
Glucose → 2 pyruvate; net 2 ATP and 2 NADH; no O₂ needed.
With pyruvate oxidation: 6 CO₂, 8 NADH, 2 FADH₂, 2 ATP.
Final electron acceptor at the end of the electron transport chain; forms water.
About 30–32 (2.5 per NADH, 1.5 per FADH₂, 4 direct). Older books: 36–38, using 3 and 2.
H⁺ pumped across a membrane by an electron transport chain flows back through ATP synthase, which makes ATP. Used in both mitochondria and chloroplasts.
Regenerates NAD⁺ so glycolysis can keep making 2 ATP per glucose without oxygen.
Lactic acid: pyruvate → lactate (muscle, yogurt bacteria). Alcoholic: pyruvate → ethanol + CO₂ (yeast).
Aerobic: needs O₂, about 30 ATP per glucose, CO₂ + H₂O. Fermentation: no O₂, 2 ATP, lactate or ethanol + CO₂.
Interphase: G1 (growth) → S (DNA replication) → G2 (preparation); then M phase: mitosis and cytokinesis.
G1 about 11 h, S about 8 h, G2 about 4 h, M about 1 h.
After S phase a chromosome has two identical sister chromatids joined at the centromere; it is still one chromosome. Count centromeres to count chromosomes.
Prophase → metaphase → anaphase → telophase (then cytokinesis).
Chromosomes condense; spindle forms; nuclear envelope breaks down.
Chromosomes line up at the middle of the cell, attached to spindle fibers from both poles.
Sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles; chromosome count in the cell briefly doubles.
Chromosomes reach the poles; nuclear envelopes re-form; chromosomes uncoil.

cards.front: Cytokinesis in animal vs plant cells
cards.back: Animal: cleavage furrow pinches the cell. Plant: a cell plate forms and becomes a new wall.
(cells in mitosis ÷ total cells) × 100%

cards.front: Time in a stage from a snapshot
cards.back: Time in stage = (cells in stage ÷ total cells) × length of the cell cycle.
G1: size, nutrients, growth factors, DNA damage. G2: DNA fully and correctly copied. Spindle (metaphase): all chromosomes attached.
A non-dividing state outside the cycle (mature nerve and heart muscle cells); cells are active but not dividing.
Cyclin levels rise and fall each cycle; a CDK is active only when bound to its cyclin and then phosphorylates targets to drive the next phase.
Programmed cell death that removes damaged or unneeded cells without inflammation.
Proto-oncogene = gas pedal (RAS); overactive mutation → oncogene, one copy enough. Tumor suppressor = brake (p53, RB); usually both copies must be lost.
Tumor suppressor that halts the cycle when DNA is damaged and triggers apoptosis if repair fails; mutated in about half of human cancers.
Benign stays in place. Malignant invades nearby tissue and can metastasize (spread through blood or lymph).
N = N₀ × 2ⁿ; 10 doublings ≈ ×1,000; 30 doublings ≈ ×1 billion.
Totipotent: every cell type including placenta (zygote). Pluripotent: every body cell type (embryonic stem cells, iPSCs). Multipotent: several related types (blood stem cells).
Body cells reprogrammed by adding four genes to act like embryonic stem cells (Yamanaka: mouse fibroblasts 2006, human skin cells 2007).
Diploid (2n): two sets of chromosomes, as in body cells (human 46). Haploid (n): one set, as in gametes (human 23).
Homologs: one from each parent, same genes, possibly different versions. Sister chromatids: identical copies made in S phase.
Meiosis I separates homologs (2n → n, reduction). Meiosis II separates sister chromatids (like mitosis).
Mitosis: 1 division, 2 identical diploid cells. Meiosis: 2 divisions, 4 genetically different haploid cells; homologs pair and cross over.

cards.front: Three sources of genetic variation in sexual reproduction
cards.back: Crossing over (prophase I), independent assortment (metaphase I), random fertilization.
2ⁿ, where n = number of homologous pairs; humans 2²³ = 8,388,608.

cards.front: Nondisjunction in meiosis I vs II
cards.back: Meiosis I: all four gametes abnormal (two n + 1, two n − 1). Meiosis II: two normal, one n + 1, one n − 1.
Each female meiosis gives one egg plus polar bodies; each male meiosis gives four sperm.
A gene is a unit of inheritance (a stretch of DNA affecting a trait). Alleles are the different versions of one gene, such as P (purple) and p (white).
Genotype: the alleles an individual has (PP, Pp, pp). Phenotype: the observable trait (purple or white).
Homozygous: two identical alleles (PP or pp). Heterozygous: two different alleles (Pp).
A dominant allele shows its effect with one copy (in a heterozygote). A recessive allele shows only when there are two copies. Dominant does not mean common or beneficial.
The two alleles of a gene separate into different gametes, each gamete getting one, with equal probability. Physical basis: homologous chromosomes separate in anaphase I.

cards.front: Aa × Aa: genotype and phenotype ratios
cards.back: Genotypes 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa. Phenotypes 3 dominant : 1 recessive.
Cross a dominant-phenotype individual of unknown genotype with a homozygous recessive. All dominant offspring suggests AA; any recessive offspring proves Aa (expected 1 : 1).

cards.front: Of the dominant-phenotype offspring of Aa × Aa, what fraction are heterozygous?
cards.back: 2/3 (two Aa boxes out of three non-aa boxes).

Alleles of different (unlinked) genes go into gametes independently. Physical basis for genes on different chromosomes: each homologous pair orients at random at metaphase I. Genes close together on one chromosome travel together unless crossing over separates them.
9 : 3 : 3 : 1 (two dominant : first dominant only : second dominant only : both recessive), out of 16.
For independent events, P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B). Example: P(aabbcc) from AaBbCc × AaBbCc = (1/4)³ = 1/64.
For mutually exclusive events, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B). Example: P(AA or aa) from Aa × Aa = 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2.

cards.front: Number of gamete types from n heterozygous unlinked genes
cards.back: $2^n$. AaBbCc makes 8; homozygous genes add no variety.

cards.front: Probability that exactly k of n children are affected (probability p each)
cards.back: $\binom{n}{k}p^k(1-p)^{n-k}$. For two carrier parents and 2 children, exactly one affected = 2 × (1/4)(3/4) = 3/8.
Incomplete dominance: heterozygote is intermediate (pink from red × white). Codominance: heterozygote shows both traits fully (AB blood, roan cattle).
1 : 2 : 1 for both genotypes and phenotypes (red : pink : white), since each genotype has its own phenotype.
A: $I^AI^A$ or $I^Ai$. B: $I^BI^B$ or $I^Bi$. AB: $I^AI^B$. O: $ii$. $I^A$ and $I^B$ are codominant; both dominant to $i$.
A: A antigen, anti-B antibodies. B: B antigen, anti-A. AB: both antigens, no antibodies. O: no antigens, both antibodies.
A trait controlled by many genes with small additive effects (height, skin color); gives continuous, bell-shaped variation.
Pleiotropy: one gene affects many traits (sickle-cell allele). Epistasis: one gene masks another (ee Labradors are yellow; 9 : 3 : 4).

cards.front: Why X-linked recessive traits are more common in males
cards.back: Males have one X, so one recessive allele is expressed. Females need two copies.
Sons: 1/2 affected. Daughters: none affected, 1/2 carriers. Any child: 1/4 is an affected son.

cards.front: Affected father × homozygous normal mother (X-linked recessive)
cards.back: All daughters are carriers; no sons are affected (sons get the father's Y).
Square = male, circle = female, filled = affected, dot or half-filled = carrier, horizontal line = mating, Roman numerals = generations.

cards.front: Pedigree clues: autosomal recessive vs dominant vs X-linked recessive
cards.back: Autosomal recessive: unaffected parents can have an affected child. Autosomal dominant: affected people have an affected parent; affected parents can have an unaffected child. X-linked recessive: mostly males, never father to son.

cards.front: Nondisjunction in meiosis I vs meiosis II
cards.back: Meiosis I: all four gametes abnormal (two n + 1, two n − 1). Meiosis II: two normal, one n + 1, one n − 1.
Down syndrome: 47,+21 (trisomy 21). Turner syndrome: 45,X. Klinefelter syndrome: 47,XXY.
Deletion (segment lost), duplication (repeated), inversion (flipped), translocation (moved to a non-homologous chromosome).

cards.front: Chi-square formula and degrees of freedom
cards.back: $\chi^2 = \sum \dfrac{(O-E)^2}{E}$ using counts; df = number of categories − 1.
df 1: 3.84; df 2: 5.99; df 3: 7.81; df 4: 9.49. Below the value: fail to reject. At or above: reject.

cards.front: Griffith, Avery, Hershey–Chase: what did each show?
cards.back: Griffith (1928): something from dead S bacteria transforms R bacteria. Avery (1944): only destroying DNA stops transformation, so the transforming principle is DNA. Hershey–Chase (1952): phage DNA (³²P), not protein (³⁵S), enters bacteria.
A phosphate group, a five-carbon sugar (deoxyribose in DNA, ribose in RNA) and a nitrogen base.
DNA: A–T (2 hydrogen bonds), G–C (3 hydrogen bonds). RNA: A–U, G–C. Each pair is one purine (A, G) with one pyrimidine (T, C, U).
In double-stranded DNA, %A = %T and %G = %C, so %A + %G = 50%. Example: 22% G gives 22% C and 28% each of A and T.
The two DNA strands run in opposite directions: under 5′-ATG-3′ lies 3′-TAC-5′.
Generation 0: one heavy band. Generation 1: one hybrid band (rules out conservative). Generation 2: half hybrid, half light (rules out dispersive). Replication is semiconservative.
Helicase unwinds → primase lays RNA primers → DNA polymerase builds 5′ → 3′ (leading strand continuous, lagging strand in Okazaki fragments) → primers replaced → ligase joins fragments.
Leading: built continuously toward the replication fork. Lagging: built in Okazaki fragments away from the fork, because polymerase adds only to 3′ ends.
DNA → RNA → protein. Transcription makes RNA from DNA; translation makes protein from mRNA.
DNA: deoxyribose, thymine, usually double-stranded. RNA: ribose, uracil, usually single-stranded.
mRNA carries the codons; tRNA brings amino acids and has the anticodon; rRNA forms the ribosome core and makes peptide bonds.
Initiation (RNA polymerase binds the promoter) → elongation (RNA built 5′ → 3′, complementary to the template strand) → termination. In eukaryotes: add cap and tail, splice out introns.
The template strand is read by RNA polymerase. The coding strand has the same sequence as the mRNA, with T in place of U.
64 triplet codons; AUG = start (Met); UAA, UAG, UGA = stop; redundant (several codons per amino acid), unambiguous, nearly universal.
Find the first AUG from the 5′ end, read non-overlapping triplets, look each codon up in the table, stop at the first stop codon (which adds no amino acid).

cards.front: Codons vs amino acids in a coding region
cards.back: A coding region of $n$ codons (start through stop) makes $n - 1$ amino acids; it has $3n$ nucleotides.

Initiation (small subunit finds AUG, Met-tRNA pairs, large subunit joins) → elongation (tRNAs match codons, peptide bonds form, ribosome moves one codon) → termination (release factor at the stop codon).
No lactose: repressor binds the operator, genes off. Lactose present: lactose binds the repressor, which leaves the operator, genes on.
RNA polymerase binds the promoter; the repressor binds the operator, blocking polymerase.
Transcription factors and enhancers, DNA packing and epigenetic tags (DNA methylation, histone changes), RNA splicing, mRNA lifespan, microRNAs, and protein activation or breakdown.
Silent: codon changes, same amino acid. Missense: different amino acid (sickle cell GAG → GUG, Glu → Val). Nonsense: becomes a stop codon, protein cut short.

Insertion or deletion of a number of bases that is not a multiple of three; every codon after it changes and an early stop often appears. Deleting exactly 3 bases removes one amino acid and keeps the frame.
Somatic: in body cells, not inherited (may contribute to cancer). Germline: in cells that make eggs or sperm, can be passed to offspring.
Denature (~95 °C) → anneal primers (~50–65 °C) → extend (~72 °C). Copies after $n$ cycles: $N = N_0 \times 2^n$.
DNA is negative and moves toward the positive electrode. Small fragments move farthest. Distance is roughly linear in log(size), so estimate sizes from a ladder on a log scale.
$n$ cuts give $n + 1$ fragments of a linear DNA molecule but $n$ fragments of a circular one (such as a plasmid).
Cut plasmid and gene with the same restriction enzyme → sticky ends pair → ligase seals → put into bacteria → select with antibiotic → bacteria express the gene (for example, human insulin).

cards.front: How DNA profiling excludes or matches
cards.back: Compare STR lengths at about 20 regions. One mismatch excludes a person; a match at every region is strong evidence (identical twins share a profile).

Fossil record (order, transitional fossils), radiometric dating, homologous and vestigial structures, embryos, molecular similarities, biogeography, and evolution observed directly (antibiotic resistance).
Fraction left after $h$ half-lives $= \left(\tfrac12\right)^h$; age $= h \times$ half-life. Carbon-14: 5,730 years (up to ~50,000 years). Potassium-40: 1.25 billion years.
Homologous: same structure from a common ancestor, possibly different jobs (human arm, bat wing). Analogous: same job, different structure and origin (bird wing, insect wing).
Hip bones in whales and some snakes, the human tailbone, small human ear muscles: reduced remnants of ancestral structures.
A fish with neck, lungs and limb-like fin bones (~375 million years old), found by predicting the age and type of rock where a fish–tetrapod transition should be.
More differences in a gene or protein (like cytochrome c) between two species means a longer time since their common ancestor.
Variation + inheritance + overproduction + differential reproductive success → heritable traits that help become more common over generations.
Reproductive success relative to others in the population, not strength or speed.
Resistant colonies existed on a plate never exposed to the antibiotic: mutations arise randomly before selection; the environment selects, it does not create them.
Drought left large, hard seeds; deeper-beaked medium ground finches survived; the next generation had deeper beaks on average. Wet years later reversed the direction.
Multiply each group by its survival rate, then divide: dark share $= \dfrac{n_D s_D}{n_L s_L + n_D s_D}$.

cards.front: Directional vs stabilizing vs disruptive selection
cards.back: Directional: one extreme favored, average shifts. Stabilizing: average favored, spread narrows. Disruptive: both extremes favored, middle declines.
Artificial: people choose which individuals breed (dogs, cabbage and broccoli). Natural: the environment determines who survives and reproduces.
Change individuals (populations evolve), plan ahead, create needed mutations, or pass on traits acquired during life.
$p + q = 1$ (alleles); $p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 1$ (genotypes $AA$, $Aa$, $aa$).
No mutation, no gene flow, very large population (no drift), random mating, no natural selection.
$q = \sqrt{\text{frequency of } aa}$, $p = 1 - q$, carriers $= 2pq$. Example: 1 in 2,500 affected → $q = 0.02$, carriers ≈ 0.039 (about 1 in 25).
$p = \dfrac{2(\text{number } AA) + (\text{number } Aa)}{2N}$, because each individual carries two copies.
Mutation, gene flow, genetic drift (bottleneck and founder effects), nonrandom mating, natural selection. Only selection consistently produces adaptation.
Bottleneck: a population crashes and regrows from few survivors (northern elephant seals). Founder: a few individuals start a new population (Ellis–van Creveld syndrome among the Old Order Amish).
Populations that can interbreed in nature and produce fertile offspring, isolated from other such groups. Does not work for asexual organisms or fossils.
Prezygotic (before fertilization): habitat, temporal, behavioral, mechanical, gametic. Postzygotic: hybrid inviability, hybrid sterility (mules), hybrid breakdown.
Allopatric: a geographic barrier splits the population (snapping shrimp across the Isthmus of Panama). Sympatric: no barrier, for example polyploidy in plants or a host shift in apple maggot flies.
Nodes are common ancestors; tips are the groups compared (usually living ones). Two groups are most closely related if they share the most recent node. Rotating branches changes nothing.
A clade is an ancestor and all its descendants. Clades are identified by shared derived traits that arose in their common ancestor (hair for mammals).
Paleozoic 539–252 million years ago, Mesozoic 252–66, Cenozoic 66–present. Everything before 539 is the Precambrian, nearly 90% of Earth's history.

cards.front: Key dates in the history of life
cards.back: Earth 4.54 billion years ago; first fossils ~3.5 billion; oxygen builds up ~2.4 billion; eukaryotes ~2 billion; Cambrian explosion ~539 million; Homo sapiens ~300,000 years.
End-Ordovician (~445), Late Devonian (~372), End-Permian (~252, the largest), End-Triassic (~201), End-Cretaceous (66, asteroid impact). Dates in millions of years ago.
Gradualism: slow, steady change. Punctuated equilibrium: long stability broken by relatively rapid change (Eldredge and Gould, 1972). Both occur.

An archaeal host cell, related to today's Asgard archaea, took in an oxygen-using bacterium that became the mitochondrion; later one eukaryote lineage took in a cyanobacterium that became the chloroplast. So many trees show eukaryotes branching from within the archaea.
Domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species ("Dear King Philip Came Over For Good Soup").

cards.front: Rules for writing a binomial name
cards.back: Genus capitalized, species epithet lowercase, both italicized (or underlined): Homo sapiens. Genus may be abbreviated after first use: E. coli.
Bacteria, Archaea, Eukarya (Woese, from ribosomal RNA comparisons). Current evidence suggests eukaryotes arose from within the archaea, closest to the Asgard archaea.
Groups should reflect ancestry: each group contains an ancestor and all its descendants. Classifications change as DNA evidence comes in.
A series of paired, mutually exclusive choices about observable features that leads step by step to an identification.
Both lack a nucleus. Bacteria: peptidoglycan walls, ester-linked lipids, many pathogens. Archaea: no peptidoglycan, ether-linked lipids, eukaryote-like gene machinery, no known human pathogens.
Gram-positive: thick peptidoglycan wall, stains purple. Gram-negative: thin wall plus outer membrane, stains pink.
$N = N_0 \times 2^{n}$, where $n$ = elapsed time $\div$ generation time.

cards.front: Phases of a bacterial growth curve
cards.back: Lag, exponential (log), stationary, death.
$\text{CFU/mL} = \dfrac{\text{colonies}}{\text{dilution} \times \text{volume plated}}$; count plates with 30–300 colonies.
Lytic: virus replicates at once and bursts the cell. Lysogenic: viral DNA joins the host chromosome and is copied silently until a trigger switches it to lytic.

cards.front: Why antibiotics don't work on viruses
cards.back: Viruses have no cell wall, ribosomes or metabolism of their own for antibiotics to target.
An RNA virus whose reverse transcriptase copies its RNA into DNA, which integrates into the host genome.
Any eukaryote that is not a plant, animal or fungus; not a natural evolutionary group.
Pseudopods (amoeba), cilia (Paramecium), flagella (Euglena).
Caused by the protist Plasmodium, spread by Anopheles mosquitoes; multiplies in liver and red blood cells.
Fungi: heterotrophs, chitin walls, store glycogen, digest externally and absorb. Plants: photosynthesize, cellulose walls, store starch.
A hypha is one thread-like filament; a mycelium is the whole branching network of hyphae.
Mycorrhiza: fungus + plant roots (minerals for sugar). Lichen: fungus + alga or cyanobacterium.

cards.front: Four plant groups and their innovations
cards.back: Mosses (no vascular tissue), ferns (vascular tissue), gymnosperms (seeds on cones, pollen), angiosperms (flowers and fruit).
Haploid gametophyte makes gametes by mitosis; zygote grows into diploid sporophyte, which makes spores by meiosis. Sporophyte dominant in ferns and seed plants.
Xylem: dead tubes, water and minerals up from roots. Phloem: living sieve tubes, sugars from source to sink (up or down).
Transpiration pulls water out of leaves; cohesion (hydrogen bonds) transmits the pull down unbroken xylem columns; adhesion helps; roots take in water by osmosis. Powered by the sun.
Volume = tube cross-section area × distance bubble moves; rate = volume ÷ time.
Stamen = anther + filament (male). Carpel/pistil = stigma + style + ovary with ovules (female). Ovule → seed; ovary → fruit.
Darwin: the seedling tip senses light. Went: the signal is a chemical that diffuses into agar (auxin), which makes the shaded side elongate.
Radial: many planes through a central axis (jellyfish). Bilateral: one plane, left and right halves, front end with cephalization.
Notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord, pharyngeal slits, post-anal tail (at some stage).
Protostome: first embryo opening becomes mouth (mollusks, annelids, arthropods). Deuterostome: it becomes the anus (echinoderms, chordates).
Endotherm: heat from metabolism, constant body temperature, high food cost (birds, mammals). Ectotherm: heat from environment, body temperature tracks surroundings.

cards.front: Three parts of a homeostatic control loop
cards.back: Sensor (receptor), control center (often the brain), effector (muscle or gland).
Negative: response opposes the change (temperature, glucose). Positive: response amplifies the change until an event ends it (childbirth, clotting).
Sweating and vasodilation of skin vessels, triggered by the hypothalamus.
Vasoconstriction of skin vessels and shivering.
Dendrites (receive), cell body (nucleus), axon (carries impulse away, often myelinated), axon terminals (release neurotransmitter).
Rest at about −70 mV; threshold reached; sodium channels open, Na⁺ in (inside becomes positive); potassium channels open, K⁺ out (restores negative).
Every action potential has the same size; stimulus strength is coded by firing frequency.
Stimulate at two distances; speed = difference in distance ÷ difference in time (mm/ms = m/s).
Impulse arrives; neurotransmitter released; diffuses across gap; binds receptors on next cell; then broken down or taken back up.
Nervous: electrical plus neurotransmitter, milliseconds, brief, targeted. Endocrine: hormones in blood, seconds to hours, longer lasting, any cell with the receptor.
Insulin (beta cells): lowers blood glucose; cells take up glucose, liver stores glycogen. Glucagon (alpha cells): raises it; liver breaks down glycogen.
Type 1: autoimmune destruction of beta cells, little insulin. Type 2: cells respond poorly to insulin (insulin resistance).

cards.front: Path of blood through the heart
cards.back: Right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body → veins → right atrium.
Artery: away from heart, thick elastic wall. Vein: toward heart, thin wall, valves. Capillary: one cell thick, exchange.
Heart rate × stroke volume; about 70 × 70 mL ≈ 5 L/min at rest.
Volume at end of filling − volume left after contraction.
The heart pumps thousands of liters a day, far more than is eaten or contained in the body, so blood must circulate.

cards.front: Path of air into the lungs
cards.back: Nose/mouth → pharynx → larynx → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli.
Diaphragm contracts and flattens, ribs lift, chest volume up, lung pressure down, air flows in.
Rising carbon dioxide, which lowers blood pH, detected in the medulla.
Minute = tidal volume × rate. Alveolar = (tidal volume − dead space) × rate.
About 20 kJ per liter of oxygen; resting use about 3.5 mL O₂ per kg per minute.
Filtration (glomerulus), reabsorption (tubule back to blood), secretion (blood into tubule).
Released when blood is too concentrated; makes collecting ducts reabsorb more water, giving concentrated urine (negative feedback).
Carbohydrates → simple sugars; proteins → amino acids; fats → fatty acids and glycerol; nucleic acids → nucleotides.

cards.front: Roles of stomach, small intestine, large intestine
cards.back: Stomach: acid, pepsin, churning. Small intestine: most digestion and nearly all absorption (villi). Large intestine: water absorption, gut bacteria.
Carbohydrate 4 kcal, protein 4 kcal, fat 9 kcal (1 kcal = 4.184 kJ).
Innate: fast, general, from birth (barriers, inflammation, phagocytes). Adaptive: slower first time, specific, memory (B cells, antibodies, T cells).
Primary: about 1–2 weeks to peak, smaller. Secondary: within days, much larger, because of memory cells.
$1 - \dfrac{1}{R_0}$; e.g. $R_0 = 15$ gives about 93%.

glossary.definition: The maintenance of stable internal conditions (temperature, water, pH, sugar levels) within the range cells need, despite changes outside; usually achieved by negative feedback.
A property that appears at a higher level of organization from the way the parts are arranged and interact, and that the parts alone do not have, such as a heart's ability to pump.
A proposed, testable and falsifiable explanation for an observation, often leading to an "if…then" prediction.
The one factor an experimenter deliberately changes between groups; plotted on the x-axis.
The factor measured in an experiment to see the effect of the independent variable; plotted on the y-axis.
A factor that could affect the result and is kept the same in every group, so that only the independent variable differs.
The group of subjects that does not receive the treatment being tested (or receives the standard condition) and serves as a baseline for comparison.
In science, a broad, well-tested explanation that ties together many observations and has survived repeated attempts to disprove it. Not a guess; a law describes a pattern, a theory explains it.
Carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, phosphorus and sulfur: the six elements that make up about 98% of the mass of living things.
A molecule with an uneven distribution of charge, slightly negative at one end and slightly positive at another, as in water.
A weak attraction between a slightly positive hydrogen atom on one polar molecule and a slightly negative oxygen or nitrogen atom on another (or on another part of the same large molecule).
The attraction of water molecules to one another through hydrogen bonds; it causes surface tension and holds water columns together in plants. (Adhesion is attraction of water to other substances.)
The energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 g of a substance by 1 °C; about 4.18 J/(g·°C) for water, which is unusually high.
A measure of hydrogen ion concentration: $\text{pH} = -\log[\text{H}^+]$. Below 7 is acidic, 7 neutral, above 7 basic; each unit is a tenfold change.
A pair of chemicals that resists changes in pH by taking up H⁺ when acid is added and releasing H⁺ when base is added, such as the bicarbonate buffer in blood.
A small molecule that can bond to others like it to form a polymer, such as a glucose, an amino acid or a nucleotide.
A large molecule made of many monomers bonded in a chain.
A reaction that joins two monomers with a covalent bond and releases a water molecule; $n$ monomers in a chain release $n - 1$ waters.
A reaction that breaks a bond in a polymer by adding a water molecule across it; the reverse of dehydration synthesis, and the basis of digestion.
A sugar or polymer of sugars made of C, H and O (about 1:2:1), used for quick energy (glucose), storage (starch, glycogen) and structure (cellulose, chitin).
A member of a diverse group of mostly nonpolar molecules that do not dissolve in water, including fats, phospholipids and steroids; not a true polymer.
A polymer of amino acids folded into a specific 3-D shape that determines its job, such as an enzyme, transporter, antibody or structural fiber.
The monomer of proteins: a central carbon with an amino group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen and a variable R group. There are 20 common amino acids.
A polymer of nucleotides (each a sugar, a phosphate and a nitrogen base) that stores and transmits genetic information: DNA or RNA.
Deoxyribonucleic acid: the double-stranded nucleic acid that stores hereditary information, with the sugar deoxyribose and the bases A, T, G and C.
Ribonucleic acid: a usually single-stranded nucleic acid with the sugar ribose and the bases A, U, G and C; it helps carry out genetic instructions.
A biological catalyst, almost always a protein, that speeds up a specific reaction by lowering its activation energy and is not used up.
The molecule an enzyme acts on; it binds to the enzyme's active site.
The pocket or groove on an enzyme where the substrate binds and the reaction takes place; its shape and chemistry make the enzyme specific.
The energy needed to start a chemical reaction; enzymes lower it without changing the overall energy released or absorbed.
Loss of a protein's 3-D shape (and so its function) caused by high temperature, extreme pH or certain chemicals; usually permanent.
A molecule that reduces an enzyme's activity. A competitive inhibitor blocks the active site (overcome by adding substrate); a noncompetitive inhibitor binds elsewhere and changes the enzyme's shape.
A living part of an ecosystem, or material made by living things: plants, animals, fungi, bacteria, fallen leaves, dung.
A nonliving condition in an ecosystem, such as sunlight, temperature, water, soil minerals, pH or salinity.
An organism that makes its own organic molecules from an outside energy source, usually by photosynthesis (plants, algae, cyanobacteria) or by chemosynthesis. Producers form the first trophic level.
An organism, mainly a bacterium or fungus, that breaks down dead material and wastes and returns simple nutrients to the soil and water.
A feeding step in a food chain: producers are level 1, primary consumers (herbivores) level 2, secondary consumers level 3, and so on.
All the feeding relationships in a community, drawn as many interlinked food chains. Arrows point from the food to the organism that eats it.

The rate at which producers store energy as new biomass, after subtracting their own respiration from gross primary productivity (GPP): NPP = GPP − respiration. It is the energy available to consumers.
The total dry mass of living organisms in an area or trophic level, usually given in g per m².
The rule of thumb that about 10% (typically 1–20%) of the energy at one trophic level becomes available to the next; most of the rest is lost as heat from respiration.
The path an element or compound (carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, water) takes as it moves between living things and the air, water, soil and rocks.
The conversion of nitrogen gas (N₂) into ammonia or ammonium that organisms can use, done by certain bacteria (some in legume root nodules), by lightning, and industrially by the Haber–Bosch process.
The conversion of nitrate back to nitrogen gas by bacteria in low-oxygen soils and sediments, returning nitrogen to the atmosphere.
Population growth in which the increase is proportional to the population size, $dN/dt = rN$ (or $N_t = N_0\lambda^t$), giving a J-shaped curve. It occurs only while resources are unlimited.
Population growth that slows as the population nears carrying capacity, $dN/dt = rN(K-N)/K$, giving an S-shaped curve that is steepest at $N = K/2$.
The largest population of a species that an environment can support over the long term, written $K$.
A limiting factor whose effect grows stronger as population density rises, such as competition, predation, disease and parasites.
A limiting factor that affects a population the same way whatever its density, such as a freeze, drought, flood or fire.
A method of estimating population size: mark $M$ animals, later catch $C$ animals of which $R$ are marked, and estimate $N = MC/R$.
The role a species plays in its community: what it eats, where and when it feeds, the conditions it tolerates, and what eats it.
An interaction in which one organism (the predator) kills and eats another (the prey); it benefits the predator and harms the prey (+/−).
A close relationship between two species in which both benefit (+/+), such as legumes and nitrogen-fixing bacteria, or flowers and pollinators.
A close relationship in which one species benefits and the other is neither helped nor harmed (+/0), such as barnacles on a whale.
A close relationship in which one species (the parasite) lives on or in another (the host) and feeds on it, harming but usually not quickly killing it (+/−).
A species whose effect on its community is far larger than its abundance suggests, so removing it changes the community greatly (for example, the sea star Pisaster or sea otters).

The gradual, fairly predictable change in the species of a community after a disturbance. Primary succession starts without soil (bare rock); secondary succession starts with soil in place (after fire or farming).
A large region with a characteristic climate and the community of organisms adapted to it, such as tundra, desert or tropical rainforest.
The variety of life, measured at three levels: genetic diversity within species, species diversity within communities, and ecosystem diversity across regions.
A measure of species diversity that accounts for richness and evenness: $D = 1 - \sum n(n-1)/[N(N-1)]$, the probability that two individuals picked at random belong to different species.
A species introduced to a region outside its native range that spreads and causes ecological or economic harm, often because its natural predators and competitors are missing.
The theory that all living things are made of one or more cells, the cell is the basic unit of structure and function, and all cells come from preexisting cells.
How many times larger an image is than the real object. For a compound microscope, total magnification = ocular × objective; actual size = image size ÷ magnification.
The circular area visible through a microscope; its diameter shrinks in proportion as magnification increases.
The smallest distance between two points at which they can still be seen as separate; about 0.2 µm for a light microscope and about 1 nm or better for an electron microscope.

A microscope that uses a beam of electrons instead of light, giving far higher resolution. A transmission EM (TEM) shows thin slices; a scanning EM (SEM) shows surfaces. Specimens must be dead and in a vacuum.
The thin, flexible boundary of every cell, a phospholipid bilayer with proteins, that controls what enters and leaves.
A small structure of RNA and protein, not surrounded by a membrane, that builds proteins; found in every cell.
A single-celled organism (a bacterium or archaeon) whose cell has no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles; its DNA lies in a nucleoid region.
An organism whose cells have a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles: animals, plants, fungi and protists.
A noncellular infectious particle of DNA or RNA inside a protein coat (capsid), sometimes with an envelope; it has no metabolism and reproduces only inside a host cell.
The organelle that holds a eukaryotic cell's DNA, surrounded by a double nuclear envelope with pores; it contains the nucleolus, which makes ribosome parts.
A network of membranes continuous with the nuclear envelope. Rough ER has ribosomes and makes proteins for export and membranes; smooth ER makes lipids, detoxifies and stores calcium.
A stack of flattened membrane sacs that modifies, sorts and packages proteins from the ER into vesicles for secretion or delivery.
A membrane sac of digestive enzymes with an acidic interior that breaks down food particles, engulfed bacteria and worn-out organelles.
The double-membrane organelle where cellular respiration releases energy from food and stores it in ATP; it has its own DNA and ribosomes.
The double-membrane organelle in plants and algae where photosynthesis captures light energy to make sugar; it contains chlorophyll and its own DNA.
A rigid layer outside the plasma membrane of plants (cellulose), fungi (chitin), bacteria (peptidoglycan) and archaea that supports the cell and prevents bursting.

The theory that mitochondria and chloroplasts descend from free-living prokaryotes engulfed by an ancestral host cell, supported by their double membranes, circular DNA, bacteria-like ribosomes, division by splitting and DNA sequences.
A lipid with a polar, hydrophilic phosphate head and two nonpolar, hydrophobic fatty acid tails; in water phospholipids form the bilayer of cell membranes.
The model of a membrane as a fluid phospholipid bilayer in which a mosaic of proteins (and cholesterol, in animals) floats and moves sideways.
Letting some substances cross easily (small nonpolar molecules) while blocking or controlling others (ions, large polar molecules).
The net movement of particles from higher to lower concentration (down a concentration gradient) by random motion, needing no energy from the cell.
Passive diffusion of a substance down its concentration gradient through a channel or carrier protein.
The diffusion of water across a selectively permeable membrane, from the side with lower solute concentration to the side with higher solute concentration.

How a solution compares with a cell in solute concentration. Hypertonic: more solute than the cell, so the cell loses water. Hypotonic: less solute, so the cell gains water. Isotonic: equal, so no net change.
Movement of a substance against its concentration gradient (low to high) by a pump protein, using energy, usually from ATP; e.g. the sodium–potassium pump.
Surface area divided by volume; for a cube of side $s$ it is $6/s$, so it falls as size increases, which limits how large cells can be.
The process by which a cell becomes specialized in structure and function by switching particular genes on and others off; its DNA stays the same.
A group of similar cells that work together to perform a common function, such as muscle or epithelial tissue.
A structure made of two or more tissue types working together for a particular function, such as the stomach or a leaf.
All the chemical reactions in an organism, organized into enzyme-catalyzed pathways that break molecules down (catabolism) or build them up (anabolism).
Metabolic pathways that break large molecules into smaller ones and release energy, such as cellular respiration.
Metabolic pathways that build large molecules from smaller ones and require energy, such as protein synthesis or the Calvin cycle.
Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only converted from one form to another.
Every energy conversion turns some energy into heat that can no longer do work, so the disorder (entropy) of the universe increases; no conversion is 100% efficient.
A reaction that releases free energy; its products hold less usable energy than its reactants, so it can proceed on its own.
A reaction that absorbs free energy; its products hold more usable energy than its reactants, so it needs an energy input, usually from ATP.
Using the energy released by an exergonic reaction (usually ATP hydrolysis) to drive an endergonic one, often by transferring a phosphate group.
Loss of electrons by a molecule (often along with hydrogen). The molecule that loses electrons is oxidized.
Gain of electrons by a molecule (often along with hydrogen). The molecule that gains electrons is reduced.
Adenosine triphosphate: a nucleotide with three phosphate groups that is the cell's energy currency. Hydrolysis to ADP + Pi releases about 30.5 kJ/mol under standard conditions.
Adenosine diphosphate: ATP with one fewer phosphate group; recharged to ATP by adding a phosphate (phosphorylation).
The reduced form of the electron carrier NAD⁺. It carries high-energy electrons from glycolysis and the Krebs cycle to the electron transport chain.
The reduced form of the electron carrier NADP⁺. Made in the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis, it supplies electrons to the Calvin cycle.
The process by which plants, algae and some bacteria convert light energy into chemical energy in sugar: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + light → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂.
An organism that makes its own organic food from inorganic materials, such as a plant using light energy.
An organism that gets its food by eating other organisms or their products, such as animals and fungi.
The main photosynthetic pigment, found in thylakoid membranes. It absorbs mostly blue-violet and red light and reflects green.
A graph of how much light a pigment absorbs at each wavelength.
A flattened membrane sac inside the chloroplast, stacked into grana; its membrane holds chlorophyll and runs the light-dependent reactions.
The fluid inside the chloroplast that surrounds the thylakoids; the Calvin cycle takes place there.
The first stage of photosynthesis, in the thylakoid membranes: light energy splits water, releases O₂, and makes ATP and NADPH.
A series of membrane proteins that pass electrons along, using the released energy to pump H⁺ ions across the membrane. Found in thylakoids and in the inner mitochondrial membrane.
A membrane enzyme that makes ATP from ADP and phosphate, powered by H⁺ ions flowing through it down their gradient.
Making ATP using the energy of an H⁺ gradient across a membrane, as H⁺ flows back through ATP synthase.
The second stage of photosynthesis, in the stroma: the enzyme rubisco fixes CO₂, and ATP and NADPH reduce it to the sugar G3P.
Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate: the three-carbon sugar produced by the Calvin cycle; two G3P make one glucose.
The factor in shortest supply (such as light, CO₂ or temperature) that sets the rate of a process; raising other factors does not help until it is raised.
The pathway that breaks down glucose and other food molecules to make ATP: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy.
Requiring oxygen. Aerobic respiration uses O₂ as the final electron acceptor.
Not requiring oxygen. Glycolysis and fermentation are anaerobic.
The first stage of respiration, in the cytoplasm: glucose is split into 2 pyruvate, with a net gain of 2 ATP and 2 NADH. It needs no oxygen.
Acetyl coenzyme A: a two-carbon acetyl group attached to a carrier, made from pyruvate in the mitochondrion; it feeds carbon into the Krebs cycle.
The cycle of reactions in the mitochondrial matrix that breaks acetyl groups down to CO₂ and loads electrons onto NADH and FADH₂; also called the citric acid cycle.
The reduced form of the electron carrier FAD, made in the Krebs cycle; each yields about 1.5 ATP in the electron transport chain.
ATP production powered by the electron transport chain and chemiosmosis; it makes most of the ATP in aerobic respiration.

Anaerobic pathways that regenerate NAD⁺ by passing NADH's electrons to pyruvate or a product of it, so glycolysis can continue making 2 ATP per glucose. Lactic acid fermentation makes lactate; alcoholic fermentation makes ethanol and CO₂.
The life of a cell from its formation by division to its own division: interphase (G1, S, G2) followed by the M phase (mitosis and cytokinesis).
The long part of the cell cycle between divisions: G1 (growth), S (DNA replication) and G2 (preparation for division).
A single long DNA molecule wrapped around proteins, carrying many genes; after S phase it consists of two sister chromatids joined at the centromere. Human body cells have 46.
One of the two identical copies of a chromosome made during S phase, joined to its sister at the centromere until anaphase.
The constricted region where sister chromatids are held together and where spindle fibers attach.
Division of the nucleus that gives two nuclei with the same chromosome number as the parent; stages are prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase.
Division of the cytoplasm into two cells, by a cleavage furrow in animal cells or a cell plate in plant cells.
A framework of microtubules that attaches to chromosomes at their centromeres and moves them during mitosis and meiosis.
First stage of mitosis: chromosomes condense, the spindle forms, and the nuclear envelope breaks down.
Stage of mitosis in which chromosomes line up along the middle of the cell, attached to spindle fibers from both poles.
Stage of mitosis in which sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles.
Last stage of mitosis: chromosomes reach the poles, nuclear envelopes re-form, and chromosomes uncoil.
The percentage of cells in a sample that are in mitosis: (cells in mitosis ÷ total cells) × 100%.
A control point in the cell cycle (G1, G2, spindle) where the cell checks conditions such as size, signals, DNA damage or chromosome attachment before going on.
Programmed cell death: an orderly self-destruction that removes damaged or unneeded cells without inflammation.
A regulatory protein whose level rises and falls during the cell cycle; it activates cyclin-dependent kinases.
Cyclin-dependent kinase: an enzyme that, when bound to a cyclin, phosphorylates target proteins to move the cell into the next phase of the cycle.
A group of diseases in which cells divide uncontrollably and can invade other tissues, caused by accumulated mutations in genes that regulate the cell cycle.
A normal gene whose protein stimulates cell division (a "gas pedal"), such as RAS; when mutated to be overactive it becomes an oncogene.
A mutated, overactive form of a proto-oncogene that pushes a cell to divide; one mutated copy is enough to have an effect.
A gene whose protein slows division, repairs DNA or triggers apoptosis (a "brake"), such as p53 or RB; usually both copies must be lost to contribute to cancer.
The spread of cancer cells from a malignant tumor through blood or lymph to form new tumors elsewhere in the body.
An unspecialized cell that can divide to renew itself and can also give rise to specialized cells.
Able to become every cell type of the body (but not the placenta), as embryonic stem cells and iPSCs are. Compare totipotent (every type) and multipotent (several related types).
Induced pluripotent stem cell: a body cell reprogrammed (first done by adding four genes, in 2006) to behave like an embryonic stem cell.
A two-stage division that turns one diploid cell into four genetically different haploid cells, used to make gametes.
A pair of chromosomes, one from each parent, with the same size, centromere position and genes in the same order, though possibly different versions of those genes.
Having two complete sets of chromosomes, one from each parent (2n); human body cells are diploid with 46 chromosomes.
Having one set of chromosomes (n); human gametes are haploid with 23 chromosomes.
A haploid sex cell (egg or sperm) that joins another gamete at fertilization to form a diploid zygote.
Exchange of matching segments between chromatids of homologous chromosomes during prophase I of meiosis, producing new combinations of genes.

The random, independent orientation of each homologous pair at metaphase I, giving 2ⁿ possible chromosome combinations in gametes (n = number of pairs). It is the physical basis of Mendel's law of independent assortment for genes on different chromosomes.
Failure of homologous chromosomes (meiosis I) or sister chromatids (meiosis II) to separate, producing gametes with an extra or missing chromosome.
A unit of inheritance: a stretch of DNA, at a particular place on a chromosome, that affects one or more traits.
One of the different versions of a gene, such as the purple and white flower-color alleles in peas. A diploid individual has two alleles of each gene, one from each parent.
Describes an allele whose effect shows even when only one copy is present (in a heterozygote). Written with a capital letter, e.g. P.
Describes an allele whose effect shows only when no dominant allele is present (in a homozygote, or in a male for an X-linked gene). Written with a lower-case letter, e.g. p.
The pair of alleles an individual has for a gene (or its alleles for several genes), e.g. PP, Pp or pp.
The observable trait an individual shows, such as purple flowers or blood type A; it results from the genotype acting with the environment.
Having two identical alleles of a gene (PP or pp).
Having two different alleles of a gene (Pp).
Mendel's first law: the two alleles of a gene separate when gametes form, so each gamete gets one allele, each with probability one half. Caused by homologous chromosomes separating in meiosis I.
A grid that lists one parent's possible gametes on one side and the other parent's on the other; each box is an equally likely offspring genotype.
Crossing an individual with the dominant phenotype but unknown genotype to a homozygous recessive individual; any recessive offspring show the unknown parent is heterozygous.
A cross that follows two genes, typically between parents heterozygous for both (AaBb × AaBb), which gives a 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 phenotype ratio when the genes are unlinked and fully dominant.

Mendel's second law: alleles of different genes go into gametes independently of each other. For genes on different chromosomes the physical basis is the random orientation of each homologous pair at metaphase I; genes far apart on one chromosome also behave independently, but only because crossing over between them is so frequent.
The probability that independent events all happen is the product of their probabilities: $P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A)\,P(B)$.
The probability that one or another of mutually exclusive events happens is the sum of their probabilities: $P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B)$.
A relationship between alleles in which the heterozygote has an intermediate phenotype, such as pink flowers from red × white; the phenotype ratio equals the genotype ratio.
A relationship between alleles in which a heterozygote fully shows both alleles' traits at once, such as AB blood type or roan cattle with both red and white hairs.
Three or more alleles of one gene existing in a population (each individual still has only two), such as the ABO blood-group alleles $I^A$, $I^B$ and $i$.
A trait controlled by many genes, each adding a small effect, such as human height or skin color; it varies continuously, often in a bell-shaped distribution.
